In response, the European Union is developing standardized transparency mechanisms, most notably the Digital Product Passport (DPP). Despite its imminent adoption in the fashion industry, research on the DPP remains scarce, especially from the perspectives of its direct stakeholders: retailers and consumers. This study examines how retailers and consumers perceive transparency tools like the DPP, focusing on the key drivers and barriers to its adoption. Using signaling theory and the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT/UTAUT2) framework, the research involved a qualitative analysis of retailers' perceptions followed by a mixed‐method exploration of consumer views. The findings reveal that although retailers as signal strategists can enhance product oversight and discourage unethical practices through the DPP, benefiting from signal observability and credibility, they face challenges due to signal cost (implementation costs) and signal observability (standardization issues). Consumers, on the other hand, recognize that the DPP can improve their decision‐making and increase awareness of sustainability in a pleasant way, thereby enhancing their purchasing experience. The benefits of the DPP may help mitigate cultural barriers and skepticism about green initiatives by providing comparable information. This paper advances theory by using signaling theory to interpret stakeholders' qualitative perceptions of the DPP as a transparency signal, while applying UTAUT/UTAUT2 to examine consumers' intention to use DPP. It offers guidance for retailers and policymakers on overcoming adoption barriers and maximizing transparency benefits.

title: Internal Drivers and Financial Outcomes of Global Hospitality Chains' Green Strategies: An Application of the Natural Resource–Based View
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite growing concerns for protecting the natural environment, research on how eco‐friendly practices of firms in the hospitality industry impact their performance is relatively limited. Using the natural resource–based view of the firm as a theoretical platform, we propose a conceptual model focusing on the internal drivers and performance outcomes of environmental strategies, which was tested with secondary data collected from 116 global hospitality chains. The results indicate a strong association between the hospitality chain's green human resource management, strategic proactivity, and environmental targeting with each of the four environmental strategies examined, namely, product/service eco‐friendliness, resource efficiency, waste/emissions management, and green procurement. However, although the first two strategies were found to positively affect the firm's operating ROA, the last two strategies had a negative effect on it.

title: From Message Framing to Purchase Intention: The Mediating Role of Attitude Towards the Message in Pro‐Environmental Food Communication
abstract: ABSTRACT Developing effective communication for pro‐environmental foods requires understanding the persuasive link between message stimuli and consumer response. This study integrates message framing theory with the dual mediation hypothesis to examine attitude towards the message as a key mediator between induced emotions and purchase intention. A between‐subjects experiment ( N = 1483) employing multigroup SEM in Spain and Denmark shows that attitude towards the message constitutes the primary mechanism through which emotions—particularly positive ones—exert their influence. Crucially, cross‐national variation in the estimated structural pattern was observed. While Denmark exhibits a model of total mediation through attitude towards the message, Spain displays a dual pathway in which mediated and direct emotional effects coexist. These findings advance research on pro‐environmental food communication by indicating that framing‐induced emotions are associated with more favourable purchase intentions primarily through positive evaluations of the message, with differences in the strength of these estimated pathways being consistent with broader contextual variation in pro‐environmental market maturity and product involvement.

title: Green Intellectual Capital, Sustainability Control Systems, and Environmental Performance: Bridging Natural Resource Orchestration and Levers of Control Perspectives
abstract: ABSTRACT Understanding how organizations translate sustainability‐oriented intangible assets into tangible environmental outcomes remains an important challenge in sustainability accounting and management control research. Drawing on the natural resource orchestration perspective, this study examines how sustainability control systems, grounded in Simons' levers of control framework, help translate green intellectual capital (GIC) components into improved environmental performance. Using survey data from 175 listed Indian firms and applying partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS‐SEM), the results show that GIC is positively associated with environmental performance, and the sustainability control systems variable mediates this relationship. The study contributes to the sustainability management control literature by integrating natural resource orchestration theory with the levers of control framework. The findings offer firm‐level implications by showing that merely possessing green knowledge assets does not necessarily lead to improved environmental performance. Instead, firms need to orchestrate these assets through sustainability control systems by effectively structuring, bundling, and leveraging them to translate GIC into stronger environmental outcomes. The findings also provide practical insights for managers and regulators seeking to strengthen environmental performance through the strategic integration of GIC and sustainability control systems.

title: Adult-only: When excluding children reveals a flaw in hospitality management approach
abstract: This research note explores social servicescape in hospitality settings, considering recent regulatory debates questioning the exclusion of children. Although children are often positioned as either sovereign consumers or a marginalised group, their impact on guest satisfaction remains largely unexplored. Drawing on 90,045 TripAdvisor reviews from 72 international resorts, we applied advanced natural language processing techniques, including BERT-based sentiment analysis and child-reference classification using a local Large Language Model to examine whether references to children influence customer evaluations. By comparing satisfaction scores across reviews that mention or omit children, we explore whether these differences reflect broader managerial, academic, and policy-related challenges. This study contributes to ongoing debates on adult-only vs inclusive hospitality by highlighting how children’s presence is addressed in guest feedback, and by raising questions about the potential limitations in current hospitality management practices.

title: Why and when customer-related social stressors impair service performance: A conservation of resources perspective
abstract: Building on the conservation of resources theory, we investigate how customer-related social stressors impact service performance among hospitality employees. To explore this, we gathered data from 350 supervisor-employee pairs across twelve hotels in China through a three-wave survey. The results show that customer-related social stressors detrimentally affect work engagement, which in turn reduces service performance. Furthermore, job social support and employees’ social skills emerge as two key moderators, buffering both the direct impact of customer-related social stressors on work engagement and the indirect effect on service performance via work engagement. These findings provide a nuanced understanding of the interactions among customer-related social stressors, work engagement, and service performance, offering significant implications for both theory and practice.

title: Leveraging big data analytics for sustainable competitive advantage: A model of operational performance
abstract: Big Data Analytics (BDA) has become an important organizational capability for strengthening firm performance and sustaining competitive advantage. This study examines how Big Data Acceptance, Big Data Assimilation, and Big Data Routinization contribute to Organizational Performance with Big Data Analysis (OPBDA), and how the resulting organizational benefits, such as smarter management decisions, increased innovation and agility, and improved organizational efficiency, relate to sustainable competitive advantage. Survey data collected from 414 respondents in China were analyzed using IBM SPSS 23.0 and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS 4. The findings show that acceptance, assimilation, and routinization of big data positively and significantly influence OPBDA. OPBDA, in turn, significantly improves management's decision-making and organizational efficiency, while its relationship with Increased Innovation and Agility is not statistically significant. The study highlights the importance of effectively assimilating and routinizing BDA within organizational processes to strengthen managerial decision-making, operational efficiency, and sustained competitive positioning.

title: Conceptualising a scale to measure customers’ off-premise dining experience (OPDineX) with third-party food delivery services
Caught in the line of fire: tariffs and the global hospitality workforce
abstract: Purpose This critical reflection article critically examines how contemporary tariff regimes, particularly reciprocal and retaliatory trade measures, are reshaping the global hospitality workforce. Moving beyond traditional economic analyses of tariffs, by developing three propositions, it foregrounds labour dynamics to explore how trade policy functions as an indirect but powerful determinant of employment stability, mobility, equity and workforce development in hospitality. Design/methodology/approach This critical reflection paper synthesises interdisciplinary literature from international trade, tourism economics, labour studies, hospitality management and shock/crisis literature. The macro-meso-micro analytical framework is used to conceptualise how tariff policies cascade from geopolitical and institutional contexts to firm-level responses and individual worker outcomes. Findings The analysis reveals that tariffs generate second- and third-order labour effects that are largely absent from trade and tourism policy debates. These include heightened labour-market volatility, suppressed wages, growth in informal and precarious employment, constrained international labour mobility, weakened global talent pipelines and underinvestment in workforce training. These impacts disproportionately affect migrant workers, women and early-career professionals, while intensifying regional and demographic inequalities, particularly in tourism-dependent and developing economies. Practical implications The paper outlines forward-looking interventions for firms, industry bodies and policymakers, including regionalised supply-chain strategies, investment in workforce multiskilling, inclusive adoption of technology, strengthened policy-industry coalitions and scenario-based workforce planning. It argues for embedding labour mobility, skills recognition and workforce protection into future trade frameworks to enhance sectoral resilience. Originality/value This study reframes tariffs as labour-shaping mechanisms rather than purely macroeconomic tools, offering one of the first workforce-centred conceptualisations of trade policy impacts in hospitality. By repositioning the hospitality workforce at the centre of tariff discourse, the paper advances theory, informs policy and provides a foundation for future empirical research on trade-labour-tourism interdependencies.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: How accessibility barriers accumulate across the guest journey: a dual-perspective inquiry
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how hotel accessibility barriers accumulate across customer journey touchpoints, creating exclusion for people with disabilities (PWDs). Design/methodology/approach Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 13 PWDs and 10 hotel managers in Singapore. PWDs’ accounts were analyzed phenomenologically; managers’ accounts were analyzed through applied thematic analysis. Customer journey mapping was informed by the social relational model, embodiment theory and the capability approach. Findings Barriers accumulated across journey stages. Inadequate pre-arrival information carried forward into the entrance, room, bathroom and staff-mediated barriers during the stay. PWDs prioritized functional transparency, bathroom usability and proactive service recognition. Managers framed accessibility in terms of retrofit constraints, perceived low demand and ableist assumptions, resulting in implementation gaps despite goodwill. Research limitations/implications The study is based on qualitative interviews conducted in Singapore and does not capture all types of disability or stakeholder perspectives. Future research could examine these mechanisms across hotel segments, national contexts and longitudinal accessibility interventions. Originality/value This research explains failures in hotel accessibility by integrating embodied guest experiences with managerial decision-making. It extends accessible hospitality research by showing how barriers cascade across journey stages and by distinguishing the provision of accessible features from capability enablement in use.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: On and off the podium: long-term impact evaluation of European R&D Grants on patenting performance
abstract: Abstract This study evaluates the impact of the European SME Instrument (SMEi) on patent performance and technological specialization in small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs). More specifically, using data from Phase 2 of the European program (2014–2018), we compare SMEs that received funding with those that were evaluated as eligible but remained unfunded due to budget constraints. This comparison enables a robust causal analysis of the policy’s long-term effects. By applying entropy balancing and interaction-weighted estimators for dynamic treatment effects, we examine how R&D funding affects not only the scale of patenting but also the quality, novelty, and the technological direction of firms’ innovation activities. First, funded firms statistically decreased their overall patent output, while facing a short-term increase. Second, we observe an increase in technological specialization among funded firms, suggesting that SMEi funding promotes focused R&D efforts. The performance gap between funded and eligible firms narrows down over time, which suggests that eligible firms have a high potential, since they are also capable of advancing their innovation trajectories, albeit at a slower pace in comparison to funded ones. Overall, the results confirm a short-term effectiveness of SMEi grants in stimulating innovation while revealing the latent potential of high-quality, non-funded applicants. These findings contribute to the literature on innovation policy and offer actionable insights for designing complementary innovation support mechanisms that combine financial assistance with broader capability-building interventions capable of sustaining long-term innovation trajectories in SMEs.

title: Opposing effects of authentic pride and hubristic pride on funding outcomes in new venture pitches: The mediating role of competence and warmth
abstract: We investigate how entrepreneurs’ pride expressions influence funding outcomes in new venture pitches. Drawing on Social Functional Theory of emotions, we argue that authentic and hubristic pride have opposing effects on investors’ decisions through perceptions of competence and warmth. Across three experimental studies with crowdfunders (N1 = 196, N2 = 593, N3 = 159), we examined verbal and bodily pride expressions. Verbal expressions of authentic pride indirectly increased funding intentions via perceived competence, whereas hubristic pride indirectly decreased funding through reduced perceptions of both competence and warmth. These effects did not vary across variations in campaign size and technological innovation. Bodily expressions replicated the negative indirect effect of hubristic pride compared to authentic pride. Our findings suggest entrepreneurs should convey authentic pride during pitches, as hubristic pride may undermine success by signaling arrogance and diminishing perceived competence and warmth.

title: The typology of learning from successive failures—the overconfidence effect on judgment errors
abstract: While entrepreneurial failure has been widely studied, it remains unclear why repeated failures do not always lead to learning, particularly when decision-making is shaped by cognitive biases. This study examines how interacting biases distort learning from successive failures, drawing on a longitudinal case of an entrepreneur who experienced repeated venture failures. Overconfidence, reinforced by optimism, motivational reasoning, and confirmation bias, produced persistent judgment errors in opportunity identification and venture evaluation. Applying attribution theory, we show that initial internal attributions at the organizational level enabled only superficial learning, while deeper learning emerged when the entrepreneur critically reassessed beliefs through hybrid attributions across individual, organizational, and environmental levels. The study’s key contribution lies in demonstrating that overconfidence operates through interactions with other biases, delaying reflective learning and allowing errors to persist. By theorizing these dynamics, the research clarifies when and why failure leads to transformative rather than repeated misjudgment.

title: The interplay of social capital, digital transformation and sustainability for designing international marketing strategies: a systematic literature review
abstract: Purpose This study systematically reviews the current literature on the role of social capital in adopting digital technologies and achieving sustainability. The current investigation identifies key insights across social capital, digital transformation and sustainability paradigms, and highlights how these findings guide business organisations in designing international marketing strategies. Design/methodology/approach A systematic literature review (SLR) was conducted using the PRISMA protocol. In total, 92 peer-reviewed articles out of 403 manuscripts, based on Scopus and Web of Science (WoS) database searches from 1980 to 2025, were identified and selected for conducting a thematic analysis and proposing a theoretical framework. Findings The analysis of this SLR revealed three main themes: (1) social capital for digital transformation, (2) social capital for achieving sustainability and (3) social capital for both digital transformation and achieving sustainability. Several sub-themes were also synthesised under each theme. Key findings include how social capital permits sustained customer-oriented culture, inter-organisational trust and artificial intelligence-based social networks – critical aspects for designing international market strategies. A potential theoretical framework is also proposed to explain how social capital influences the adoption of digital technologies and the achievement of sustainability goals, and how firms can entrench these identified attributes into sustained knowledge management, improved strategic positioning and market-oriented innovation. Originality/value This is the first study to propose a theoretical framework that connects social capital to digital transformation and sustainability in the context of international marketing. It offers practical insights for firms seeking to integrate social capital, digital technologies and sustainability initiatives into global strategy development.

title: Cultural echoes in e-WOM: the role of self-presentation in brand agility perception
abstract: Purpose This study seeks to expand the current understanding of perceived social media agility (PSMA) within the dynamic capabilities perspective by exploring its influence on positive electronic word-of-mouth (e-WOM) across culturally diverse settings. Specifically, it examines how cultural orientation (collectivist versus individualistic) and self-presentation behaviors moderate the relationship between PSMA and positive e-WOM. Design/methodology/approach Three experimental studies were conducted using online adult samples to test the research hypotheses. Studies 1 and 2 utilized a cross-national design with participants drawn from Türkiye (representing a collectivist culture) and the United Kingdom (representing an individualistic culture). In these studies, standard linear regression was used to evaluate the primary baseline relationship, while the PROCESS macro in SPSS (Models 1 and 3) was employed to test moderation and moderated moderation structures, exploring the conditional effects and interaction patterns among PSMA, self-presentation, and cultural context. Additionally, a post hoc analysis was performed to validate the use of nationality as a proxy for cultural orientation. Finally, Study 3 was conducted within a single-country framework (the United Kingdom) to rigorously evaluate and replicate the model at the individual psychographic level, utilizing a refined experimental design, an alternative operationalization of PSMA, and an individual-level measure of collectivism. Findings The findings across all three studies demonstrate that PSMA consistently and significantly enhances consumers' intentions to engage in positive e-WOM. In the cross-national framework (Studies 1 and 2), this main effect is heavily conditioned by cultural context and self-presentation tendencies. Specifically, the positive impact of PSMA on e-WOM is greater for Turkish participants than for UK participants, and a significant three-way interaction reveals that self-presentation behaviors play a more pronounced moderating role for UK consumers. Crucially, the single-country framework of Study 3 successfully replicates this cultural boundary condition at the micro-psychological level within an individualistic market, revealing a statistically significant interaction between brand agility and individual-level collectivism. Johnson-Neyman threshold analysis further demonstrates that even within an individualistic society, the positive returns of brand agility are significantly unlocked and amplified once a consumer's individual collectivism score crosses a critical activation baseline. Originality/value This research advances the literature on social media agility by positioning PSMA within the dynamic capabilities perspective, incorporating a psychological perspective through the lens of self-presentation, and addressing the scarcity of cross-cultural comparative studies through an explicit integration of cultural analysis. It offers a multilayered, cross-level framework that highlights culture not merely as contextual background, but as a central interpretive lens through which consumers understand and evaluate agile brand behavior on social media. In this way, the study provides robust multi-method validation demonstrating how both macro-level national culture and micro-level individual cultural traits systematically shape consumers' engagement with agile brands.

title: Impact of artificial intelligence in international business – a comprehensive review
abstract: Purpose The aim of this research article is to review the existing literature on the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the international business (IB) phenomena. In particular, a comprehensive bibliometric method as well as a literature review is conducted, followed by focused future research directions for scholars. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a systematic literature review approach, in which we conducted a thorough bibliometric analysis as well as a systematic literature review by analyzing each of the papers. Bibliometric analysis is performed using the Biblioshiny software, which merges data from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. In some cases, where the merged data do not show significant results, we used the VOSviewer software for analysis. Furthermore, we read the selected papers and created a detailed spreadsheet of the papers and then crafted themes to present our literature review. We then analyzed the gaps in existing literature to provide future research directions. Findings We could identify trends and patterns of AI's influence on IB scholarship, where there is a sudden jump in the articles post-COVID, i.e., 2020 onward. Furthermore, there is a diverse range of streams currently publishing on this topic indicates the infancy of an evolving research domain. In addition, there is a wide range of countries that are publishing on this topic, which suggests growing awareness and adoption of AI; however, several African, Asian and South American countries require significant catch-up. Next, our themes derived from the findings of the literature reveal that AI is driving innovation and efficiency, amplifying cultural and behavioral dynamics, facilitating critical knowledge and improving governance for MNEs to impact IB. Finally, we suggest five future research directions, i.e., geopolitical environment, regulatory frameworks, dark side of AI, ESG and culture, which are critical to any MNE's success in a foreign country. We encourage scholars to study IB through the lens of AI's impact on these research agendas. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is one of the first systematic and bibliometric analyses of AI's influence on the IB. Furthermore, ours is one of the few attempts to merge the two databases, i.e., Scopus and the Web of Science, to provide a comprehensive set of articles for the bibliometric analysis. We also provide the R-code on how to merge the two databases. Finally, we review the existing literature by providing four novel themes and present five unique future research directions.

title: Microfoundations of Adaptive Decision‐Making Capability: How Chief Supply Chain Officers Convert Technology‐Enabled Visibility Into Coordinated Action
abstract: ABSTRACT Supply chain leaders increasingly operate with extensive technology‐enabled visibility, yet many firms still struggle to convert shared signals into timely, coordinated action. We frame this tension as the visibility‐to‐action problem in supply chain management (SCM): executives observe more than they can process and often fail to route, prioritize, and execute quickly enough for information to translate into coordinated outcomes. We examine how Chief Supply Chain Officers (CSCOs) close this gap. Drawing on dynamic capabilities and microfoundations research, we adopt a theory‐elaborating qualitative design that pairs a theories‐in‐use approach with the Gioia methodology, analyzing 25 CSCO interviews spanning manufacturing, retail, logistics, and technology sectors. Informants theorize that technology‐enabled advantage depends less on tool acquisition than on the intentional design of interoperable data architectures, conversion routines that filter and route exceptions to accountable owners, and learning stabilizers that preserve reliable adjustment over time. We conceptualize these as the microfoundations of adaptive decision‐making capability (ADMC), a higher‐order managerial capability linking information, judgment, and action into self‐reinforcing learning cycles. As a theorized downstream implication, participants further suggest that ADMC supports the development of adaptive supply chain capability (ASCC), reflected in agility, resilience, alignment, and learning velocity. The study extends microfoundations and dynamic capabilities research by specifying the cognitive, governance, and exception‐management mechanisms through which technology‐enabled visibility becomes coordinated action in data‐intensive SCM settings.

title: Shaping sustainable investment through digital technologies: Strategic perspectives for the transformation era
abstract: This paper examines the importance of technological infrastructure in influencing sustainable investment, with particular reference to gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) and foreign direct investment (FDI). We use principal component analysis (PCA) and data envelopment analysis (DEA) to uncover the structural interdependences among digital readiness, innovation capacity and macroeconomic stability. Countries that are identified as DEA-efficient, with high internet penetration, extensive mobile uptake and strong high-tech exports, are consistently receiving greater investment. Inflation impacts economies in different ways, it prevents capital accumulation in less efficient economies and it helps promote investment in more efficient economies. This highlights the importance of context sensitive macroeconomic strategies. Unemployment is still a big hurdle to sustainable investment, limiting GFCF and FDI especially in economies with structural rigidities. The outlier analysis identifies Vietnam, China and Malta as examples of ICT-driven investment resilience, while Sudan illustrates how structural and labor-market constraints can impede capital accumulation despite moderate digital progress. A robust digital infrastructure, innovation capacity and a stable macroeconomic and labor-market are essential to sustain competitive investment strategies. This alignment of factors strategically promotes inclusive growth and long-term investment resilience in countries. It provides actionable guidance to policy makers and business leaders to advance sustainable economic development.

title: From standards to patent pools: SEP-owner heterogeneity and the staged formation of collective licensing
abstract: Patent pools enable owners of standard-essential patents (SEPs) to coordinate licensing for standards-based technologies, but doing so requires agreement among firms with divergent competitive positions, technological capabilities, and commercialization interests. We develop a staged governance framework in which SEP-owner composition is associated with patent pool formation through theorized stage-contingent mechanisms. The conditions that increase the governance necessity and coalition feasibility of collective licensing in Stage 1 need not be the same conditions that enable rapid agreement in Stage 2; in some cases, the same compositional feature can operate in opposite directions across the two stages. Using a new dataset covering nearly 1000 ICT standards, of which 57 became viable pool candidates, we estimate a two-stage survival-selection model that jointly examines whether a standard enters the pool-formation process and, conditional on entry, the time required to launch a pool. We find that greater heterogeneity in SEP owners' knowledge domains increases the likelihood of pool candidacy but slows formation, suggesting that fragmented technological ownership raises governance necessity while impeding execution. Business-domain heterogeneity is associated with slower formation but has no detectable association with candidacy, a pattern consistent with an execution-stage friction. SEP-quality dispersion is associated with lower candidacy and slower formation, a pattern consistent with asymmetric outside options weakening coalition feasibility and bargaining efficiency. The findings provide ex ante observable indicators of licensing-coordination delay risk and suggest that standard establishment alone is insufficient for timely commercialization when IP ownership is fragmented across heterogeneous SEP owners.

title: Unveiling the dynamics of data driven innovation in human resource analytics: A grounded theory of strategic approach to HRM
abstract: Data-driven innovation (DDI) in Human Resource Analytics (HR Analytics) presents a significant potential for strategic organizational change. A persistent gap exists between the theoretical promises of HR Analytics and its practical, value-generating implementation within organizations. This study aims to develop a conceptual model for the effective implementation of HR Analytics within private-sector organizations in a developing economy (Iran), framed through the lens of DDI. Employing a Grounded Theory (GT) approach, specifically the systematic coding methodology of Strauss and Corbin, this research gathered rich qualitative data through in-depth, semi-structured interviews with HR Analytics and Business Analytics experts operating within the Iranian organizational context. Data analysis, facilitated by MAXQDA, involved rigorous open, axial, and selective coding until theoretical saturation was achieved, with study rigor confirmed via Lincoln and Guba's criteria. The resulting conceptual model elucidates the complex interplay of causal conditions (e.g., transformation in human resource management, data-driven approach), context (e.g., technology adoption, cultural contexts), strategies (pre-adoption, decision-making, adoption phases), intervening obstacles, and possible outcomes. By highlighting the contextual features of the Iranian economic environment, this model offers a coherent framework to assist private enterprises in comparable settings to more effectively navigate their transition toward data-driven HR management, offering insights for organizations aiming to leverage HR Analytics as a driver for strategic innovation and business value enhancement.

title: The Age‐Fit Hypothesis: Celebrity Age, Content Type, and Consumer Engagement on Social Media
abstract: ABSTRACT Although prior work has examined celebrity influence in digital contexts, how celebrity age shapes follower responses to sponsored versus non‐sponsored content remains underexplored. Integrating role congruity theory with the ageing stability hypothesis, we propose an age‐fit hypothesis. We test this proposition across three studies using a multimethod design. Study 1 analyzes 22,619 posts from 286 celebrities. Study 2 applies sentiment analysis to 67,778 follower comments. Study 3 employs a 2 × 2 between‐subjects experiment ( N = 290) to replicate the interaction effect and test the underlying mechanism. Results consistently reveal that older celebrities elicit lower engagement and less positive emotional responses for sponsored posts relative to non‐sponsored posts, whereas younger celebrities elicit higher sponsored posts, with followers expressing more positive emotional responses toward their sponsored content. Study 3 further demonstrates that this interaction effect is sequentially mediated by perceived interest fit and social identification: reduced congruence between older celebrities and sponsored content diminishes followers’ interest alignment and identification, ultimately undermining engagement. By theorizing age‐based role congruity as a boundary condition in celebrity endorsement effectiveness, this research advances understanding of how stereotype‐driven identity processes shape consumer digital engagement.

title: Guidelines for Meta‐Analytic Structural Equation Modeling: Steps, Resources, and Illustrations
abstract: ABSTRACT The goal of science is to build incremental, structured, and reliable knowledge over time. Yet, many strands of marketing and related disciplines exhibit symptoms of cumulative stagnation, including lack of replicability and weak theoretical integration. Existing remedies such as replication studies, multistudy investigations, and open science practices offer safeguards for future research, but they are not designed to reconcile past evidence now under scrutiny. Meta‐analytic structural equation modeling (MASEM) offers a complementary route to improving the cumulative character of marketing research by aggregating past fragmented evidence into a multivariate test of an overarching theory. Given that such examination occurs at the cumulative level, MASEM offers higher‐level contributions by exposing structural inconsistencies, adjudicating contested mechanisms, and revealing obscured mediating mechanisms across entire literature streams. Uptake, however, remains limited as its implementation requires a long chain of technical decisions that are rarely reported in a reproducible form. Moreover, methodological recommendations remain fragmented across studies, leaving researchers to integrate the overall workflow on their own. This article develops an integrated set of guidelines for conducting MASEM that address these barriers in three important ways. First, the guidelines provide a six‐step methodological guide that integrates fragmented methodological knowledge into a coherent workflow. Second, the guide is operationalized through an empirical illustration, providing a practical application of the six steps. Third, the guidelines are accompanied by modular open resources to facilitate accessible MASEM implementation. In sum, the guidelines support a more rigorous and widespread application of MASEM.

title: EXPRESS: Platform Complementors’ Diversification Strategies and the Role of Venture Capital
abstract: Digital entrepreneurs play a critical role as complementors in platform ecosystems yet often face formidable power imbalances vis-à-vis platform owners and venture capitalists (VCs). To explore how entrepreneurs buffer against powerful platforms and enhance their own bargaining power, we conceptualize their diversification strategies as “escape routes”—across product categories (portfolio diversity) and across platforms (multihoming)—through the lens of native platform choice and VC funding. We propose three distinctive models of complementors’ diversification choices that arise when the VC’s interests align with those of the complementor, platform or neither, illustrating the triadic platform-complementor-VC dynamics. Using data on iOS and Android app developers, and their VC funding status, we find that originating on Apple’s iOS platform correlates with relatively narrow portfolio breadth but a stronger tendency to serve multiple platforms. Conversely, originating on Google’s Android platform is associated with greater portfolio diversity yet a lower propensity for cross-platform expansion. Interestingly, neither VC funding nor native platform choice alone fully predict all diversification choices; rather, the additive effects of these factors reveal the “escape routes” or “all-in” focused approaches. Notably, regardless of the native platform, developers securing VC funding appear to specialize, suggesting a ‘VC standalone’ model, whereby independent of the platform power dynamics, external capital may prefer strategic depth over breadth. Our conceptual model and findings highlight how powerful platforms and scarce venture capital shape entrepreneurial choices, offering new insights into how these stakeholders’ interests may converge or diverge in collective enterprises such as platform ecosystems.

title: EXPRESS: A CONFIGURATIONAL THEORY OF BUSINESS COLLECTIVE ACTION
abstract: Firms facing institutional pressures often respond collectively through established organizations such as trade associations. However, they may also create new organizations that supplement, redirect, or challenge these incumbent vehicles. Yet we know little about what shapes firms’ choice among these different forms of collective action. Adopting a configurational approach, we theorize how collective responses reorganize the set of organizational vehicles through which business interests are aggregated, represented, and coordinated in organizational fields – the BCA infrastructure. We identify critical contingencies related to institutional pressures, field structure, and existing BCA infrastructure, and we theorize how combinations of these contingencies generate four recurrent coordination problems––contribution problems, distributional conflict, capacity gaps, and representational authority problems––that give rise to distinct BCA infrastructure outcomes: consolidation around incumbent vehicles, complementation through new BCA vehicles offering functional differentiation, cooptation of existing vehicles, or competition via rival BCA vehicles. In doing so, we offer a conceptual lens for understanding the proliferation of business associations, coalitions, platforms, and initiatives across organizational fields.

title: Recurrent and eroding challenges in creative tourism: A longitudinal study of entrepreneurial resilience among urban handicraft artisans
Renovating for Relevance: How to Rewrite a Traditional Manuscript for Academy of Management Perspectives
The innovation tug‐of‐war: Local grit versus global grit in emerging markets
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Drawing on vicarious learning, competition‐driven innovation incentives, and the temporal dynamics of competitive activity, this study explores which type of competition, local versus foreign, most benefits advanced economy MNEs' (AEMNEs) emerging market (EM) innovation performance, when and in what temporal patterns. We predict that local competition contributes more to AEMNEs' EM innovation performance and that this positive impact is reinforced by foreign competition. We further predict that irregular local competition amplifies the innovation performance‐enhancing effect of local competition, whereas irregular foreign competition diminishes the benefits of foreign competition for innovation performance. Our multi‐level analysis of AEMNEs operating in China's high‐tech sector supports these predictions. The findings offer novel insights into how competition heterogeneity and its temporal dynamics shape the innovation performance of AEMNEs in EMs. Managerial Summary AEMNEs face competition from both local and foreign rivals, but not all competition equally drives innovation. Our study of AEMNEs operating in China shows that competing with local counterparts delivers greater innovation performance, and the innovation benefits of engaging with one type of rival are reinforced by the other. Competitive rhythm also matters. Local competition enhances innovation when local rivals act irregularly, while irregular moves by foreign peers reduce their innovation benefits. Managers should strategically track both competitor types and align innovation efforts with the rhythm of market dynamics to maximize innovation outcomes.

title: Classified Boards and Corporate Environmental and Social Performance
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This study examines the relationship between classified boards and firms' environmental and social (E&S) performance. We ask whether the insulation associated with classified boards is related to firms' sustainability outcomes and whether external monitoring and investor horizon condition this relationship. Research Findings/Insights Using 14,066 US firm‐year observations from 2002 to 2020, we find that firms with classified boards exhibit significantly lower overall E&S performance. This negative association is concentrated in the environmental dimension. The adverse association with E&S performance is weaker among firms subject to stronger institutional monitoring and, in particular, among firms with greater long‐term institutional ownership. We further find that classified boards are associated with a higher incidence of negative E&S events and greater disagreement across ESG rating providers. Finally, classified boards are negatively associated with firm value, and our path analysis is consistent with E&S performance and rating disagreement serving as channels linking board structure to valuation. Our results are robust to using instrumental variable estimation, and entropy balancing. Theoretical/Academic Implications Our findings are consistent with the managerial entrenchment view of classified boards. Although classified boards may provide stability and protection from short‐term market pressures, the evidence suggests that this insulation can be associated with weaker accountability and lower engagement in sustainability‐related activities. The study contributes to the corporate governance literature by showing that the implications of classified boards extend beyond conventional shareholder outcomes to stakeholder‐oriented, non‐financial outcomes. It also contributes to the ESG literature by identifying board structure as an important correlate of both corporate E&S performance and disagreement among ESG rating providers. Practitioner/Policy Implications The findings have implications for investors, corporate boards, and policymakers evaluating the costs and benefits of classified boards. Shareholders may wish to consider the potential E&S consequences of board classification, particularly in firms where external monitoring is weak. More broadly, the results suggest that institutional monitoring and long‐term ownership can play an important role in mitigating the adverse E&S associations of classified boards. For policymakers, the evidence is relevant to debates over board declassification, director accountability, and the governance of corporate E&S activities.

title: Theoretical Foundations for a Sustainability and Climate Change Strategic Leadership Typology: Towards Regenerative Leadership
abstract: Abstract The interlinked climate and ecological crises have profound implications for future human success. Temperatures are set to rise by 3–4 0 C by the end of the century and there is already a sixty-nine per cent global average biodiversity abundance loss since 1970. Most of our business and management literature continues to rely on traditional, anthropocentric, leadership and strategy theories as a route to change without considering the embedded, systemic, heterogeneous, and future-orientated nature of the problem. Given this multifaceted grand challenge, and the compounding lack of adequate business and management theoretical foundations for such research investigations, we propose six strategic leadership types (and their underpinning values and capabilities) that help to differentiate leadership for the complex climate and ecological crises we face. The leadership types, greenwash, resilience, eco-innovation, ecocentric visionary (sustainability), degrowth and regenerative leadership, are calibrated against known ontological and strategic perspectives, which provide plurality and fluidity of thought, allowing connection between the natural and social sciences, to aid understanding of research towards sustainability and climate change. We reframe the leadership literature by locating our theoretical contribution within environmental ethics, linking our understanding of the natural world, human ethics, and related business ethics, identifying regenerative leadership as the most ethical and most promising type.

title: When Oversight Falters: Ethical Opportunism and Corporate Tax Avoidance under Governance Failure
Artificial Intelligence Disclosure and the Value Relevance of Earnings
When Responsibility Compensates for Ownership: Agency Theory, State Capitalism, and the Scale of Chinese OFDI
abstract: This paper investigates how the ownership structures of Chinese enterprises shape their outward foreign direct investment (OFDI) outcomes, and whether corporate social responsibility (CSR) performance alters that relationship. Drawing on agency theory and a firm-level panel dataset of companies listed on China’s Shenzhen and Shanghai Stock Exchanges covering 2008 to 2017, the study asks two related questions: does state ownership systematically disadvantage firms in international investment relative to their privately held counterparts, and does CSR performance function as a moderating force capable of offsetting whatever ownership-driven effects emerge? The empirical analysis indicates that state-owned enterprises (SOEs) tend to underperform private firms in OFDI, yet reveals that the degree of government intervention, whether a firm is controlled by the central government or by a provincial or municipal authority, does not itself produce a statistically distinguishable difference in OFDI outcomes within the SOE category. Crucially, the study finds that stronger CSR performance can partially offset the OFDI disadvantage associated with state ownership, but this moderating effect is not uniform across all SOEs: it operates specifically among locally governed SOEs, whose primary obstacle in foreign markets is a reputational deficit rather than the institutional pressure and risk aversion that constrain centrally governed counterparts.

title: Making Water Investible : Development Banking, Regulatory Governance, and the Institutional Production of Sanitation Infrastructure in Brazil
abstract: ABSTRACT Why did long‐horizon private investment in Brazilian water and sanitation expand after 2016 despite fragmented authority and persistent political contestation? This article places the Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES) inside, rather than outside, the credible‐commitment framework. It argues that the bank operated as a credibility intermediary: it assembled service territories at investible scale, financed and coordinated project preparation, translated statutory goals into comparable contracts, and linked concessions to long‐term finance. These functions complemented courts, legislatures, the national standard‐setting role of the National Water and Basic Sanitation Agency (ANA), and post‐award supervision by infranational regulators. Process tracing of laws, concession documents, regulatory instruments, auction records, corporate filings, and attributable investor statements shows how this architecture was repeated across the Temer, Bolsonaro, and Lula administrations, albeit under different political framings. The mechanism is sequence‐sensitive but not universally necessary: Chile demonstrates an alternative route through regional utilities and a central regulator, while Colombia illustrates the continuing constraints of fragmented provision. The article also distinguishes investibility from legitimacy. Financial and contractual discipline can make commitments more legible to investors, but it neither replaces public‐law oversight nor resolves disputes over affordability, participation, and the human right to water.

title: The Right Key for the Right Lock: How Government Response Methods and Demand Types Affect Citizen Satisfaction
abstract: ABSTRACT Faced with diverse and complex demands from citizens, the government has consistently sought ways to enhance its ability to respond. Metaphorically, citizens' needs can be viewed as locks, and the government requires keys to unlock them. Artificial intelligence (AI) is an innovative new key offering a fresh paradigm for unlocking the door to high citizen satisfaction. Drawing on government responsiveness theory, this study applies a 2 × 3 between‐subjects survey experiment to explore the impact of government response methods (traditional responses, AI‐enabled responses) and citizen demand types (consultation, complaint/help‐seeking, suggestions) on citizen satisfaction. Findings show that AI‐enabled government responses significantly increase citizen satisfaction compared to traditional approaches. Among demand types, consultation yields the highest satisfaction, while suggestion results in the lowest. Further, the satisfaction level is significantly influenced by the interaction effect between response method and demand type. Perceived fairness mediates the relationship between government responses and citizen satisfaction, with citizen participation experience having a moderating effect. This study offers new insights into increasing citizen satisfaction from the perspective of government responses. It reveals the content‐dependent nature of AI‐enabled government responses, helping the government create unique AI response strategies and enhance digital interaction with citizens.

title: The few, the loud: platform-mediated articulation of conspiratorial discourse by political elites on X and Facebook
abstract: Despite growing concerns about the role of political elites in producing and amplifying conspiracy theories, little is known about which politicians engage in this behavior, how prevalent it is across countries and platforms, and what ideological patterns it follows. We address these questions by identifying a narrow set of elite conspiracy entrepreneurs who disproportionately produce conspiratorial discourse, challenging the bounds of acceptable debate across three European democracies. Using gradient threshold analysis, logistic regression, and close reading, we analyze a manually annotated sample of posts by political elites (N = 702) in Belgium, Finland, and Poland to identify conspiracy entrepreneurs, characterize them, and examine their cross-platform communication. Results indicate that conspiratorial discourse is driven by a narrow set of predominantly far-right politicians, who generate higher engagement than their colleagues, despite comparable following and posting rates. Conspiratorial discourse also differs across platforms, with Facebook enabling more fully articulated conspiratorial narratives and X favoring more fragmented, context-dependent communication. These findings illuminate how political elites cultivate epistemic crisis and how social media platforms may algorithmically reward conspiratorial content by providing tools for politicians to generate engagement.

title: Quantitative analysis of multi-factor coupled safety risks for automated driving: Empirical evidence from 232 accident cases
When harm does not simply reverse: Asymmetric within-child associations between child maltreatment allegations and behavioral problems
Increasing the number of released rice varieties with higher yield potentials alone do not necessarily improve farm yields: Evidence from double-season rice in China
Does the Evidence Refute the Male Choice Hypothesis? A Response to Wilczkowski (2026)
Cloud-ground mapping matching for enhanced regional distributed PV power forecasting
abstract: Accurate forecasting of distributed photovoltaic (PV) power remains a significant challenge due to the lack of on-site meteorological measurements. Satellite cloud images (SCIs) offer a promising alternative. However, existing methods that directly utilize SCIs as input features often yield suboptimal performance in distributed PV scenarios. This is primarily attributed to the broad spatial coverage of SCIs, which introduces substantial irrelevant information unrelated to PV sites, thereby impairing model learning efficiency and increasing computational complexity. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a cloud–ground mapping framework to improve the forecasting accuracy of distributed PV cluster power. First, a cloud–ground mapping model is developed to identify SCI feature regions that directly obstruct the distributed PV sites. Second, a feature region attention enhanced 3D-CNN is constructed to forecast future SCIs accurately. Third, a similar cloud condition matching method is developed to extract similar historical power as meteorological features based on SCIs. Finally, both the similar historical power and temporally adjacent PV outputs are integrated as input features for the forecasting model. Extensive case studies on a real-world dataset comprising 638 distributed PV sites demonstrate that, compared with existing PV power forecasting methods, the proposed framework reduces nMAE by approximately 14.6% and nRMSE by up to 16.5%, confirming its effectiveness and superiority in regional distributed PV power forecasting.

title: Peak demand estimation in distribution systems: impacts of plug-in electric vehicle charging on load coincidence
abstract: Increasing transport electrification is expected to substantially alter electricity demand patterns in distribution systems (DSs). In particular, large-scale adoption of plug-in electric vehicles (PEVs) may modify the temporal coincidence of customer loads, challenging peak-demand estimation methods calibrated under historical demand conditions, such as Velander’s formula. This study investigates how PEV charging affects load coincidence and peak-demand estimation in a real urban DS in Stockholm County, Sweden. A probabilistic Monte Carlo framework is used to generate stochastic PEV charging demand across penetration scenarios ranging from the 2023 baseline conditions to full fleet electrification. The resulting charging profiles are integrated into a detailed DS model, enabling the analysis of system operation, coincidence factors, and the performance of the Velander formulation across different aggregation levels, customer groups, and seasons. The results show that increasing PEV penetration markedly alters coincidence behaviour, with secondary substations exhibiting a pronounced U-shaped response across the penetration range: the median coincidence factor falls from about 0.96 at the 2023 baseline to 0.61–0.62 near 15–20% penetration, and recovers to about 0.91 at full electrification. Consequently, the relationship between annual energy consumption and coincident peak demand changes substantially, leading to systematic errors in peak-demand estimation. To address these shortcomings, a set of analytical and data-driven formulations that explicitly account for PEV demand characteristics are developed and evaluated. These models improve predictive accuracy by up to 70% relative to the classical approach and provide more robust performance across PEV penetration scenarios. Overall, the findings provide new insights into how PEV charging affects coincidence behaviour across DS aggregation levels, reveal limitations of the classical Velander formulation, and demonstrate how alternative formulations can improve peak-demand estimation under transport electrification.

title: Grid-interactive data centers for sustainable and resilient energy systems: Evolution, trends, and future directions
abstract: Data centers (DCs) are becoming some of the most energy-intensive and grid-influential infrastructures in modern power systems, driven by the explosive growth of artificial intelligence (AI) workloads, cloud computing, and data-intensive digital services. Conventional facilities were designed primarily for reliable computing service delivery, but high-density AI workloads and fast load transients now demand more flexible and controllable energy-computing integration. Grid-interactive data centers (GDCs) provide a pathway for this transition by coordinating computational workloads, energy storage, renewable generation, cooling infrastructure, and grid-facing control functions. However, existing studies continue to address energy management, workload flexibility, demand response, power quality, dynamic load modeling, and ancillary-service participation as largely disjoint research streams. To address this fragmentation, this review provides a systems-level synthesis of next-generation GDCs for sustainable and resilient energy systems. It traces the evolution from conventional and energy-aware data centers to AI-optimized DCs and next-generation GDCs. The review identifies key enabling technologies, including grid-forming interfaces, flexible workload scheduling, distributed energy storage systems, AI-based control, digital twins, and cybersecurity, and introduces a six-layer GDC architecture that integrates physical infrastructure, energy systems, communication and control, intelligence and co-optimization, grid interfaces, and stakeholder-market interaction. The review further examines operational management strategies, grid integration challenges, sustainability metrics, and deployment barriers, and highlights digital-twin-based operation, coordinated smart inverters, and fast multi-timescale optimization frameworks as critical research directions for future GDC deployment.

title: Cost comparison of low- and zero-emission heavy-duty vehicles: a case route analysis
Progress and prospects of amine-based chemical absorption for post-combustion CO2 capture in thermal power plants
abstract: To meet the greenhouse-gas (GHG) mitigation targets pledged under the Paris Agreement, signatory countries are accelerating the deployment of commercial carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) projects. The power sector is responsible for more than 36% of global carbon emissions, and amine-based chemical absorption is widely regarded as the leading option for post-combustion CO 2 capture in thermal power plants. However, commercial CCUS operating experience has exposed persistent economic and environmental challenges. These issues continue to hinder wider implementation of CCUS in the power sector. This review systematically summarizes advances in chemical absorption technologies tailored for thermal power plants, emphasizing cost-reduction energy-saving strategies across solvent development, capture process configurations, high-efficiency equipment integration, and advanced operational control. The evolution of absorbents is first traced, and current strategies to reduce regeneration energy while improving key performance attributes are summarized, including corrosion resistance, amine-emission mitigation, and resistance to amine degradation. Energy-saving process technologies are presented as complementary levers for reducing regeneration energy. Representative energy-saving configurations and intensified equipment are classified, and their applicable scenarios and remaining limitations are analyzed. In addition, the contribution of intelligent methods to accelerating the discovery of energy-efficient solvents and the development of energy-saving technologies is highlighted, together with the potential of intelligent control for automated and economically optimized operation. Finally, future challenges and research directions for flue-gas CO 2 capture in power plants are outlined to support practical CCUS deployment in the electricity sector.

title: Advanced machine learning and hybrid deep learning models for performance prediction of conducting polymer-based supercapacitor systems
Critical review of hybrid solar thermal desalination system for sustainable potable water production
Constraint-guided multi-agent deep reinforcement learning for multi-microgrid energy management with mobile electric vehicles
Temporal and spatial patterns of the Sealed-to-Artificial area Ratio in European urban areas
abstract: Land take is primarily driven by urbanisation and infrastructure development and is closely linked to soil sealing, which involves covering soil with impervious materials. Over recent decades, both processes have steadily increased in European urban areas, significantly impacting ecosystem services. To stop these processes, the European Commission has set two distinct targets: "no net land take" and ”no net soil sealing”. To examine the relationship between the two processes, we introduce the Sealed-to-Artificial area Ratio (SAR), a novel indicator defined as the ratio between sealed areas and artificial areas in a certain region. We computed SAR for 661 Functional Urban Areas (FUAs) in the 27 countries of the European Union plus the UK, and its change between 2012 and 2018. Two hypotheses were tested: (1) SAR tends to decrease in FUAs with predominant agricultural land cover, as opposed to artificial; and (2) SAR tends to increase as urban form becomes more compact, as opposed to sprawling. Results show a general decrease in SAR (median of –0.36), indicating a possible trend toward lower-intensity urban development. However, regional variations emerge, with the UK-Ireland showing a greater decrease and the Southern region a smaller reduction. As expected, SAR increased in FUAs with a high share of artificial land cover and a tendency towards a more compact urban form, while those with larger availability of agricultural land and a sprawling development showed the opposite trend. The proposed indicators can be used to support urban planning and local policies to achieve European targets.

title: Coupled hydrogen-corrosion degradation in hydrogen-blended natural gas pipelines: A critical review
Thermal management of power lithium-ion batteries under extreme fast charging conditions: From heat generation mechanisms to a coordinated control framework
abstract: Extreme fast charging (XFC) can substantially reduce recharging times for battery electric vehicles, but high-rate charging generates large, spatially nonuniform heat loads within a short period. The resulting temperature gradients, localized hotspots, and cold regions affect polarization, ion transport, and lithium plating. Consequently, maximum and average temperatures alone cannot adequately characterize the electrochemical safety and aging state of the battery. This review uses a problem-driven semi-systematic approach to examine heat generation and transfer, temperature nonuniformity and its consequences, and pathways for regulating the thermal field. Under XFC conditions, the magnitudes and effects of irreversible heat generation and reversible entropic heat are jointly governed by several interacting factors. These include charging rate, state of charge, temperature nonuniformity, aging state, and cell chemistry. Heat-transfer pathways and cooling boundary conditions determine temperature differences between the cell interior and exterior, gradient direction, and hotspot duration. Their consequences are further constrained by cell configuration, system scale, and operating conditions. On this basis, the review restructures thermal management into three stages: thermal-state shaping before charging, temperature-field regulation during charging, and thermal recovery after charging. It also proposes a coordinated control framework coupling charging protocols with the battery thermal management system, together with a unified evaluation framework. Together, these frameworks are intended to guide thermal management pathway optimization, control strategy development, and system-level solution design for power lithium-ion batteries under XFC conditions.

title: China’s power market reform for a high-renewable future: Key drivers, market design, and prospects
Advanced sintering of solid oxide fuel cells: Microstructure and interfaces
abstract: Sintering in solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) is traditionally regarded as a consolidation step. However, grain-boundary topology, crystallographic stabilization, defect chemistry, and interfacial compatibility are established during sintering, pre-determining electrochemical performance and durability. This review repositions sintering as a governing design variable rather than a passive densification process. A unified mechanistic framework classifies sintering strategies by their dominant driving forces: diffusion-controlled thermal equilibration, field- and current-assisted nonequilibrium densification, pressure-mediated low-temperature consolidation, and spatially confined energy-beam processing. This perspective links energy input modality to grain growth, pore collapse, crystallographic evolution, and interfacial reactions across electrolytes, electrodes, and multilayer architectures. Comparative analysis shows that key SOFC bottlenecks, including ohmic loss in ultrathin electrolytes, triple-phase-boundary degradation, and interdiffusion-induced reaction layers, are strongly processing-dependent rather than purely material-intrinsic. Conventional furnace sintering remains robust yet thermally severe, whereas microwave and field-assisted routes provide controllable acceleration. Ultrafast and flash-assisted techniques exploit kinetic asymmetry to suppress coarsening, while cold sintering and sol–gel approaches redefine low-thermal-budget integration. Intense pulsed light and laser-based methods enable spatially selective consolidation with potential relevance to scalable manufacturing, although validation remains limited. These comparisons are compiled in five tables covering paired grain-boundary responses, reported processing conditions, published single-variable sweeps, demonstrated formats and operating records, and route selection across eleven component-and-requirement combinations; a closing section converts them into a five-question selection procedure graded by the confidence of the supporting evidence. By bridging microstructural physics with manufacturability metrics, this review advances a process-informed design paradigm for durable, efficient, and scalable SOFC systems.

title: Grain refinement control strategy for Mg-based hydrogen storage materials: Severe plastic deformation
Solar-driven photothermal and thermoelectric CO2 catalytic reduction: A review of mechanisms, materials, and reactor systems
Bridging criticality assessment and supply chain resilience: a structured framework for operationalizing mitigation actions
abstract: Critical raw materials underpin the energy transition, defense, and digitalization, yet criticality assessments remain diagnostic: they quantify supply risk and vulnerability without prescribing how to act. This gap is addressed through a structured review, from which 139 mitigation actions across mechanisms, capability types, and disruption pathway categories were compiled, harmonized, and classified. A dependency matrix encodes 278 relationships between actions. To operationalize the resulting catalog, a five-stage decision funnel is introduced to filter it by actor-specific structural boundaries and operational readiness. The illustrative application to vehicle electronics shows that no single action is universally applicable, and the set of suitable actions varies with the actor, temporal horizon, degree of control, and disruption profile. By making actor-specific feasibility and inter-action dependencies explicit, the framework enables companies and countries to assemble coherent mitigation portfolios rather than deploying isolated actions whose prerequisites, amplifications, or contradictions remain unexamined.

title: Catalytic Shunt for Sustainable Photosynthesis of Hydrogen Peroxide from Hypersaline Organic Wastewater
abstract: Abstract Photosynthetic hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) production from organic wastewater offers a sustainable alternative to the energy-intensive anthraquinone process, yet it is severely hindered by rapid quenching of reactive precursors by concentrated salts in hypersaline organic wastewater. Inspired by biological metabolic shunts, we propose a catalytic shunt strategy that spatially and functionally separates salts and organic contaminants through dynamic modulation of the catalyst electronic structure. Using an unsaturated Cr single-atom model catalyst, chloride ions (Cl–) are preferentially adsorbed onto active sites to enhance electron enrichment, while organic contaminants serve as proton donors. This system achieves a H2O2 production rate of 1.81 mM g–1 h–1, 172.3-fold higher than that of a representative photocatalytic system in pure water, and complete degradation of bisphenol A within 15 min, without external reagents. Mechanistic studies reveal that Cl– adsorption weakens *OOH binding to promote a two-electron oxygen reduction pathway, while contaminant protonation facilitates interfacial proton-coupled electron transfer. Life cycle assessment demonstrates substantially lower environmental burdens across 17 impact categories and a levelized H2O2 cost of $70.6 per ton, well below the commercial price ($140 per ton). This catalytic shunt paradigm transforms waste into a resource, enabling carbon-minimal, decentralized H2O2 production and sustainable remediation of hypersaline organic wastewater.

title: Transforming Cadmium in Paddy Soils into a Catalytic Driver for Chlorantraniliprole Degradation: Implications for an Integrated Strategy for Tackling Heavy Metal–Organic Cocontamination
abstract: Abstract Developing remediation strategies for heavy metal–organic cocontamination in paddy soils is imperative to ensure food safety. Current soil remediation strategies typically address these pollutant classes separately, often creating trade-offs in which mitigating one class of contaminants exacerbates the mobility or persistence of the other. Here, we demonstrate an integrated strategy that transforms heavy metal contaminants into a functional driver for organic contaminant degradation. Using cadmium (Cd)–chlorantraniliprole (CAP) cocontaminated paddy soil as a model system, we show that amendment with 0.5 wt % porous calcium-doped iron oxide (P-Ca@Fe2O3) achieves efficient Cd sequestration via Ca–Cd isomorphous substitution. This structural incorporation restructures the mineral electronic environment, generating abundant oxygen vacancies that activate ambient oxygen and water to produce reactive oxygen species, which drive the catalytic degradation of CAP applied during rice cultivation. Accordingly, Cd and CAP concentrations in rice grain are reduced by 77% and 61%, respectively, at the end of the 140-day rice cultivation experiment. By repurposing a soil pollutant into a functional component of the remediation process, our strategy provides a scalable, closed-loop catalytic process that restores contaminated croplands with minimal external inputs while safeguarding food safety.

title: Rate and Stoichiometry of Ytterbium Release during Ligand-Promoted Goethite Dissolution
abstract: Abstract Goethite is widely present in weathering environments and can host structurally incorporated trace elements, including heavy rare earth elements (REEs). The stability of goethite-hosted REEs in the presence of low molecular weight organic acids will impact their accumulation and mobility in regolith-hosted deposits, major sources of heavy REEs. This study assessed oxalate-promoted dissolution of Yb-incorporated goethite in flow-through and batch reactors, focusing on the kinetics and stoichiometry of Yb release at pH 4–6. Oxalate enhanced the kinetics of Fe and Yb release and promoted stoichiometric dissolution in flow-through experiments (1 mM oxalate at pH 4–5). In flow-through experiments with lower oxalate concentrations (0–0.1 mM at pH 5) and in batch experiments (1 mM oxalate at pH 4–6), the dissolution was non-stoichiometric with preferential release of Yb over Fe. Non-stoichiometric preferential Yb release is consistent with possible Fe retention by the mineral, while the dissolution of Yb-goethite may overall be stoichiometric. Experimental observations demonstrated that ligand-promoted dissolution can mobilize Yb at lower pH values (4–5), but they also showed that Yb may adsorb to the goethite surface via ternary surface complexation at higher pH values (5–6). Overall, the observed behavior has implications for understanding trace element mobility in weathering environments.

title: Trifluoroacetic Acid Competitively Inhibits Lactate Dehydrogenase to Disrupt Endothelial Glycolysis and Impair Vascular Development
abstract: Abstract Trifluoroacetic acid (TFA) is a two-carbon ultrashort-chain per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) and constitutes the most abundant PFAS in the environment. TFA has historically been regarded as a compound of relatively low acute lethality, yet its adverse effects on sensitive targets at environmentally relevant levels are largely unknown. Due to extreme hydrophilicity and anionic form in the aqueous phase of blood, TFA manifests high accessibility to the innermost layer of vasculature. In this study, we investigated the vascular toxicity of TFA using human umbilical vein endothelial cell and zebrafish embryo models at concentrations of 0.8–2000 μg/L. The results showed that TFA exposure reduced ATP content, lactate production, and glycolytic flux, concomitantly increasing pyruvate accumulation. The benchmark dose lower confidence limit (BMDL5) values ranged from 0.44 to 2.65 μg/L, falling within the range of environmental levels. Enzyme kinetics and molecular docking indicated that TFA competitively inhibited lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) at the pyruvate-binding site. In addition, TFA inhibited endothelial migration, induced cellular F-actin disruption, and impaired vascular development in zebrafish larvae. The AI-aided vascular phenomics revealed the most prominent defect in the subintestinal venous plexus. A quantitative adverse outcome pathway was subsequently established, and key-event relationships were robustly fitted, with R2 values exceeding 0.72. This study unravels a metabolic perturbation pathway of TFA-induced vascular toxicity and reinforces the need to reassess the health risks of TFA.

title: A Multi-Model Assessment of the Air Quality and Health Impacts of U.S. Energy Decarbonization
abstract: Abstract Net-zero transitions are expected to reduce ambient fine particulate matter (PM2.5) concentrations and the associated mortality burden. The magnitude and distribution of these health effects are substantially affected by energy technology choices and the resulting precursor emissions that contribute to ambient PM2.5. On the basis of a multi-model analysis using three leading energy system models for the United States (US-REGEN, GCAM-USA, and REPEAT), we demonstrate that a net-zero transition yields robust nationwide reductions in ambient PM2.5 concentrations and associated mortality. Under the net-zero scenarios, national PM2.5-attributable mortality rates in 2050 declined by 28–73% compared to 2017 across the three models. This result confirms substantial health benefits from reducing energy-sector pollution, despite concurrent population growth and aging trends that place upward pressure on mortality. Differences across the models result from how CO2 mitigation efforts are allocated across sectors and associated energy technology choices. For instance, the scale of carbon dioxide removal deployment in 2050 varies by a factor of three across the net-zero scenarios developed by the three models, influencing the amount of fossil fuel use that remains in a deeply decarbonized future and, consequently, the precursor emissions contributing to ambient PM2.5. By exploring sensitivity analyses that vary the projected emissions from non-energy activities such as wildfires, we also find that potential future increases in non-energy emissions can offset energy-sector health benefits.

title: Improving UAV Magnetic Surveys with a Theory-Guided Empirical Model for Locating and Characterizing Undocumented Orphaned Oil and Gas Wells
abstract: Abstract Undocumented orphaned oil and gas wells can pose risks through unintended releases of substances, yet they remain difficult to locate because records are incomplete and surface indicators are often absent. Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) magnetometry is increasingly used to identify steel-cased wells, but surveys commonly stop at target detection and provide limited guidance on how sensor height affects anomaly strength, burial-depth estimates, or confidence in non-detection. Here, we develop a physics-informed, calibrated empirical model between peak magnetic-anomaly amplitude and distance from the magnetometer to the top of steel casing.
