Using anomaly amplitude measured at known sensor height, the model provides three practical outputs: estimated casing-top burial depth where casing is not visible, maximum sensor height at which casing at a specified depth remains detectable, and correction of variable-height anomalies to a common reference height. We calibrate the relationship using multi-altitude UAV surveys at Wildcat Canyon Regional Park, California, and Osage Ranch, Oklahoma, and apply it at Hillman State Park, Pennsylvania, identifying one undocumented-well candidate supported by ground magnetometry and estimating burial depths for three documented wells consistent with independent depth constraints.

title: LED Light at Night Alters Amphibian Redox Physiology and Development across Ontogeny
abstract: Abstract Artificial light at night (ALAN) is a pervasive environmental stressor, yet its effects are often assessed without considering ontogeny, cross-group variation, or interactions between spectral composition and illuminance. The transition to LED lighting makes this issue increasingly relevant. Amphibians may be vulnerable because many species rely on natural light cycles and undergo habitat transitions during development. We tested direct and carryover effects of ecologically realistic LED light in crested newts (Triturus macedonicus, T. ivanbureschi) and reciprocal hybrids. Larvae were exposed to warm (2700 K) or cool (6500 K) light at 5 or 30 lx. We quantified oxidative status, development, and growth; carryover was assessed only in T. ivanbureschi after 5 lx larval exposure. ALAN altered oxidative physiology and life-history traits, with responses depending on spectrum, illuminance, and cross group. Warm light at 30 lx reduced catalase activity and glutathione and increased protein carbonyls, whereas cool light at 30 lx most strongly delayed development and reduced growth. In juvenile T. ivanbureschi, carryover responses were clearest after cool 5 lx exposure. Observed cross-group patterns were exploratory because cross type was confounded with family composition and breeding mesocosm. These findings identify LED-based ALAN as a multidimensional stressor and challenge spectrum-only mitigation strategies.

title: Demand-side drivers for low-carbon concrete: Provenance, certification and cultural legitimacy for construction uptake
Reducing the idle times of forest machines: A scenario analysis with machine big data in Finland
abstract: The idling of forest machines reduces the energy and cost efficiencies of logging operations. This study aimed to estimate the idle times and fuel consumption during idling using automatically collected machine big data. Furthermore, a scenario approach was used to describe the influence of idle times on the volume and price of carbon dioxide (CO 2 ) emissions. The dataset included monthly data from 2021 to 2024, covering 10 logging enterprises with a total of 28 harvesters and 23 forwarders. The results showed that the proportion of idle time of harvesters and forwarders regarding the total operating hours was 14.0% and 11.1%, respectively. Average fuel consumption during idling was 4.28 L h −1 for harvesters and 3.38 L h −1 for forwarders. Annual idle-related CO 2 emissions for wood-harvesting machines in Finland were roughly estimated at around 11,000 metric tonnes (t) with costs equivalent to approximately €50 million. Reduction in idling by 25–50% could cut emissions by around 3000–5000 t CO 2 and generate additional revenue roughly up to €55 million when the reduced idle engine hours were transferred into productive hours. This study concluded that understanding, as well as acknowledging, the influence of idling has a positive impact on energy and cost-efficiencies, while also ensuring more environmentally friendly logging operations. While more research is needed regarding the effects of idling in non-road machinery, this study provides a solid foundation for promoting low emissions non-road machinery operations.

title: System archetypes shaping e-waste circular economy transitions: A participatory system dynamics study
abstract: Socio-technical transitions in e-waste systems are increasingly recognised as a distinct class of technological change, in which the co-evolution of reverse logistics infrastructure, extended producer responsibility regimes, and informal recovery networks determines the pace and direction of circular economy diffusion. Understanding how feedback structures within these systems accelerate or obstruct the scaling of circular technologies is therefore central to designing effective transition interventions. This study examines circular economy transition pathways in Brazil's e-waste sector through the lens of socio-technical change, employing a participatory System Dynamics methodology that integrates co-created causal loop diagrams (CLDs), backcasting exercises anchored to a 2030 normative vision, and archetype analysis. CLDs were developed in a participatory workshop engaging heterogeneous stakeholder groups, including manufacturers, waste cooperatives, policymakers, and industry practitioners operating across Brazil's hybrid extended producer responsibility and informal governance landscape. The diagrams were further validated through multi-round interviews with the same stakeholders. The analysis spans the full product life cycle, from circular design and manufacturing to reverse logistics and end-of-life recovery. This study develops participatory causal loop diagrams that capture how stakeholders represent circular economy dynamics across the manufacturing, policy, and recycling subsystems of the Brazilian e-waste system. It moves beyond causal mapping by identifying system archetypes such as Limits to Growth, Shifting the Burden, Fixes That Fail, and Success to the Successful, which reveal recurrent feedback structures associated with transition bottlenecks, unintended consequences, and persistent coordination failures. Finally, it derives subsystem-specific policy and management implications, showing that circular economy interventions need to be aligned with the distinct structural dynamics that shape each part of the system.

title: Assessing recycling potential of critical materials in European electric vehicle fleet
abstract: The rapid expansion of electric mobility in the European Union (EU) is driving a significant increase in end-of-life (EoL) lithium-ion battery (LiB) flows. This study develops a dynamic material flow analysis (MFA) framework to quantify the future recycling potential of critical materials from electric vehicles (EVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs). A temporally explicit stock-flow model is constructed, integrating vehicle adoption projections, survival functions (including cross-border dynamics), and battery characteristics (chemistry shares and material intensities) to estimate in-use stocks and resulting material flows. EoL pathways include second-life allocation to stationary storage and recycling processes. Results indicate a sharp rise in recoverable materials by the late 2020s, driven by the temporal mismatch between rapid EV uptake and delayed battery retirement. However, even under optimistic assumptions, EU targets for recycled content in new batteries (for the years 2031/2036) are unlikely to be met under current assumptions and without additional policy intervention, particularly for cobalt. Scenarios with extended second-life use further delay material recovery, reducing near-term recycling outputs by up to 20%–25%. The findings highlight critical timing and capacity gaps in recycling infrastructure, providing actionable insights for industry and policymakers to support strategic planning and alignment with EU circular economy objectives.

title: Environmental and carbon footprint performance of biochar-augmented concrete: A cradle-to-gate life cycle assessment
Life-cycle and carbon-cost trade-offs in configuration and operation choices of a solid oxide fuel cell integrated hybrid desiccant cooling trigeneration system

Energy, exergy and economic analysis of bioinspired wick solar desalination leaf
abstract: Freshwater scarcity and energy constraints have driven the development of low-carbon and efficient solar desalination technologies. To address the salt accumulation and thermal bridge heat loss commonly encountered in conventional wick solar stills, this study proposes a bioinspired leaf-shaped reverse wick solar distiller. The leaf still employs a gravity-driven flowing liquid film to continuously rinse the evaporator surface, thereby mitigating salt crystallization. Meanwhile, a leaf-tip guttation mechanism physically breaks the continuous brine pathway, significantly reducing sensible heat loss and improving thermal efficiency. A thermodynamic theoretical model was established to analyze the heat loss and exergy loss of different components in the distiller, and validated through indoor experiments. The results demonstrate that under 1000 W/m 2 irradiation, the steady-state water production rate and solar thermal efficiency of the leaf distiller reach 0.93 kg/m 2 /h and 60.1 %, respectively. Theoretical calculation results reveal the distribution characteristics of the salinity field and temperature field within the leaf evaporator, as well as the effects of water supply flow rate and salinity on the distiller’s water production performance. Furthermore, outdoor testing in Beijing weather indicates that the designed distiller achieves a daily exergy efficiency of 4.4 %. Economic analysis shows that the water production cost is only $0.019/L, highlighting the novelty and practical potential of the proposed bioinspired reverse-distillation configuration for sustainable freshwater production.

title: Implementation of the myopic approach in the long-term energy planning and capacity expansion model; examination in a multizonal case
The atmospheric-surface Nexus in a hyper-arid coastal metropolis: Compound heat and pollution risk across Doha's urban morphologies (2018–2025)
abstract: Rapid urbanization in hyper-arid coastal cities can generate compound environmental risks through interacting surface heat, biometeorological stress, and atmospheric pollution. This study characterizes the Atmospheric–Surface Nexus in Doha, Qatar, by integrating seven satellite-derived environmental variables across six morphologically distinct urban zones in 2018 and 2025. Land Surface Temperature (LST), Approximate Wet-Bulb Globe Temperature (AWBGT; used as an uncalibrated biometeorological proxy), tropospheric NO₂, SO₂ and CO, Aerosol Optical Depth (AOD), and Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) were evaluated using a multi-tier statistical framework incorporating non-parametric tests, correlation analysis, and multivariate regression with multicollinearity and residual spatial-dependence diagnostics. Results show that thermal change was strongly season-dependent rather than uniformly increasing, with the largest upward shift occurring during March–May. This shift was particularly evident in rapidly developing peri-urban areas, indicating an encroachment of elevated heat conditions into the climatologically mild part of the year. Multivariate models identified urban morphology and NO₂ among the strongest statistical predictors of AWBGT, while the NO₂–LST Spearman correlation increased from ρ = +0.103 in 2018 to +0.493 in 2025, suggesting stronger statistical coupling between atmospheric pollution and surface thermal conditions. The analysis also reveals a Green–Blue Paradox. Vegetation and water features can reduce LST while their association with moisture may limit corresponding reductions in humidity-sensitive AWBGT under coastal conditions. Although the absence of in-situ meteorological calibration limits interpretation of absolute biometeorological risk, the findings identify morphology-specific and seasonally shifting patterns of compound heat exposure and provide a transferable framework for urban heat-risk assessment in rapidly urbanizing hyper-arid coastal cities.

Dynamic Techno-economic Assessment of Carbon Capture and Utilisation for E-methanol Production Integrated in a Local Danish Energy System
abstract: This study evaluates the techno-economic performance of integrating a carbon capture and utilisation (CCU) power-to-methanol pathway into a Danish Waste-to-Energy (WtE) plant within a local energy system context. Using a dynamic hourly model based on a real-world case (Thisted Varmeforsyning), the analysis captures the interaction between electricity price variability, carbon capture, grid-connected electrolysis, methanol synthesis, storage systems, and district heating operation. The results showed that the levelised cost of methanol (LCOMeOH) remains high, ≈ 1,288 €/t, and is dominated by hydrogen production, with electrolyser electricity consumption accounting for 60% of total costs. Sensitivity analysis revealed that system economics are highly dependent on electricity-related conditions: a 50% change in electricity prices changes LCOMeOH by 21%, while full tariff exemption reduces costs by 17%. In contrast, even substantial direct subsidies, modelled as financial credit per tonne of utilised CO 2 , have a limited impact (<4%). Integrating CCU with WtE fundamentally alters the plant from a modest net electricity exporter (+13,285 MWh/a) to a major grid consumer (-419,732 MWh/a), while simultaneously becoming a key heat supplier, displacing over 70% of heat purchases from other units. Overall, the study highlights that the viability of WtE-based power-to-methanol depends primarily on access to low-cost electricity as well as favourable regulatory conditions, and requires evaluation within an integrated energy system framework rather than at the process level alone.

The European making of circular economy for transport megaprojects. Insights from a Trans-Alpine Tunnel
abstract: The European Union is undergoing a shift: over the past decades, what was once a framework built primarily on economic growth, acceleration, and intensifying connectivity is now being driven to integrate environmental concerns. The development of the Trans-European Transport Network (TEN-T), based on several infrastructure megaprojects that must comply with environmental requirements such as reducing waste production, illustrates this transition. However, many of these projects involve underground construction, including tunnels, which generate substantial quantities of excavated material. One proposed solution is the circular economy (CE), which focuses on reusing these materials. Our article first retraces the institutionalization of environmental concerns within European directives, particularly those related to CE. This top-down analysis reveals that developments in this field result from a co-production process between public and private actors aligned with industrial interests and constraints, leading to conflicting commitments. Second, drawing on an ethnography-inspired approach, we analyze how these legal evolutions materialize in practice, within a specific TEN-T project: the construction of the Lyon–Turin tunnel. The findings from the bottom-up approach reveal that industry actors deploy technical strategies and engage in regulatory negotiations to promote CE practices. Combining these two analytical scales highlights the inherent structural tensions in the construction of megaprojects, between the imperative to increase productivity and the pursuit of environmental sustainability and circularity. This dual perspective demonstrates that CE is simultaneously shaped at multiple levels (European, national, and local) and by diverse actors (industries, regulators, and policymakers), which reinforces the contradictions between growth logics and a greening policy agenda.

title: Hybrid water governance in Nigeria: Modelling the integration of traditional institutions through empirical insights and community-led data
abstract: Persistent challenges in ensuring reliable access to safe, equitable, and sustainable water services, including inadequate infrastructure, institutional coordination, and uneven service coverage continue to undermine formal governance efforts in Nigeria, despite the presence of statutory agencies, established policy frameworks, legal provisions, and regulatory instruments. This study aims to design an integrated model that formally incorporates traditional institutions, long-standing, culturally legitimate actors with deep community trust, into Nigeria’s water governance framework. By employing a bimodal research approach, this study combines an extensive literature review, which traces the historical and contemporary roles of traditional institutions in water governance in Nigeria and across Africa and Asia, with a cross-zonal online survey, capturing community perspectives. The literature reveals that traditional institutions have historically played pivotal roles in water resource management through community-led systems, yet their contributions remain largely informal and underrecognized in policy discourse. The national survey with over 85% youth participation and representation from all six geopolitical zones highlights widespread support for hybrid governance models that integrate traditional and state systems. Respondents emphasized the roles of traditional leaders in community mobilization, infrastructure provision, and cultural enforcement, while also identifying challenges such as limited technical expertise, short-term interventions, and inadequate institutional support. The resulting model comprises four interrelated components: institutional integration, capacity and knowledge development, community engagement, and equity and inclusivity. By providing a structured framework for integrating traditional institutions into water governance, this study advances hybrid governance, offering a context-sensitive approach to addressing persistent water governance challenges in Nigeria.

title: Recycling biowaste with mechanical biological treatment technologies: The rise and fall of a socio-technical imaginary
abstract: In France, the development of fermentable waste recovery sectors has been shaped by the emergence of so-called “mechanical-biological treatment” facilities – more commonly known as “MBT” plants – throughout the 2000s and 2010s. Promoted by major actors in the waste-management industry, these plants offered a turnkey technological solution capable of sorting and treating fermentable waste while converting it into compost. For local authorities, MBT plants represented a convenient technological fix that eliminated the need to mobilize citizens to adopt source-separation practices. However, this rapid expansion came to a halt in 2015 following the adoption of the Energy Transition for Green Growth Act (LTECV), which, in its Article 70, mandates “the widespread implementation of source separation of bio-waste.” This regulatory shift marked the culmination of a long-standing socio-technical dispute that had set advocates of MBT facilities against detractors for nearly two decades. Beneath this controversy lies a struggle for control over the “socio-technical imaginary” of biowaste recovery. In this paper, I show how the sociotechnical imaginaries associated with these recovery methods were shaped by waste-management stakeholders – specifically, how the imaginary of MBT plants gained traction in the 1990s and early 2000s, only to be subsequently discredited in the years that followed.

title: The broken promise of plastic recycling: How the recycling narrative became a barrier to effective plastic governance
Governance barriers to climate change adaptation in regional catchment management
Forest Vapor Pressure Deficit Sensitivity: A Potential Indicator of Soil Carbon Stability Under Atmospheric Drying
abstract: ABSTRACT This Short Report examines an underexplored link between atmospheric drying and soil organic carbon (SOC) stability. Rising atmospheric vapor pressure deficit (VPD) is becoming an increasingly important hydroclimatic stressor for terrestrial ecosystems. We propose that VPD sensitivity, the degree to which evapotranspiration (ET) and photosynthesis co‐vary with atmospheric demand, is a potentially useful and context‐dependent indicator of forest soil carbon resilience. Operationally, VPD can be quantified as the covariate‐adjusted slope or elasticity of ET or gross primary production (GPP) with respect to VPD. A short‐term reduction in VPD sensitivity may reflect protective stomatal regulation; only persistent changes accompanied by reduced carbon uptake or root‐derived inputs are proposed as a potential warning signal. Recognizing VPD sensitivity as a candidate indicator rather than a direct measure of SOC change provides a new lens through which to evaluate forest carbon stability under global drying.

Intergroup Contact, Empathy Education, and Refugee-Native Integration in Lebanon
abstract: Abstract Intergroup contact interventions often yield limited results in deeply divided societies. We test contact and empathy education in Lebanon, where Syrian refugees comprise a quarter of the population. In a fully cross-randomised field experiment with 887 Lebanese and Syrian youth embedded in a psychosocial support programme, we find that contact has little effect on outgroup attitudes and behaviour, while empathy education consistently improves attitudes for Lebanese youth and behavioural engagement for both. The combined treatment achieves little beyond empathy alone, with no evidence of spillovers to parents (n = 595). In polarised settings, empathy education should precede — or replace — contact.

title: From Efficiency to Engagement: Leveraging Emerging Technologies for Sustainable Manufacturing Transformation
abstract: ABSTRACT The manufacturing sector is undergoing a substantial transformation driven by emerging technology and sustainable practices, offering new opportunities to improve efficiency and communicate with customers. Drawing on perspectives such as the resource‐based view (RBV) and technology adoption frameworks, this study empirically examines the influence of emerging technologies and sustainable practices on manufacturing, with connections between efficiency, sustainability, and customer engagement. The research uses confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine and enhance sustainability and customer engagement in the manufacturing industry by leveraging digital technologies. The results indicate meaningful relationships, including adoption of new technologies, implementation of sustainable practices, operational effectiveness, sustainable product development, supply chain sustainability, sustainable manufacturing performance, and customer engagement and satisfaction. Adopting emerging technologies has a good effect on operational efficiency and product sustainability. Similarly, sustainable practices positively influence supply chain and product sustainability; moreover, increased operational efficiency results in sustained production performance and higher customer involvement and satisfaction. The study provides novel insights into how technology‐driven sustainability initiatives can simultaneously strengthen operational performance and customer‐centric outcomes in manufacturing firms. This study is significant for manufacturing firms as it influences their operational strategy, innovation initiatives, and adaptation efforts to meet the changing market expectations for sustainability and customer satisfaction.

title: AI guest personalization as driver of hotel performance and hotel guest behavior: A dual-model analysis

Navigating digital transformation in bed and breakfasts: a grounded theory framework from Italian case studies
abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how bed & breakfasts (B&Bs) navigate digital transformation under resource constraints, focusing on technology adoption, customer experience and organizational adaptation in micro-hospitality. Design/methodology/approach The authors use grounded theory to analyze 31 interviews with owners of 55 Italian B&Bs already undergoing digital transformation, using a Gioia-style data structure to present the coding progression transparently. Findings The authors introduce guest-centric digital synergy: digital transformation as a paradox-driven capability system. Six propositions explain this capability system. They show how digital empathy, sociotechnical integration, cooperation and trust-based governance align technology, market demands and the hospitality ethos. Research limitations/implications The qualitative design and focus on Italian B&Bs limit generalizability; cultural and regulatory contexts may shape outcomes differently elsewhere. Future research should test the proposed framework quantitatively and extend comparisons across countries to validate portability. Studies on inclusivity and labor dynamics are also needed to address risks of job displacement and digital divide. Originality/value This research contributes to theory by reframing digital transformation in Italian micro-hospitality as a capability-dependent, contextually embedded process. It moves beyond descriptive accounts to offer a systemic perspective that integrates paradox management, cooperative strategies and sociotechnical design, providing a foundation for empirical testing and actionable guidance for small hospitality firms.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: What Do Analyst Financial Modelling Mistakes Tell Us? Evidence from the Properties of Accounting
abstract: This study develops a novel measure of sell‐side analyst financial modelling mistakes, based on whether an analyst's simultaneous forecasts of earnings, book value of equity, and dividends are internally consistent with the accounting clean surplus relation. I find that the discrepancy of an analyst's forecasts from clean surplus (a proxy for financial modelling mistakes) is positively associated with the analyst's contemporaneous forecast errors and price target errors. This is consistent with financial modelling playing an important role in analysts’ forecasting and valuation process. More experienced analysts, analysts who work for larger brokerage firms, and analysts who are less busy produce forecasts that are less discrepant from clean surplus. This is consistent with analysts learning to avoid modelling mistakes over time and making fewer mistakes when they have better access to resources and sufficient time to prepare a careful analysis. The market reaction to earnings forecast revisions is significantly weaker when the contemporaneous analyst forecasts are discrepant from clean surplus, consistent with the market viewing these forecasts as lower quality. In sum, the results reveal the importance of financial modelling to analyst information processing.

title: A Good Cry or Gratifying Revenge? The Effects of Culture and Mixed Emotions on Choice
abstract: ABSTRACT Content marketers often employ mixed emotional appeals to engage viewers. Prior research suggests mixed emotions would appeal to collectivists, but not individualists. In contrast, the current research proposes that both individualists and collectivists choose content (e.g., in movies and comics) intended to signal mixed emotions, if the mixed emotions align with their cultural values. Building on established theoretical links between collectivism and self‐transcendence values, and individualism and self‐enhancement values, the authors find that collectivists (individualists) process affection‐sadness (pride‐anger) more fluently, and that this relative fluency is consistent with their choices. Data from 8 years of box office revenue (2015‐2022) and six experiments (including three in the Web Appendix), along with an internal meta‐analysis, are consistent with the hypotheses. Practically, the findings suggest that content platforms can increase recommendation effectiveness by personalizing emotional tags and images to match viewers' cultural orientations. The authors discuss implications for content personalization, consumer experience, and recommendation effectiveness.

title: When stability becomes a liability: the negative effects of supplier network stability on green innovation diversity and quality
abstract: Purpose Drawing on the network embeddedness perspective, this study aims to investigate how supplier network stability affects two distinct facets of green innovation – diversity and quality – and how these relationships are moderated by absorptive capacity. Design/methodology/approach The proposed relationships are tested using ordinary least squares regression based on a sample of 1,655 firm-year observations from 577 Chinese publicly listed firms over the period 2009–2023. To address potential endogeneity and selection bias, we conduct a series of analyses. Findings We find that supplier network stability is detrimental to both green innovation diversity and green innovation quality. Furthermore, absorptive capacity plays a differential moderating role, alleviating the detrimental influence of supplier network stability on green innovation quality while having no significant moderating effect on green innovation diversity. Originality/value By integrating the network embeddedness perspective with the green innovation literature, this study uncovers the unintended consequences of supplier network stability for green innovation diversity and quality and underscores the important role of absorptive capacity in mitigating these adverse effects.
journal_name: International Journal of Operations & Production Management

title: The Causes and Outcomes of Meaningful Work: An Integrative Model
abstract: Despite rapid growth, claims about the causes and outcomes of meaningful work remain diminished by reliance on correlational evidence. We review 70 longitudinal and experimental studies in which meaningful work is modeled as an antecedent, mediator, or outcome to evaluate what can be concluded about its causes and effects. Drawing exclusively on causally informative evidence, we develop an integrative model that advances prior frameworks and unifies leading perspectives, including the job characteristics model, self-determination theory, person-environment fit, and positive organizational scholarship. In doing so, we provide a rigorously grounded and integrative account of how meaningful work emerges and the outcomes it produces. Our hope is that this model provides a roadmap for future research and evidence-backed interventions to foster and prosper from meaningful work.
journal_name: Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior

title: Ambidexterity Across Levels and Over Time
abstract: Ambidexterity is a multilevel capacity for balancing competing imperatives such as adaptability and alignment. If left unmanaged, these imperatives create tensions that challenge performance and continued viability. The construct of ambidexterity has a long and varied history in the organizational literature, generating hundreds of articles, meta-analyses, and literature reviews. Findings regarding performance effects are mixed, and research has been plagued by fragmentation due to different levels of analysis and operationalizations, and samples derived from vastly different economic and industry environments. Many open issues remain, with critics arguing for greater conceptual clarity, multilevel frameworks, and more contemporary perspectives that account for an ever-changing organizational environment. Our review assesses progress in the field, integrating macro-, meso- and micro-level approaches to ambidexterity, providing particular attention to recent research on team- and individual-level applications of the concept. In doing so, we aim to expand our understanding of ambidexterity to include an embedded, contingent, episodic perspective.
journal_name: Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior

title: Functional Substitution and Particularized Trust: Governance Mechanisms in Hourglass Socio‐Economic Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Governance research shows that cooperation can persist despite dysfunctional state institutions, often through trust‐based mechanisms. This paper extends these debates by examining a complex collective action problem: the engagement of small‐ and medium‐sized enterprises (SMEs) in vocational education and training (VET) in post‐communist contexts. Drawing on the concept of “hourglass societies”, where trust concentrates among elites and local actors but is weak at the meso‐level, the paper argues that VET schools act as functional substitutes to meso‐level business associations by leveraging particularized trust and local networks. Evidence from Albania and Slovakia, based on 62 interviews and network analysis, demonstrates how face‐to‐face interaction, reciprocity, and localized knowledge enable SMEs to overcome prisoner's dilemma dynamics. These findings contribute to governance theory by showing how functional substitution and micro‐level trust structures sustain cooperation in fragmented socio‐economic systems, offering insights for designing policies for collective good provision such as education politics beyond Western contexts.

Elevation Amplifies Carrier-Type Differences in Nitrogen Cycling and N 2 O Dynamics in Lake Biofilms
abstract: Abstract Lake biofilms are microbial habitats for nitrogen transformation, but how carrier type and elevation influence N2O dynamics remains unclear. We examined abiotic- and biotic-carrier biofilms from 12 lakes spanning 4–4272 m using anoxic incubations, 15N tracing, selective inhibition, isotopocule analysis, and metagenomics. Net N2O emission potential increased with elevation in both carrier types, with the largest carrier contrast at high elevation, where biotic-carrier biofilms showed the highest net N2O emission potential. 15N partitioning showed a marked shift in emission sources. At low elevation, heterotrophic nitrification dominated abiotic-carrier biofilms (∼91%), whereas denitrification contributed ∼57% in biotic-carrier biofilms. At high elevation, denitrification accounted for 67–97% of net N2O emission across both carriers, and bacterial denitrification dominated the total denitrification rate potential. Metagenomic profiles provided mechanistic support: high-elevation biotic-carrier biofilms showed higher relative representation of genes for dissimilatory nitrate reduction to ammonium and nitrogen fixation, but had few nosZ-carrying genomes, indicating weak terminal N2O reduction capacity. Overall, carrier type and elevation jointly shape nitrogen transformation pathways. High-elevation lake ecosystems, particularly those with abundant biotic substrates, may harbor disproportionately important biofilm N2O hotspots under global change.

title: Neurodevelopmental Toxicity of Tris(2,4-di- tert -Butylphenyl)phosphate: Mechanistic Insights from Laboratory Models and Implications for Human Health
abstract: Abstract Organophosphite antioxidants (OPAs) and their transformation products, novel organophosphate esters (NOPEs), are ubiquitous environmental contaminants, yet their toxicological profiles remain poorly understood. This study systematically characterized the neurodevelopmental toxicity of these compounds and evaluated their associated environmental risks within the adverse outcome pathway framework. Molecular docking and radioligand binding assays identified integrin αvβ3 as a primary molecular target for all tested OPAs and NOPEs, with tris(2,4-di-tert-butylphenyl)phosphate (AO168═O) exhibiting high binding affinity. Exposure to AO168═O at environmentally relevant concentrations (≥50 μg/L) triggered significant behavioral deficits in zebrafish larvae, including reduced locomotion, altered exploratory preference, and irregular locomotor patterning. In vivo imaging and molecular analyses revealed that AO168═O induced motor neuron abnormalities and suppressed neurogenesis markers. Transcriptomic profiling elucidated that AO168═O disrupted MAPK and calcium signaling pathways via integrin αvβ3 targeting, driving the observed neurotoxicity. Crucially, the derived integrin αvβ3 binding threshold (0.7 μg/L) is comparable to reported environmental concentrations, providing a critical early warning for aquatic ecosystems. Furthermore, “Genes-to-Pathways” analysis demonstrated high conservation of this toxicological pathway between zebrafish and humans, highlighting a potential human health risk. These findings deliver strong evidence for the hazard assessment of AO168═O and offer valuable insights for managing other emerging NOPEs.

Optimal Time-Consistent Debt Policies
abstract: Abstract We study a dynamic trade-off model where shareholders can freely adjust debt but lack commitment to future debt policies. A debt policy is time-consistent if shareholders prefer it to deviating and losing credibility ex post. We characterize the optimal time-consistent policy in a class. It includes a stable regime, where shareholders actively manage liabilities to maintain the target interest coverage ratio, and a distress regime triggered by large negative shocks, where shareholders temporarily abandon the target. This policy has realistic properties and bridges the gap between the static trade-off theory of debt and theory based on the leverage ratchet effect. (JEL G32, C73)

title: The Coherence Side of Rationality Theory and Evidence from Firm Plans
abstract: Abstract Using the Duke Survey data on firms’ internal plans, we show that over 80% of Chief Financial Officer (CFO) forecasts align closely with simple heuristics taught in MBA textbooks. We introduce forecast coherence—internal consistency across forecasts of jointly determined variables—as a benchmark for evaluating these heuristics. Nearly half of CFOs issue forecasts closely aligned with incoherent heuristics. Such forecasts are associated with predictable reversals in forecast errors, lower firm performance, and underinvestment. We develop a parsimonious model illustrating how reliance on restricted forecasting heuristics can generate incoherence and resource misallocation within firms, consistent with our evidence (JEL D84, D22, L2, M2, G32)

Index Insurance and Food Security Among Smallholder Farmers in Southern Mali
abstract: ABSTRACT Climate extremes increasingly threaten food security in low‐ and middle‐income countries, where vulnerable smallholder farmers often lack access to risk mitigation tools. Although index‐based insurance has been promoted as a promising adaptation measure to climate shocks, evidence on its welfare effects, especially on food security, remains limited. This study addresses this gap by evaluating the relationship between index insurance ownership and food security among approximately 1300 smallholder maize farmers in southern Mali. Using self‐assessed food security measures and applying a rich set of different regression models to mitigate endogeneity concerns, we find that owning an index insurance product statistically significantly improves food security. Our results suggest that this effect operates primarily through reduced ex‐post consumption adjustments. The findings are particularly relevant for policymakers and development practitioners exploring scalable and climate‐resilient financial instruments for food security.

title: Announcements
Competing for commoditization or platforming for de-commoditization: The role of salient thinking
abstract: Consumer preferences are often context-dependent, with attention naturally drawn to a product’s most prominent attribute. Applying the behavioral framework of “salient thinking,” this paper examines how firms strategically design channel architecture to manipulate consumer focus. We reveal a fundamental asymmetry in the incentives for firms to transition from direct competitors to cooperative complementors. Under direct competition, markets often devolve into a “commoditized,” price-salient equilibrium. However, we demonstrate that relative product quality allows firms to escape this trap. When a lower-quality firm resells a premium competitor’s product, the resulting contrast shifts consumer focus from price to quality; this “de-commoditization” fosters a market environment that can overcome double marginalization, particularly when quality-production costs remain moderate. Crucially, this mechanism is structurally asymmetric: it fails if the high-quality firm acts as the reseller, as low-quality firms prefer price-salient competition. These insights provide a novel, cognition-driven rationale for why premium and budget brands selectively co-locate in modern retail ecosystems.

title: Willing to pay for security: A discrete choice experiment to analyse labour supply preferences
abstract: This paper investigates workers’ valuations of the job attributes that distinguish atypical work arrangements from traditional employee relationships. Using a vignette-based discrete-choice module fielded to samples of UK and US workers, I estimate willingness-to-pay distributions for contract security, work-related benefits, flexibility, autonomy, and tax treatment. Across both countries, workers place substantially higher value on job security and employment protections than on flexibility-related attributes. Interestingly, this pattern holds even among the self-employed: almost two-thirds of UK self-employed workers and just under half of US self-employed workers are estimated to prefer the traditional-employment bundle. Despite institutional differences between the UK and US, average valuations are closely aligned. The heterogeneity analysis shows that most observable characteristics account for only limited variation in preferences, but risk aversion and parenthood are notable exceptions, with both substantially increasing the value workers attach to contract security.

Bankruptcy Experience and Corporate Hedging
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether managers’ prior exposure to corporate bankruptcy shapes corporate risk‐management policies. Using detailed executive employment histories and hand‐collected derivative disclosures for a large sample of US public firms, we find that firms led by bankruptcy‐experienced (BE) CEOs are more likely to use cash‐flow hedges and hedge more intensively. Consistent with the “hot stove” hypothesis, exposure to an extreme left‐tail event appears to heighten managers’ sensitivity to downside risk. Several findings support an experience‐based interpretation over managerial sorting or fixed traits: The relation is stronger when the bankruptcy is more recent, when the manager served as CEO of the failed firm, when the failure occurred during a recession, and when career consequences were more severe. Hedging operates as a flexible risk‐management margin; the effect is stronger when managers do not reduce leverage or build cash reserves, suggesting substitution with balance‐sheet conservatism, but complements reductions in investment. The relation weakens under stronger board monitoring, and boards respond to BE CEO appointments by increasing risk‐taking incentives. Above‐predicted hedging is generally associated with higher firm value, but these benefits are significantly weaker when undertaken by BE CEOs; the incremental hedging also attenuates after anti‐recharacterization laws strengthen hedging incentives economy‐wide. At the same time, experience‐driven hedging predicts lower future distress risk and fewer credit downgrades, indicating a trade‐off between downside‐risk reduction and value maximization. The results are robust to firm fixed effects, CEO turnover analyses, matched samples, and controls for managerial characteristics.

title: “That great cosmic principle of becoming”: elucidating Ludwig von Mises’s multifaceted account of the origin, development and function of the division of labour
abstract: Ludwig von Mises propounded a social theory grounded in the division of labour. However, he used different language to describe the phenomenon that he regarded as constitutive of society: an “insight,” “principle,” “theory,” “law,” “discovery,” “disclosure” and even “that great principle of cosmic becoming.” The variability of this language creates a degree of ambiguity surrounding exactly how Mises conceived the development and function of the division of labour. This article seeks to elucidate Mises’s understanding of the division of labour as a social phenomenon and suggests several implications for contemporary social theory.
journal_name: The European Journal of the History of Economic Thought

title: Stability of multiple cartels in differentiated markets
abstract: Abstract We characterise stable market structures under price competition in differentiated markets when multiple cartels may form – this is a marked departure from the predominant assumption in the existing literature that supposes without further justification that at most one cartel may be formed. We find that market structures without cartelisation are never stable and, in stark contrast to the above-mentioned a priori assumption made in the literature, we establish that in markets that are sufficiently differentiated, whenever the formation of multiple cartels is possible (i.e. there are at least four firms in the market), at least one market structure involving multiple small cartels is stable. Furthermore, except for the case where there are only four firms in the market, stable market structures are exclusively characterised by multiple small cartels. Combined with the result that the unique stable market structure under quantity competition is also characterised by multiple small cartels, this underscores the importance of considering the possibility of multiple cartels in competition policy. Comparing stable market structures under price and quantity competition, we find that prices and profits are higher under price competition whenever the market is sufficiently differentiated or sufficiently concentrated.
