Intersectional Gender Representation in Corporate Social Media and Corresponding AI-Generated Images: Hallucinatory AI or Anamorphic AI in a House of Illusions?
abstract: Abstract This study examined how companies visually constructed intersectional gender representation in their social media posts and how Generative AI may reproduce or reshape these practices. Drawing on gender representation research in corporate communication, the Stereotype Content Model, and visual social semiotics, we analyzed 300 Instagram posts from the top 100 Fortune 500 B2C companies alongside 300 AI-generated images created to mirror them. Using mixed-methods visual social semiotic content analysis, we compared compositional, interactional, and representational meanings, positioning representation as distributive and recognitional justice. Findings indicated that corporate imagery often signaled performative inclusivity in compositional and interactional meanings, while reinforcing persistent hierarchies in representational meanings. In contrast, AI-generated imagery appeared anamorphic, sometimes reflecting dominant representational patterns and other times distorting or reversing them in ways that rendered identity markers ambiguous or exaggerated. These findings highlight ethical challenges in integrating AI into corporate communication and underscore the need for organizational reflexivity, transparency, and accountability in visual content creation. This study contributes to emerging scholarship on AI ethics and gender representation in corporate communication and offers practical guidance for managers seeking to ensure that the use of AI supports inclusivity and social justice.

title: Sensitivity of established driving simulator metrics to varying doses of alcohol during a brief motorway task
abstract: Driving simulators are valuable for investigating driving impairment since ethical and safety considerations limit the ability to conduct such research on roads. Although simulators have generally demonstrated relative validity, alcohol is often referred to as a reference for impairment due to well-established legal limits and its known effects on driving ability. However, there is a relative lack of large-sample studies that systematically assess the sensitivity of established driving performance metrics to alcohol-induced impairment, alongside the application of rigorous methodological approaches designed to minimise bias in estimating alcohol-related effects on driving performance. Therefore, this study employed a between-subjects alcohol dose–response experimental design using a driving simulator to assess the effects of alcohol on driving performance. Participants (N = 165, 77 females, mean age = 34.62 years) were randomly allocated to one of three single-blind conditions (range BAC: 0.020% − 0.085) and completed a short motorway driving task while wearing an eye tracker. A causal framework was employed to identify and adjust for potential confounders, and Bayesian modelling was used to estimate alcohol-related effects on driving performance and quantify uncertainty. The study showed first that simulator sickness is unlikely to bias driving performance estimates in driving simulator studies using alcohol. Then, the study assessed the sensitivity of established driving performance metrics as a result of alcohol. The largest effects were found on speed selection and lateral control while driving on a motorway, followed by reaction time during an emergency braking event and longitudinal control when following a vehicle. Limited changes in gaze patterns were found on this simple motorway drive. The findings of this study provide the basis for the development of models of impairment that are anchored on BAC levels, which is currently the sole impairment with widely accepted levels in the road safety domain.

title: Regulating Microplastics in Drinking Water: Treatment First, Measurement in Parallel
Impact of social violence on mining global value chains in Africa
abstract: This study examines how social violence, a major constraint to economic development in resource-rich African countries, shapes their participation in global value chains (GVCs) in the mining sector. Combining disaggregated indicators of forward, backward, and mixed mining GVC participation with conflict data from Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED) for 51 African countries over the period 1997–2022, we analyze how violence affects the structure of GVC integration. Findings show that social violence is associated with a reallocation toward down-stream, export-oriented participation, and adversely affects upstream and mixed forms of integration. These effects, however, are strongly conditional on structural factors. Attacks targeting transport infrastructure and inward foreign direct investment in violent contexts reinforce export-oriented integration, whereas greater reliance on renewable energy helps mitigate the adverse effects on segments requiring stable energy supply and coordination. Overall, the results indicate that higher GVC participation under violent conditions reflects constrained specialization rather than productive upgrading, underscoring the role of infrastructure security and energy resilience in fostering sustainable mining development in Africa.

Assessing urban carbon emissions from a water-energy-food nexus perspective: An intensity-structure-pressure framework for differentiated management in Chinese cities
abstract: The classic Kaya identity lacks integration of water-energy-food (WEF) nexus elements, and conventional geographical zoning fails to capture the structural heterogeneity of urban carbon emissions. To address these gaps, this study extends the Kaya identity to construct an intensity–structure–pressure chain decomposition equation covering the energy-economy-agriculture-land-water system. A three-stage analytical framework, macro-driving decomposition, structure type identification, and conditional associations analysis, is then applied. Using city-level panel data from China (2000−2020) and integrating Logarithmic Mean Divisia Index (LMDI) decomposition, Partitioning Around Medoids (PAM) clustering, and panel quantile regression, the study decomposes the structural factors of carbon emissions, identifies city clusters with homogeneous resource structures, and reveals heterogeneous factor associations across emission levels. The results indicate that: (1) Economic growth emerges as the dominant positive factor in carbon emission growth, with its decomposed proportion exhibiting significant north–south regional divergence; (2) cities can be classified into six distinct structural typologies in terms of resource use and emissions, high-emission clusters are typically constrained by a dilemma of improving efficiency while still expanding in scale, whereas low-carbon clusters have systematically entered a phase of decoupling economic growth from carbon emissions; and (3) regression analysis further suggests that the direction and magnitude of the conditional association of the same decomposition factor differ significantly between low- and high-carbon cities, with the marginal association of most factors diminishing as emission levels increase. This study provides a basis for transcending the limitations of geographical proximity and establishing intensity-structure-pressure-oriented, precise, and differentiated carbon management strategies.

title: Pathways to premium: How habits and benefits shape conversion and retention in freemium subscription models
abstract: Abstract Numerous digital services rely on freemium models, yet the mechanisms that move users from free usage to premium subscriptions remain poorly understood. This research examines how expected benefits of premium access, experienced benefits during trials, and habit development in free and premium contexts jointly shape conversion and retention. Across four empirical field studies in a freemium subscription setting, we show that habits in the free version are double‑edged: they can increase conversion by reinforcing expected benefits of the premium version, yet also anchor users in continued free usage through inertia. Habits formed while using the premium version, together with experienced premium benefits, generally support paid conversion and long‑term retention. In discounted trial settings, we further identify an inverse‑U‑shaped relationship between premium‑side habits and retention, with very strong habits associated with lower retention than moderate levels. These insights inform the design of effective freemium and trial strategies.

title: Explaining Uneven and Reversible Gender Equality Outcomes: A Relational Open‐Systems Perspective on Gender Diversity and Inclusion in Multinational Corporations
abstract: ABSTRACT Multinational corporations (MNCs) increasingly adopt common gender diversity and inclusion (GDI) policies, yet gender equality outcomes continue to diverge across subsidiaries and may stall or reverse as institutional and political conditions change. Existing human resource management (HRM) research offers important accounts of policy design, transfer, performance rationales, and individual experience, but provides less integrated explanation of how cross‐border institutional pressures are translated into organizational rules that allocate opportunity, recognition, mobility, protection, and status. We develop a relational open‐systems perspective on GDI in MNCs. Open systems theory provides the architecture for conceptualizing GDI as embedded, interdependent, and feedback‐driven, while relational inequality theory specifies how categorization, social closure, and relational claims‐making shape resource allocation within that system. Intersectionality operates as a cross‐cutting logic that conditions actors' positions, power, and claim legitimacy across institutional and organizational settings. The resulting framework explains how formally similar GDI arrangements can generate substantive inclusion, selective advancement, symbolic maintenance, persistent exclusion, or retrenchment across subsidiaries. The paper contributes by linking the evolution and adaptation of multinational HRM systems to the concrete organizational relations through which differentiated gender equality outcomes are produced and revised over time.

title: Board Cultural Diversity and Corporate Sustainability Performance: Evidence From Hospitality and Tourism Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines whether board cultural diversity is associated with corporate sustainability performance (CSP) in the hospitality and tourism sector. Drawing on upper echelons theory and resource dependence theory, the analysis uses LSEG ESG data for 282 publicly listed firms across 49 countries, covering 1406 firm‐year observations from 2018 to 2023. The results show that board cultural diversity, board gender diversity, board independence, and sustainability committee presence are positively associated with CSP. By contrast, CEO duality and board size are negatively associated with sustainability performance. Additional analyses using lagged specifications, firm fixed effects, country‐group regressions, region‐year fixed effects and environmental and social pillar scores provide further evidence of the stability of the reported associations. The paper contributes to sustainability governance research by showing that board cultural diversity remains relevant when examined alongside established governance characteristics. The findings also offer sector‐specific evidence from hospitality and tourism, where sustainability performance is closely linked to stakeholder relationships, reputation and board‐level oversight.

title: Theories and Theoretical Approaches in Double Materiality Research: A Systematic Literature Review
abstract: ABSTRACT Double materiality has rapidly emerged as a central construct in sustainability reporting under the EU Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), yet the literature remains theoretically fragmented and descriptive. This study maps its theoretical foundations through a PRISMA‐guided systematic review combining qualitative content analysis and bibliometric mapping of 77 English‐language, peer‐reviewed journal articles published between 2019 and 7 July 2026 and retrieved from Scopus and Web of Science. Findings show that 51.9% of articles are theory‐based; Stakeholder, Institutional, and Legitimacy theories account for 60.2% of all theoretical occurrences. Theory Application represents 85.0% of theory‐based studies, whereas Extension, Refinement, and Building remain limited. The literature is heavily concentrated in Europe. The study identifies theoretical concentration, application dominance, and geographic parochialism as key vulnerabilities and proposes a research agenda examining when double materiality may move beyond regulatory compliance toward substantive organizational transformation and strategic value creation.

title: Industry 4.0 Capabilities and Sustainable Supply Chain Resilience: The Sequential Roles of Sustainability‐Oriented Dynamic Capabilities and Circular Supply Chain Practices
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how Industry 4.0 capabilities contribute to sustainability‐oriented dynamic capabilities, facilitate circular and reverse supply chain practices, and jointly produce sustainable supply chain resilience. Addressing the persistent reference fragmentation across digitalization, sustainability, circular economy, and resilience research, the study develops and empirically validates a sequential capability architecture grounded in the dynamic capabilities view (DCV) and an emerging circular intelligence perspective. Using survey data from 2503 supply chain professionals across 500 US manufacturing firms, covariance‐based structural equation modeling confirms the higher‐order structure of Industry 4.0 capabilities, sustainability‐oriented dynamic capabilities, reverse supply chain, and sustainable supply chain resilience, and tests the direct, mediating, and serial mediating relationships. Results show that I4C significantly enhances sustainability‐oriented dynamic capabilities and reverse supply chain. Sustainability‐oriented dynamic capabilities further enable circular practices and resilience, and the reverse supply chain is the dominant driver of sustainable resilience. Mediation and serial mediation analyses reveal that digital capabilities translate into resilience only when routed through sustainability‐oriented interpretation and regenerative circular operations. This study provides initial empirical support for an integrated digital, sustainability, and circular capability pathway. The study advances DCV by demonstrating how digital sensing evolves into higher‐order sustainability cognition and extends circular‐economy logic through a circular‐intelligence perspective, identifying the circular mechanisms through which sustainability capabilities produce resilient outcomes. Managerially, the findings underscore that digitalization must be coupled with sustainability learning and circular system design for firms to achieve resilience that is environmentally regenerative and operationally robust.

title: Green Taxes, Greener Firms? Institutional Influences on Corporate Environmental Responses
abstract: ABSTRACT Existing literature has paid limited attention to whether higher environmental taxation, measured as environmental tax revenue intensity, is associated with greater corporate environmental sustainability and whether the quality of national governance complements or substitutes for environmental taxation in shaping firms' environmental sustainability outcomes. To address this, we utilize a global sample of publicly listed companies covering the period from 2002 to 2020 and a sample of 51,407 firm‐year observations from 7360 companies across 48 countries. We find that environmental taxation per se is not sufficient in stimulating firms for greater environmental sustainability. It needs to be supported by national governance mechanisms such as control of corruption, government effectiveness, rule of law, absence of violence and political instability, regulatory quality, and voice and accountability. However, environmental innovation outcome is contingent upon the innovative eco‐system and financial market development of the country. Furthermore, we find that environmental tax is likely to be translated into improved environmental score in developed countries and countries with common law systems. Overall, study findings support the argument that broader institutional development is important in contributing to firm‐level resource use, emissions, and eco‐innovation outcomes.

title: Who Benefits From Compressed Workweeks? The Role of Job Autonomy and Task Interdependence in Shaping Longitudinal Changes
abstract: ABSTRACT Compressed workweeks (CWW)—compressing the regular 5‐day workweek into fewer workdays—are gaining global popularity as an alternative work arrangement for jobs that are not suitable for remote work. Yet research on CWW has stagnated over the last decade, leaving us with little evidence and knowledge about whether and under which conditions CWW brings about positive changes over time. To revitalize research on CWW and provide insights for theory advancement and effective practices, longitudinal data were collected over 6 months ( N = 147), both before and after implementation of CWW. Using conservation of resources (COR) theory, the work redesign literature, and growth curve modeling, this research reveals theoretically and practically meaningful patterns of change in employees' outcomes after CWW implementation. Specifically, significant decreases in stress and increases in health were observed among employees with greater job autonomy but not among those with lower job autonomy. Interestingly, for employees with lower job autonomy, perceived organizational support decreased over time; the same was not true for those with higher autonomy. Moreover, task performance increased for employees with less interdependent tasks, but not for those performing highly interdependent tasks. Therefore, organizations should carefully consider important job characteristics when designing and implementing CWW.

Propaganda, Administrative Deformation, and the Erosion of State Capacity: The Case of the “Censorship Industrial Complex”
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines how a propaganda frame alleging the existence of a “Censorship Industrial Complex” was institutionalized and then helped justify the dismantling of US election information resilience infrastructure across multiple federal agencies. Drawing on documentary evidence and process tracing, we show how political entrepreneurs reframed routine, non‐coercive election information coordination and communication practices as a covert censorship regime targeting conservative speech. The article argues that this case is best understood as administrative deformation: weakly evidenced claims were laundered into higher‐status venues, including congressional investigations, litigation, executive action, and budget rationales, where they altered the incentive environment facing public agencies. The result was staff reductions, program cuts, and chilling effects, and weakened state capacity in a core domain of democratic administration. We conclude with recommendations for protecting administrative resilience under conditions of narrative attack.

abstract: ABSTRACT Forests are carbon storage that can reduce carbon emissions, so deforestation (decrease in forest area) is a serious threat to environmental sustainability. Indonesia is a large carbon sink due to its large forests. However, deforestation is quite high due to economic activities that use fossil energy. In contrast to previous studies, this study uses deforestation per capita as a variable explained. The aim is to investigate the causes of deforestation in relation to economic variables with a focus on energy issues. Based on the EKC conceptual framework, control variables in the form of economic variables GRDP per capita and its square and technology in the form of proportion of internet usage. This study focuses on energy use, consisting of gas, electricity production, electricity consumption and fuel wood/charcoal/briquettes for cooking. The method is a longitudinal approach based on regional data for 8 years. The model used is dynamic panel data, which accommodates adjustments in deforestation per capita that are influenced by long‐term behavior and explores the diversity of data in the region. This study shows that the energy option that can reduce deforestation is currently gas. Indonesia has not yet reached the top of the Kuznet curve so the economy has not been able to improve environmental sustainability. The production and use of electrical energy in Indonesia is still not environmentally friendly and thus urgently requires investment in renewable energy and new technologies. In addition, the replacement of industrial machinery and household electrical appliances requires new technology to be more efficient.

abstract: Abstract Although much of the persistence literature has dealt with extractive colonial institutions, no study directly examines the persistent effects of the transition from pure subsistence to market economies as a result of such institutions. This article fills that gap by investigating the paddy commutation system of British Ceylon, which taxed native farmers in cash on the potential yield of their paddy lands. On the basis of a novel dataset on nineteenth‐century Ceylon and a two‐pronged identification strategy of neighbouring unit analysis and propensity score matching, I find that historical exposure to the paddy commutation system predicts higher wealth today. Advanced agricultural markets, higher land ownership, and an ethos of economic independence resulting from the commutation system appear to be the primary mechanisms driving these more favourable wealth outcomes.

abstract: Abstract Catastrophe‐exposed P&C insurance markets increasingly confront low‐frequency but high‐severity losses. When such risks interact with costly external financing, insurance pricing depends not only on expected losses but also on insurers' balance‐sheet conditions and capacity constraints. In this paper, we develop a dynamic competitive equilibrium framework of insurance capacity and pricing under jump‐diffusion risk and model uncertainty. We show that catastrophe jumps introduce a liability‐side gamble‐for‐resurrection mechanism through the interaction of limited liability and recapitalization options, which can generate non‐monotonic and non‐smooth pricing patterns under certain conditions. Robustness concerns raise equilibrium prices and capital buffers while attenuating excessive risk‐taking incentives. Using a market‐disciplined calibration, we show that jump risk generates substantial pricing effects beyond expected losses alone and shapes the duration of endogenous underwriting cycles.

abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines whether Toxic Secrecy Bans, state laws restricting overly broad non‐disclosure agreements, affect stock price crash risk. Exploiting the staggered adoption of these bans across US states as a quasi‐natural experiment, we find that Toxic Secrecy Bans significantly reduce crash risk. Consistent with an employee‐voice mechanism, EEOC complaints and negative workplace disclosures increase following adoption. Effects are stronger among firms with lower employee satisfaction, weaker ethical cultures, and greater ownership monitoring, but weaker in high‐unemployment environments. The bans also improve firms' governance, social, and community performance. Overall, Toxic Secrecy Bans enhance transparency and constrain managerial bad‐news hoarding.

title: Environmental Impact Shaping a Firm's Zero Leverage Decision: Analysing Debt Demand and Supply Determinants
abstract: ABSTRACT Zero‐leverage firms remain a puzzle in corporate finance. We propose a supply‐side mechanism linking environmental impact to debt access. Because creditors favour firms with high negative externalities and strong cash flows, environmentally friendly firms with high initial costs face tighter credit constraints. Using a theoretical model and a bivariate probit on 1113 firms across 54 countries (2011–2024), we show that positive environmental impact significantly reduces debt availability. The effect varies with firm development, industry environmental sensitivity, environmental regulation and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) performance. The findings highlight the importance of jointly estimating debt demand and supply.

title: Repeat SPAC Sponsors
abstract: ABSTRACT Sponsors are the key value‐generating resource for special purpose acquisition companies (SPACs). We identify a subgroup of sponsors—repeat sponsors—who have formed and managed multiple SPACs. Repeat sponsors identify target companies faster, and their SPACs merge with private companies of higher quality. However, these benefits are attenuated when sponsors manage multiple SPACs simultaneously, suggesting that overlapping commitments create conflicts of interest and dilute sponsor attention. Overall, our findings highlight a tradeoff between the benefits of sponsor expertise and experience, and the costs associated with concurrent sponsorship.

title: Conflicts of interest, ethical standards, and competition in legal services†
abstract: Abstract We study how the legal profession manages representational conflicts of interest. These conflicts arise when a single law firm represents clients with opposing interests, threatening to undermine the legal process and, ultimately, social welfare. We argue that current ethical standards, emphasizing disqualification, may actually worsen the clients’ situation. Instead, the clients’ interests are today mainly safeguarded by law firms being small, reducing the incidence of conflicts. Despite low market concentration, law firms enjoy high earnings as representational conflicts create negative network externalities at the firm level. These profits are sustained in the long run as entry occurs through firm split-ups.
journal_name: The Journal of Law, Economics, and Organization

title: When Technology Meets Inequality: The Persistent Effects of Distance Education on Gender Gaps in Rural China
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the persistent effects of China's Modern Distance Education Program (MDEP), a large‐scale educational technology initiative that provided access to high‐quality instruction for over 100 million rural primary and junior high school students. Utilising two nationally representative surveys and employing a cohort‐based triple‐difference (DDD) identification strategy, we demonstrate that MDEP significantly narrowed the gender gap in educational attainment. The programme's effects exhibit a cumulative pattern, intensifying with greater exposure duration and investment intensity. We further find that MDEP facilitated gender‐equitable access to public educational resources and weakened son‐preference distortions in household educational investment, thereby improving educational outcomes for rural girls. These educational gains also translated into persistent reductions in gender disparities in labour market outcomes, with MDEP‐exposed rural women experiencing greater improvements in formal employment, digitally intensive occupations and wages than comparable men.
journal_name: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

title: Assessing the Heterogeneous Impact of Economy‐Wide Shocks: A Causal Machine Learning Approach Applied to Colombian Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT Our paper presents a causal machine learning (ML) methodology to study the heterogeneous effects of economy‐wide shocks and applies it to the impact of the COVID‐19 crisis on exports. This method is applicable in scenarios where, due to the pervasive nature of the shock, it is difficult to identify a control group that is not affected by the shock and to determine ex ante differences in shock intensity across units. In particular, our study investigates the effectiveness of different ML techniques in predicting firms' trade and, by building on recent developments in causal ML, these predictions are used to reconstruct the counterfactual distribution of firms' trade under different COVID‐19 scenarios and investigate the heterogeneity of treatment effects. Specifically, we focus on the probability of Colombian firms surviving in the export market under two different scenarios: a COVID‐19 setting and a non‐COVID‐19 counterfactual situation. On average, we find that the COVID‐19 shock decreased a firm's probability of surviving in the export market by about 20 percentage points in April 2020. We study the treatment effect heterogeneity by employing a classification analysis that compares the characteristics of the firms on the tails of the estimated distribution of the individual treatment effects.
journal_name: Oxford Bulletin of Economics and Statistics

title: Small banks really are different: Unexpected deposit flows, loan production, and off-balance-sheet funding liquidity risk
From liability to asset: How campaign context determines whether body weight helps or hurts online fundraisers
journal_name: Journal of the Academy of Marketing Science

title: Cross-border cooperation among securities regulators and supply chain collaboration: evidence from U.S.-listed foreign firms
Temporal grammars of novelty: How carbon removal entrepreneurs frame new technologies
abstract: Abstract Research Summary This paper assesses the ways in which carbon dioxide removal ventures frame their work. Drawing on George Herbert Mead's philosophy of the present, it conceptualizes temporal grammars of novelty as a framing strategy that involves connecting two points in time, namely present and future, to elaborate novelty. Dictionary, dependency parsing, and large language model approaches trace the use of temporal grammars of novelty across the websites of carbon removal companies in the market, and connect this to venture sales volumes. Analyses show that ventures deploying newer technologies and using temporal grammars of novelty have higher sales. In contrast, explicitly causal language does not prove beneficial. This paper addresses a fundamental problem in conceptualizing novelty by arguing that it is referential without being causal, and shows this with reference to the framing strategies deployed by environmental entrepreneurs. Managerial Summary Carbon removal entrepreneurs must convince buyers that novel, often unproven technologies are credible. This paper shows that how they talk about time matters. Analyzing website language and sales across carbon removal ventures, it finds that firms using more speculative technologies sell more when they link present action to future possibility: what they are designing, building, or deploying now, and what this will make possible later, at scale. By contrast, causal language—detailed claims about why or how specific features will produce outcomes—is not helpful and is negatively associated with sales. When framing novelty, pairing present action with future promise is more credible than over‐specified causal certainty.

title: When Is It Fairer to Allocate Resources for Training to Lower Performing Versus Higher Performing Employees?
abstract: ABSTRACT Professional development and training are essential for organizational growth and success, but resource constraints often force managers into a dilemma: Should they train their lower performing or higher performing employees? While lower performers with greater skill gaps can benefit more from training than higher performers, managers must also consider employees’ fairness concerns. Using an interactive experiment, we predict and find that how employees react to their manager's allocation of training resources depends on the prevailing fairness norms in the work environment. When egalitarian norms dominate, such as when employees have little control over their job tasks, lower performers take the receipt of resources for training for granted and react negatively when the manager allocates those resources to higher performers instead. In contrast, when meritocratic norms dominate, such as when employees have more control over their job tasks, higher performers react more negatively than lower performers to not receiving training resources. Additional experiments suggest that these fairness‐norm–dependent reactions are most pronounced under tournament incentives and may disappear under individual performance‐based pay. Overall, our study highlights the importance for managers to consider both employee productivity and the prevailing fairness norms of the work environment when allocating scarce training resources.

title: Auditor-Employed Tax Experts and Audit Quality
Financial Statement Audits of Private Firms and IRS Enforcement Outcomes
Communicating Corporate Culture in Labor Markets: Evidence from Job Postings
abstract: We examine how culture information in job postings influences firms’ hiring outcomes. We utilize machine learning methods to measure five core values present in job postings and demonstrate that culture information helps attract job seekers, as it is associated with higher worker inflows. The effect strengthens when job seekers value culture in their job searches and face frictions in learning about culture from other sources. Additional analyses indicate that individual cultural dimensions in job postings are more salient to job seekers when they have heightened preferences for that particular value. Finally, culture information is associated with a higher likelihood that interviews result in offers, and greater acceptance of those offers. Overall, our results suggest that culture information in job postings helps job seekers sort into culturally aligned firms. This paper was accepted by Ranjani Krishnan, accounting. Conflict of Interest Statement: The authors declare that they have no relevant or material financial interests that relate to the research described in this paper. Funding: A. H. Huang acknowledges financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72172079]. Supplemental Material: The data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.07272 .

title: Motivated Procrastination
abstract: This study provides a rigorous empirical test for motivated memory as a cause for procrastination. In a longitudinal experiment over four weeks, individuals had to complete a cumbersome task of unknown length and receive noisy signals about their assigned workload. Varying scope for motivated memory results in more optimistic beliefs among workers who receive negative signals but not among those who receive positive ones. This suppression of negative news through motivated memory causes individuals to defer more work to the future. This paper was accepted by Marie Claire Villeval, behavioral economics and decision analysis. Funding: Financial support from the Deutsche Forschungsgemeinschaft [Grant CRC TRR 190 (project number 280092119)] is gratefully acknowledged. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.05353 .

title: Partitioning menus to nudge single-item choice
abstract: Decision makers are often called on to choose a single item from a menu of options: employees pick health plans from provider-sponsored lists, citizens vote for a representative among candidates, physicians select a treatment from an order set. Because options are often organized or grouped into subsets, the question arises whether the grouping of menu items affects the options ultimately selected by decision makers. Across ten experiments, we provide robust evidence of single-item partition dependence — decision makers are more likely to choose from response categories that are more finely partitioned, holding the underlying set of options constant. For example, an employee choosing a health plan from a menu that lists HMOs individually but groups PPOs into a single category with sub-options may be biased toward choosing an HMO. Unlike prior work on multi-item allocation decisions, the traditional explanation of partition dependence — a bias toward even allocation — cannot apply to single-item choice, because singular choices are not divisible. Instead, we find that finer partitions receive greater choice share because decision makers infer that separately listed options are more popular on average than grouped ones. More broadly, strategic partitioning of the menu space may serve as a simple and effective tool for managers, policymakers, and choice architects: listing options separately rather than grouping them together tends to increase their choice share, without fundamentally altering the underlying set of alternatives or the effort required to choose among them.
journal_name: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes

title: Research relevance in management and organization: A problematizing review, critique and proposal for moving forward
abstract: Abstract The relevance of scholarly research is a core concern for many scholars in the field of organizations and management, leading to an ever‐growing body of literature on the topic. However, discussions, regarding the challenges of attaining relevance and the proposed solutions, tend to be repetitive and reflect little progress. To advance this discussion, this article is organized into three parts. First, through a problematizing review, we identify the use of the theory‐practice gap as an overarching frame that drives the dominant discussions in the research relevance literature. Using that identification as a starting point, we organize the currently fragmented literature. Next, we delve deeper into three problematic assumptions that stem from using the theory‐practice gap as a framing device and offer a detailed critique. Finally, drawing on our review and critique and on insights from related literature beyond research relevance, we propose three alternative conceptualizations of relevance that aim to address these shortcomings. We provide a path for future research by suggesting that research relevance can be reconceptualized as practical utility, as a cyclical process, and as etched in organizational processes, and highlight how these reconceptualizations can be put into practice.

title: Forcing Transformation or Spawning Disguise? The U‐Shaped Response Mechanism of Corporate Greenwashing Triggered by Rising Temperatures
abstract: ABSTRACT Climate change inevitably shapes corporate environmental behavior, yet whether it fosters genuine green transformation or merely encourages greenwashing remains controversial. This study integrates data from listed companies and urban temperature records spanning 2009–2023 to investigate the relationship between rising temperatures and corporate greenwashing. The findings reveal as follows: (1) Rising temperatures exhibit a positive U‐shaped relationship with corporate greenwashing, and this pattern also holds for carbon greenwashing. (2) In companies with a lack of political embeddedness, severe financial constraints, and low public attention, rising temperatures are more likely to trigger greenwashing. (3) The positive effect of rising temperatures on green innovation is observed only in companies without prior greenwashing experience. These findings not only help explain the discrepancies in existing research on the impact of climate change on corporate environmental performance but also provide evidence for governments to formulate dynamic regulatory strategies to curb greenwashing under rising temperatures.

title: Hospitality and tourism industry as a primary beneficiary of artificial intelligence: A conditional optimistic scenario
abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has become a disruptive force reshaping the entire economy through automation, productivity gains, and changing labor dynamics. Under supportive labor policies, AI may drive substantial productivity gains across many sectors and generate a “leisure dividend” through increased leisure time and disposable income, driving greater demand for experience-based services central to the hospitality and tourism (HT) industry. This study develops a conditional optimistic scenario in which the HT industry may emerge as a primary beneficiary of this AI-driven shift, with AI serving not as a threat but as a conditional catalyst for the industry’s growth and the elevation of human roles. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory and the experience economy framework, a conceptual framework is proposed wherein, under certain conditions, AI may generate a positive cyclical relationship among AI-integration, HT industry expansion, employee wellbeing, and guest satisfaction. The implications of AI-driven transformation in the HT industry are discussed.

title: Practicing More of What We Profess: Turning Our Sustainability Impact Lens Inward
abstract: Universities face seemingly intractable challenges in achieving major long-term sustainability goals, despite their impressive capabilities in research and teaching. We propose concrete ways universities and, in particular, business schools, their faculty and staff, and their administrations can leverage the very challenges that plague progress by building on momentum in untapped structural and communication opportunities, existing work of insider change agents, and the psychology and practicality of small wins.

title: Transformative international marketing: an integrative review and a recursive framework of cross-border transformation
abstract: Purpose Why should transformative marketing be assumed to operate in the same way when it crosses national market boundaries? Existing research treats internationality as context rather than as a condition that shapes the meaning, legitimacy and consequences of transformation. This review addresses that gap by conceptualizing Transformative International Marketing (TIM) and developing a recursive framework that explains how cross-market discontinuities and interdependence condition the reconfiguration of international marketing and how those reconfigurations in turn transform stakeholders and market systems. Design/methodology/approach The study employs a systematic literature review to examine the knowledge structure and development of TIM research. The review applies the Theory–Characteristics–Context–Methodology and planning, operationalizing, writing, embedding, and reflecting (POWER) frameworks to 129 studies published between 1994 and 2025 in Scopus and Web of Science. The corpus was subsequently examined through theoretical foundations, substantive characteristics, geographic and international contexts, and methodological patterns. Findings The study reveals that transformative marketing has been theorized largely as a marketing phenomenon, overlooking how heterogeneous and interconnected markets alter transformation itself. It distinguishes whether change is transformative through depth, scope, durability and consequentiality, from how transformation unfolds through directionality, valence and normative contestation. It separates transformation of international marketing from transformation through it and specifies the boundary conditions under which TIM offers distinct explanatory value. Originality/value The study’s originality lies in repositioning internationality from a contextual backdrop to a constitutive element of transformative marketing theory. Rather than extending transformative marketing through additional firm- or stakeholder-level variables, it establishes TIM as a distinct and deliberately bounded domain of international marketing inquiry. The review also moves beyond importing general theories into international settings by integrating transformative marketing with international marketing mechanisms and market-system perspectives. In doing so, it provides a theoretically coherent foundation for studying transformative change under cross-market heterogeneity, interdependence, contested legitimacy and global-local tensions.

title: Turning psychic distance upside down: a dynamic, adaptive and manager-centered reconceptualization
abstract: Purpose This article reconceptualizes psychic distance (PD) from managers' perspectives as a dynamic and adaptive sense-making process. Dynamic refers to the interactive nature of PD interpretations, while adaptive emphasizes the in-the-making quality of PD assessment as it is continually recalibrated through ongoing interactions and learning. Design/methodology/approach The article employs a multi-step methodology to develop the conceptual framework, synthesizing insights from international marketing, management, psychology, and sociology literature. Findings Managers assess PD across three cognitive domains, psychological (business self), role-based (business habitus), and cultural (organizational values and priorities), which are affected by history and religion, market environment, and social structure. PD is further influenced by mental frames, behavioral observations and mindsets, evolving adaptively through perspective taking, strategic interactions, and learning. Research limitations/implications The new conceptual framework requires empirical validation across diverse cultural and institutional contexts. Practical implications Rather than treating PD as a constraint, businesses can use it as a strategic tool to navigate international marketing decisions. Originality/value This article represents a paradigm shift in conceptualizing PD, from a static, macro-level view to a dynamic, interpretive perception rooted in managerial experience.

title: Digital Transformation and Green Total Factor Productivity in China
abstract: ABSTRACT Achieving sustainable development relies on the continuous improvement of green total factor productivity (GTFP). Although existing studies have documented a positive association between digital transformation and GTFP through technological innovation, the underlying mechanism remains insufficiently understood because technological innovation is often treated as an aggregate channel. Such aggregate treatments are ineffective in clarifying the underlying mechanisms of action within it and carrying out targeted policy. In this paper, we open this black box by dividing the technology innovation caused by digitization into indigenous R&D efficiency improvement and technology spillovers increase. Through a dataset covering China's A‐share listed enterprises over the period 2012–2021, together with the Global Malmquist‐Luenberger index based on a super‐efficiency Slacks‐Based Measure model and econometric analysis, we show that digitization significantly enhances GTFP. More importantly, the increases in both indigenous R&D efficiency and technology spillovers coming from digital transformation are two important channels to promote GTFP. Our study offers insights for emerging economies aiming to achieve green growth through digital reforms.

title: Performance gift-giving and incentive systems: Conditions and effects of peer helping in a sales team
abstract: This paper presents a case study of a sales team in which members who had reached their individual performance targets helped their peers achieve theirs by gifting surplus performance. At first glance, this form of peer helping may resemble collusion and appear dysfunctional for the organisation, as it alters the attribution of individual performance and increases bonus payments within the team. However, we show that the practice also generates positive effects for both the functioning of the incentive system and team dynamics. This study contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it extends research on helping behaviour by identifying and analysing a distinctive form of peer helping—performance gift-giving—which, to our knowledge, has not previously been examined in organisational research. Second, it contributes to the management accounting literature on performance target setting by demonstrating that risk adjustments, typically addressed through formal managerial processes, may also be addressed through informal peer helping, such as performance gift-giving. Third, it contributes to research on teams in management accounting. Whereas prior work in this field has examined how the transparency produced by individual performance information versus team-based performance information influences team cooperation, our study demonstrates how the transferability of individual performance information among team members through peer helping shapes cooperation.

title: CEO political organizational experience and firm productivity
abstract: Purpose Drawing on upper echelons and imprinting theories, we examine whether chief executive officers’ (CEOs') political organizational experience is associated with firms' subsequent total factor productivity (TFP). Design/methodology/approach We conduct panel data analyses to examine the relationship between CEOs' military and political backgrounds and subsequent firm-level TFP. Using a sample of Chinese listed firms from 2004 to 2021, we distinguish Communist Party of China (CPC) or Communist Youth League of China (CYLC) committee experience from military experience and CPC school training. Findings CEOs with substantive CPC/CYLC committee experience are associated with higher subsequent TFP in SOEs, whereas military experience and CPC school training are not significantly associated with TFP. The association is also evident among firms with internal CPC organizations across ownership types. Reductions in agency costs and inefficient investment are potential mechanisms through which CPC/CYLC committee experience is associated with higher productivity in state-owned enterprises (SOEs). These findings underscore the importance of distinguishing substantive CPC/CYLC organizational experience from broader forms of political or military exposure, highlighting how political embeddedness within institutions and governance structures is associated with executive behavior and firm productivity. Originality/value This study contributes to the literature by showing the importance of distinguishing substantive CPC/CYLC organizational experience from broader forms of political or military exposure. It highlights how political embeddedness within institutions and governance structures is associated with executive behavior and firm productivity.

title: Childhood scars as a path to conformity: How CEOs’ childhood disaster experiences shape strategic distinctiveness
EXPRESS: High on Coopetition? How Collective Categories Cognitively Order Cooperation and Competition
abstract: Some organizational collectives are composed of firms that cooperate to advance collective goals while competing to pursue their own interests. Yet less is known about how such collectives navigate cooperation and competition across the practices through which collective coopetition is enacted. We argue that collective coopetition is organized through members’ categorization of practices. We examine this process during the early emergence of the U.S. recreational cannabis industry (2012–2017), where firms faced simultaneous pressures to support legalization and industry development while pursuing firm-level growth. Using Cultural Consensus Modeling, we examine how industry participants categorized 32 practices as cooperative and/or competitive and how these categorizations were associated with practice prevalence. Our findings show that collective categories enable, clarify, and constrain practice prevalence. Highly prevalent practices included professionalizing forms of competition and collective-oriented practices related to education, standards, and industry participation. Our study shows how collective categories cognitively order cooperation and competition across diverse practices.

title: EXPRESS: The Diversity Paradox: Why Board Gender Diversity Succeeds in Some Firms and Fails in Others
abstract: Why do studies on board gender diversity (BGD) and firm performance reach opposite conclusions? We argue this reflects a genuine empirical regularity: the BGD–performance relationship is not a single stable coefficient but a distribution of firm-specific associations varying substantially in magnitude and direction. Analyzing a large panel of publicly listed, non-financial firms in China, India, Japan, and Singapore over nearly two decades, we apply variance decomposition with random slopes modeling to quantify this variation. Firm-specific factors account for far more variation in performance than country or industry factors. Modeling the relationship as varying across firms reveals significant heterogeneity: it ranges from meaningfully negative in some firms to meaningfully positive in others, robust across alternative measures, specifications, and sub-periods. These findings offer a methodological explanation for decades of contradictory results and identify firm-specific factors rather than national institutions or industry context as the primary locus where the relationship varies.

title: Reflexive governance and the co-creation of socio-economic value: how macro-social marketing drives citizen-centric smart cities
abstract: Purpose Partnerships are viewed as important in social marketing for addressing wicked socio-economic problems. However, research is required to understand partnerships in macro-social marketing for complex exchange. And to uncover how socio-economic value is co-created as a process through this exchange. This study aims to explore reflexive governance as a systemic partnership platform for macro-social marketing in smart cities. It also identifies and breaks down the process of socio-economic value co-creation realised and determined by citizens. Design/methodology/approach An exploratory case study approach involved Belfast and Bristol as two UK cases at distinct stages of smart city development. Semi-structured in-depth interviews were conducted with key stakeholders from both cities alongside secondary data collection. With a structured thematic analysis approach to analyse the data collected. Findings Reflexive governance is identified as a systemic partnering platform for macro-social marketing in smart cities. Policymakers were the focal point in a boundary-spanning role to support citizen involvement in complex exchange. Involving upstream-midstream-downstream information flows facilitated by connectivity that enabled co-designed socio-economic solutions. Co-design principles were integral to a citizen-centric socio-economic value co-creation process. That was realised and subjectively determined as value through improvements in the lives of individual citizens. Research limitations/implications The study identifies reflexive governance as a systemic partnership platform for macro-social marketing. With policymakers crucial to planning and deploying digital connectivity for supporting citizen involvement in complex exchange. The role of strategic frameworks is identified for forming and resourcing reflexive governance and macro-social marketing in smart cities. Prioritising digital connectivity for upstream-downstream information flows in strategy implementation. The study also shows how systemic partnering through complex exchange co-creates socio-economic value in smart cities. With co-design principles for citizen-centric smart developments integral to a value co-creation process that improves citizens’. Practical implications The study shows that policymakers have a central role in developing and sustaining reflexive governance as a systemic partnership platform in smart cities, built upon digital connectivity and data sharing. And for deploying macro-social marketing as a tool for equitable socio-economic development. Reflexive governance and macro-social marketing therefore require integration into urban policy for tackling wicked socio-economic problems. The Bristol case provides an example of a city leveraging connectivity and data sharing to form reflexive governance that put citizens at the centre of a value co-creation process. Originality/value Reflexive governance is introduced to social marketing literature as a systemic partnering platform for macro-social marketing. The study shows how partnering for complex exchange is integral to a process of socio-economic value co-creation. The novel setting of smart cities provides insights into the powerful supporting role of digital connectivity and data sharing.

title: Corporate (Il)legal Enclosures: How Fraudulent Land Titles Override Community Rights in Forestry Land Conflicts in Bahia, Brazil
abstract: Abstract This article examines the ethical and legal dimensions of corporate land grabbing in Bahia, Brazil, focusing on the forestry sector’s use of fraud, legal manipulation, and violence to acquire land. Through a case study of Veracel Celulose, a joint venture between the Swedish-Finnish corporation Stora Enso and the Brazilian company Suzano, we analyze how corporations exploit legal ambiguity and manipulate land registries to dispossess local populations. Drawing on archival data from federal and state land governance institutions, we develop the concept of corporate (il)legal enclosure, defined as the process through which corporations transform contested, public, or informally held land into de facto corporate property by mobilizing intertwined legal and illegal practices that exclude local populations from access, use, and control over land. Our findings show how title forgery, cadastral manipulation, administrative procedures, and legal regularization operate together to convert fraudulent land claims into seemingly legitimate corporate property. We demonstrate that land grabbing increasingly occurs not only through violence or outright illegality, but through the strategic mobilization of legal and bureaucratic institutions that render dispossession lawful in practice. By integrating insights from agrarian studies, sociolegal scholarship, and business ethics, the article advances a contextually grounded understanding of land-based injustice and challenges compliance-oriented approaches to business ethics. In doing so, it highlights the need for business ethics scholarship to engage more directly with the role of law in enabling and legitimizing corporate dispossession.

title: Revealing the divide: Differential impact of inclusive leadership on marginalized and dominant group members
abstract: There have been increasing pushbacks against diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) efforts in society and organizations, revealing a deepening divide across social groups. Although inclusive leadership has been linked to positive outcomes, existing research has three critical limitations. First, research has yet to adequately account for the role of diversity in defining inclusive leadership and in shaping followers' responses to inclusive leadership. Second, prominent definitions often conflate inclusive leadership behaviors with their intentions or effects, blurring cause-effect distinctions, thereby generating overly positive findings that limit clarity about when, how, and for whom inclusive leadership may generate benefits or risks. Third, much of the empirical literature remains vulnerable to endogeneity threats, which undermine causal inferences about the impact of inclusive leadership. Aiming to address these issues, we draw on signaling theory to develop a diversity-sensitive, behavior-based reconceptualization of inclusive leadership grounded in prior literature. We further advance a conceptual model explaining how inclusive leadership differentially affects marginalized and dominant group members. By doing so, we help enhance conceptual precision and contextual sensitivity in inclusive leadership research. We also provide a roadmap that can enable stronger causal tests of inclusive leadership.

title: Workplace Interventions to Promote Employees' Pro‐Environmental Behaviour: A Meta‐Analysis
abstract: ABSTRACT This meta‐analysis quantifies the effectiveness of workplace interventions to promote employees' pro‐environmental behaviour. It examines potential moderating factors, reports several tests for small‐study effects and publication bias, and challenges existing theoretical assumptions by applying the AMO framework to pro‐environmental workplace interventions. We synthesised m = 400 effects from k = 52 studies using random‐effects meta‐analytic models with the state‐of‐the‐art robust variance estimation (RVE) procedure to account for dependencies between effect sizes. We conducted moderation analyses to assess the influence of intervention methods directed at employees' abilities (informational and feedback interventions), motivation (financial incentives, competition, and tailoring), or opportunity (infrastructural interventions). Several procedures examined (and quantified) the presence (and size of) small‐study effects and publication bias (i.e., trim‐and‐fill, Egger's regression, PET‐PEESE, TESSPSST). Workplace interventions demonstrated a significant, small‐to‐moderate, positive effect on pro‐environmental behaviour (Hedges' g = 0.325). We found an indication for small‐study effects and publication bias, but the main effect remained robust and significant after bias‐correction and outlier exclusion. Moderation analyses revealed systematic differences in effect sizes, significance, prevalence, and heterogeneity. This meta‐analysis provides robust evidence for the effectiveness of pro‐environmental workplace interventions and, thus, highlights the potential of managerial HR measures to foster corporate sustainability. Based on the results, we challenge existing theoretical frameworks focusing on the individual‐level psychological constraints and use the AMO framework to highlight the importance of design features of interventions.

title: Epistemic Capabilities of Artificial Intelligence for Public Administration and Policy Research: A Framework for Scholarship in the Age of Intelligent Machines
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) has gained much interest in public administration and public policy fields in recent years. Research on and that uses AI has so far treated it as an object or context within the broader administrative and governance discourse. In this article, we aim to shift the locus of scholarly attention on AI by focusing on its premise as a new epistemic technology that will shape how scholars conduct research. In doing so, it proposes a framework for leveraging AI as a methodological enabler that augments researchers' cognitive and analytical capabilities, thereby overcoming longstanding methodological barriers in the fields. We propose a framework distinguishing AI applications along two epistemological dimensions of research that make use of synthetic data and real‐world data: (1) inductive approaches to discover patterns and build theory to address exploratory questions (“what,” “so what”), and (2) deductive approaches to test hypotheses and establish causal relationships to serve explanatory and predictive purposes (“why,” “how”). We contend that AI has propelled the fields toward a “new normal science” characterized by human‐machine collaboration.

title: Bricolage in bureaucracies: public leadership and bricolage behaviour in turbulent situations
abstract: Public employees increasingly face turbulent challenges in which principles such as foresight, planning, and consensus-seeking fall short. We examine bricolage as a robust governance strategy and conceptualize turbulence as a contextual moderator of the relationship between public leadership and bricolage behaviour. Based on survey data from 368 German public employees, the findings suggest that bricolage is less practiced under turbulent conditions. While rule-following leadership, contrary to expectations, becomes even more strongly and positively related to bricolage behaviour as conditions grow more turbulent, the positive association between accountability leadership and bricolage behaviour weakens substantially. Surprisingly, network governance leadership does not gain in importance. This study contributes to public administration research by further conceptualizing and exploring bricolage as a micro-level behavioural capacity in response to turbulence, by operationalizing turbulence as a graded situational stressor, and by demonstrating that turbulent contexts constitute a critical boundary condition for the exercise of public leadership.

title: Difference-in-Differences with Latent Variables: A Structural Equation Modeling Framework
abstract: Difference-in-differences (DiD) is a widely used research design in the quantitative social sciences. This article demonstrates how the standard econometric DiD model can be implemented within the structural equation modeling (SEM) framework. We show that the traditional DiD estimator can be exactly reproduced in SEM and illustrate extensions that exploit SEM’s ability to model measurement error, latent variables, and model assumptions. Particular attention is given to the identification of DiD models with latent outcomes. Empirical examples examining the effect of COVID-19 vaccination on trust in government institutions are presented using lavaan and Mplus.
journal_name: Structural Equation Modeling: A Multidisciplinary Journal

title: Beyond the Habermas machine: rethinking the democratic meaning of AI-assisted deliberation
abstract: Advances in artificial intelligence have generated renewed interest in using computational systems to facilitate democratic deliberation at scale. While recent efforts, exemplified by the ‘Habermas Machine,’ promise efficiency, balance, and consensus, they raise fundamental questions about the meaning of deliberation itself. This article offers a theoretical critique of deliberation using AI, focusing on systems that operationalize deliberation as a consensus-optimizing procedure. Drawing on Habermasian theories of communicative rationality, deliberative systems scholarship, and distinctions between private and public deliberation, the article argues that current AI approaches risk translating deliberation from communicative rationality into computational rationality. This shift privileges public acceptability and formal balance over critical contestation, reflexivity, and democratic legitimacy. In response, the article reconceptualizes AI-mediated communication by foregrounding private, informal interaction as a ‘pre-public’ space within the deliberative system, where citizens can explore disagreement in judgement-free context and develop deliberative capacities.

title: Deaths of Despair among Former Military Service Members, Massachusetts (2014-2021) and Minnesota (2014-2022)
abstract: People who served in the U.S. armed forces-former service members (FSMs)-may be at increased risk of deaths of despair: alcohol-related, drug-related, and suicide deaths. We linked 2014-2021 Massachusetts and 2014-2022 Minnesota death certificates for decedents aged 18-64 years with military personnel files to describe deaths of despair in FSM and non-military populations. We calculated age- and sex-standardized proportionate mortality ratios (PMR) for all FSMs and three-year rolling average age-standardized mortality rates for FSMs with active duty experience. We mapped the geographic distribution of these deaths and describe patterns by service history. Of 176,719 decedents, 9.5% were FSMs. FSMs were more likely to die from a death of despair than non-military populations (PMR (95% Confidence Interval), MA: 111.9 (107.0, 117.0), MN: 106.7 (101.4, 112.2)), specifically suicide deaths (MA, MN) and drug-related deaths (MA). Mortality rates displayed similar trends. FSM deaths of despair occurred a median of 20-30 years after military separation and were most common among those with Coast Guard, Marine, or Army service and Bad Conduct/Dishonorable or Uncharacterized separations. FSMs have higher burden of deaths of despair than non-military populations with patterns that vary by service history, warranting further investigation into contributing military, individual, and community factors.

title: Hypothetical interventions on alcohol consumption and risk of mortality in healthy women: emulated target trials from the Norwegian women and health study
abstract: We applied target trial emulation and the parametric g-formula to evaluate the effects of sustained alcohol consumption on 23-year mortality. Healthy women aged ≥ 35 years from the Norwegian Women and Health Study who completed questionnaires in 1998-2003 were eligible for the emulated trials (A and B). Trial B included only women reporting moderate alcohol consumption before baseline. In total, 57 964 and 14 393 women met the eligibility criteria for Trials A and B, respectively. The observed 23-year all-cause mortality risk was 6.97%. In Trial A, 23-year mortality risk differences (RDs) versus no intervention were 0.29% (95% CI, 0.02%, 0.58%) for no alcohol consumption, 0.12% (95% CI, 0.07%, 0.20%) for low consumption (>0 to 2 drinks/week), and - 0.44% (95% CI, -0.66%, -0.25%) for moderate consumption (>2 to 7 drinks/week). The lower mortality associated with moderate drinking was observed only among women aged ≥ 50 years. In Trial B, the 23-year mortality RD of reducing to low/no consumption (≤2 drinks/week) versus maintaining moderate consumption was 1.07% (95% CI, 0.10%, 1.66%). The results suggest a slight decrease in mortality from moderate alcohol consumption, particularly among women aged ≥ 50 years. In addition, the results suggest slightly increased mortality when reducing alcohol consumption from moderate levels.

title: Does despair drive increases in white mortality, or did the narrative get ahead of the data?
abstract: The aim of this study is to test the central claim of the "deaths of despair" theory: that rising despair among midlife white Americans has driven increases in all-cause mortality, particularly in those with low education. We analyzed time series of annual all-cause mortality rates per 100,000 (N=92,700 individuals) and despair (N=88,872 individuals) among US midlife (aged 45-54) adults from the CDC and NIH between 1999-2015. The association between changes in despair and changes in mortality rates were estimated via Bayesian autoregressive models with AR(1) errors. Race/ethnicity and education-specific estimates were obtained via marginal standardization. All-cause mortality increased by 7.49 per 100,000 only among midlife white adults, with a larger increase among those with low education (51.4 per 100,000). Despair prevalence did not increase exclusively among midlife white adults, increasing by 0.13% (-0.03%; 0.29%) and 0.12% (-0.27%; 0.51%) among white and Black midlife adults. The observed increases in despair among whites in midlife were not associated with increases in mortality rates (-0.12 per 100,000; 95%UI=-0.54; 0.29). These findings directly challenge the central claim of this theory and highlight the need to move beyond the white despair narrative to explain US mortality trends.

title: Rationale and Design of the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities Generation 2 (ARIC Gen2) Study
abstract: Type 2 diabetes is a risk factor for cardiac arrhythmias, but it is unknown how specific aberrations in glucose (e.g., episodes of high or low glucose) might contribute to the occurrence of heart rhythm abnormalities. The overarching goal of this study is to address research questions regarding how glucose patterns might contribute to the occurrence of arrhythmias, primarily atrial fibrillation, in adults with diabetes. To fulfill this goal, the Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities (ARIC) Gen2 study recruited 507 community-dwelling adults aged 50-80 years with type 2 diabetes to wear continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) and electrocardiogram (ECG) "patch" monitoring sensors simultaneously for up to 14 days. Gen2 study had high CGM and ECG completeness: the median wear time for sensors was 14 days and approximately 80% of participants wore both sensors for ≥10 days. By combining Gen2 and data from the original ongoing ARIC cohort (aged 80+), we have the capacity to conduct a comprehensive evaluation of the impact of CGM-defined glucose patterns on arrhythmias across a wide age spectrum from middle-aged to very old adults (aged 50-100) with type 2 diabetes. The findings from this study may help inform clinical strategies for the prevention and management of arrhythmias among adults with type 2 diabetes.

title: Public policymaking under uncertain time horizons: cyclicality, synchronization, and temporal delegation
abstract: Abstract What form does public policymaking take when actors cannot tell whether they face a short emergency, a medium-term episode, or a protracted transformation? Theories of cooperation and intertemporal choice assume time horizons that are either fixed or effectively indefinite, yet in many policy domains actors cannot specify how long a problem will last nor whether it will intensify, stabilize, or recede. Under such uncertainty, policymakers rely on short, repeatable policy cycles anchored in established calendars such as budgets and elections, a pattern conceptualized here as cyclicality. Two further mechanisms follow. Where implementation is dispersed across actors whose circumstances the center cannot observe, officials delegate authority over timing; where they delegate, they require synchronizers to keep dispersed cycles aligned, though horizon uncertainty caps how binding that coordination can be. Evidence from legal documents and semi-structured interviews tracks these mechanisms across four episodes of Romania’s implementation of the EU Temporary Protection Directive after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. Officials sustained cooperation without resolving the underlying uncertainty, settling into an extended present that remained procedurally stable at the center while producing uneven temporal experiences at the periphery.
