Markup Estimation using Production and Demand Data: An Application to the US Brewing Industry
abstract: Abstract We compare and combine two distinct approaches to estimating market power in the US brewing industry—one based on production data, the other on demand. Both methods produce similar estimates of average markups and reveal a recent upward trend. We then combine the two approaches in two ways. First, we replace conventional instruments in demand estimation with a moment involving a production-based markup estimate, yielding similar results. We then evaluate the common (but controversial) assumption that retail markets operate competitively, finding that demand-based markups recovered with the assumption of competitive retail markets align with production-based estimates, as long as downstream costs are accounted for.

title: Bringing Work Home: Flexible Work Arrangements as Gateway Jobs for Women in West Bengal
abstract: Abstract There is a large latent workforce in developing countries that consists of hundreds of millions of women who prefer to have paid work and yet are out of the labor force. Often, available job opportunities are incompatible with traditional gender roles that encourage women to stay at home. In a randomized experiment with 1,670 households, we partner with a jobs platform to offer short-term data work to women who are out of the labor force. We find three main results. First, flexible work-from-home jobs are highly effective at bringing women into paid work. Job flexibility more than triples take-up from 15% for an office job to 48% for a job that women can do from home while multitasking with childcare. Second, these jobs can act as a stepping stone to less flexible work. Trying paid work from home increases take-up of less flexible jobs two to three months later among women without previous work experience. “Gateway jobs” are especially important for women from more traditional households: their labor supply is more likely to be marginal to flexibility, and in turn, work experience shifts their attitudes to become less traditional. Third, from the labor demand side, remote work comes with trade-offs in worker performance. Working from the office increases accuracy by 3% and speed by 18%. However, these performance drawbacks of work-from-home arrangements may be outweighed by the increase in available workers.

title: ANNOUNCEMENTS
Justice Good as Random?
abstract: ABSTRACT The random assignment of judges promotes fairness and underpins causal identification across the social sciences. Analyzing Chapter 11 bankruptcies, we find sophisticated parties “judge‐shop”: relative to secured hedge fund creditors, cases involving unsecured hedge fund creditors and equity holders are assigned judges with lower past conversion rates and higher unsecured recovery rates. Experienced legal counsel similarly influences assignment. Because judges are not assigned consecutive large cases, knowledgeable parties can judge‐shop by timing the filing date. We develop a method to measure the resulting bias and demonstrate the need for controls and bounded instrumental variable specifications in judge/examiner designs.

title: AMERICAN FINANCE ASSOCIATION
Knowledge diffusion, rising inequality, and the dynamics of a pulled front
abstract: Abstract A model of economic growth is presented in which workers increase their labour income by learning from higher-paid workers. They also experience individual random income shocks. A calibration of the model to U.S. wage micro data implies that these shocks are Brownian ‘noise’, with drift close to zero. Growth comes from occasional random advances at the frontier, which create novel learning opportunities for others and drive sustained growth. The long-run growth rate is increasing in both the variance of shocks and the knowledge-diffusion rate. The model closely reproduces the evolving shape of the U.S. wage distribution between 1991 and 2023.

title: The Content Moderator’s Dilemma: Removal of Toxic Content and Distortions to Online Discourse
abstract: Abstract There is an ongoing debate about how to moderate toxic speech on social media and the impact of content moderation on online discourse. This paper proposes and validates a methodology for measuring the content-moderation-induced distortions in online discourse using text embeddings from computational linguistics. Applying the method to a representative sample of 5 million US political Tweets, we find that removing toxic Tweets significantly alters the semantic composition of content. The magnitudes of the distortions are comparable to removing 4 out of 67 topics from the online discourse at random. This finding is consistent across different embedding models, toxicity metrics, and samples. Importantly, we demonstrate that these effects are not solely driven by toxic language but by the removal of topics often expressed in toxic form. We propose an alternative approach to content moderation that uses generative Large Language Models to rephrase toxic Tweets, preserving their salvageable content rather than removing them entirely. We show that this rephrasing strategy reduces toxicity while mitigating distortions in online content.

title: Threat and Assimilation: Evidence from Refugees in Germany
abstract: Abstract This paper studies how local threat shapes refugees’ cultural assimilation and economic integration, exploiting plausibly exogenous variation in their allocation across German regions between 2013 and 2016. Using representative survey data and administrative records, we measure cultural preferences alongside employment, earnings, and job characteristics, and build a threat index combining contemporaneous and historical local xenophobia. Refugees assigned to more hostile regions converge more rapidly to Germans’ stated preferences, yet do not find jobs faster and experience slower earnings growth. We show that local hostility heightens threat perceptions, prompting quicker cultural adoption, while higher discrimination slows refugees’ successful economic integration.

title: What Explains Growing Gender and Racial Education Gaps?
abstract: ABSTRACT We study why US college graduation gaps by gender and race widened across cohorts. We develop a dynamic life‐cycle model with endogenous education, labor supply, marriage, fertility, and welfare participation. Preferences are fixed across cohorts and race/ethnic groups; changes arise from family background, labor‐market opportunities, and marriage markets. Labor‐market changes account for half of growth in women's graduation from the 1960 to 1980 cohorts. Parental background accounts for one quarter and marriage markets for one fifth. These shares are similar for Whites, Blacks, and Hispanics, but absolute gains were larger for White women, which led to wider racial gaps.

title: Managing Procurement Auction Failure: Bid Requirements or Reserve Prices?
abstract: ABSTRACT This paper examines bid requirements, where the government may cancel a procurement contract unless two or more bids are received. Using a first‐price auction model with endogenous entry, we compare the bid requirement and reserve price mechanisms in terms of auction failure and procurement costs. We find that, in comparison with bid requirements, reserve prices can reduce procurement costs and substantially lower failure probabilities, especially when entry costs are high or signals are sufficiently informative. Bid requirements are more likely to result in zero entry, while reserve prices can sustain positive entry under broader conditions.

title: How Do Savings Groups Respond to Agricultural Shocks?
abstract: ABSTRACT Negative aggregate shocks lead to persistent rural poverty. Access to credit and insurance can help, but is often lacking. How do informal financial institutions, dependent on locally sourced capital, respond to shocks? We study the response of savings groups—locally run financial associations mostly embedded in rural agricultural communities—to aggregate shocks. We explore this by combining group‐level performance data for 9328 savings groups primarily in five sub‐Saharan African countries with local drought data. We use two‐way fixed‐effects and heterogeneity‐robust difference‐in‐differences analyses to assess how these informal financial groups respond to drought shocks. Groups mobilise credit during shocks by increasing the number of loans they provide. The counter‐cyclical credit response is concentrated among groups shocked in the later stages of their savings cycle, where accumulated capital permits additional lending, confirming a capital‐constraint prediction. The social fund, designed for idiosyncratic shocks, is not mobilised during droughts. We discuss implications for integrating informal savings groups into climate‐risk management strategies.

title: The impact of lying aversion and prosocial lies on cheating
abstract: Abstract This paper examines how prosocial motivations shape lying behavior in a strategic setting. Two players each privately choose a color in their mind, then draw a color at random, and report whether the two colors match. Both players receive a high payoff if at least one reports a match, so a single lie secures the payoff for both, making lies strategic substitutes. I develop a theoretical model in which individuals bear a psychological cost of lying but experience a lower cost when their lie increases their partner’s payoff. The model predicts that individuals are less likely to lie when they can rely on their partner to do so, and more likely to lie when their dishonesty benefits their partner. I test these predictions in an online experiment with four treatments that separately vary the opportunity to rely on the partner’s lie and the presence of a benefit to the partner. In this setting, prosocial motives outweigh lying aversion: participants lie more when their dishonesty benefits their partner, and they do not lie less when they can leave the lie to their partner. Lying increases only when a participant’s report is pivotal to the partner’s payoff, indicating that prosocial preferences reduce the net cost of lying when dishonesty is instrumental in generating benefits for others.

title: Recovering subjective probability distributions: a Bayesian approach
abstract: Abstract An individual reports subjective beliefs over continuous events using a proper scoring rule, such as the Quadratic Scoring Rule. Under mild additional assumptions, it is known that these reports reflect latent subjective beliefs if the individual is risk neutral. We demonstrate how to fully recover latent subjective beliefs if the individual is known to distort probabilities into decision weights using Rank Dependent Utility theory, and generalize all results for the complete class of proper scoring rules. As an immediate corollary, we can then exactly recover latent subjective beliefs using Expected Utility Theory. Using Bayesian econometric methods, we demonstrate how to recover belief distributions for individuals, and illustrate these results by recovering belief distributions about the “competitiveness” of individuals and the addictiveness of smoking. These results significantly widen the domain of applicability of proper scoring rules for eliciting latent subjective belief distributions.

title: The future of work in creativity and innovation: perspectives on on-site versus remote work policies and practices
Gifts, commodities and the ‘problem’ of NGO ambivalence
Passing on Talent: A Generativity Perspective on the Effects of Perceived Overqualification Among Older Employees
abstract: Drawing on generativity theory, we examine the positive effects of perceived overqualification among older employees. Specifically, we argue that perceptions of overqualification in older employees are positively associated with a core generativity motive—that is, a desire to support and guide the next generation and be needed by them. Further, we argue that generativity motive predicts prosocial attitudes and behaviors in the form of prosocial meaning of work for future generations and helping behavior. Additionally, we identify mature-age practices—that is, human resource practices tailored to address older employees’ needs—as a key contextual factor that strengthens the indirect pathway between perceptions of overqualification in older employees and their prosocial attitudes and behaviors. We test and find support for our hypotheses in two independent field studies—a three-wave field study of older employees (Study 1, N = 261) and a dyadic three-wave field study of employees of various ages and their respective supervisors (Study 2, N = 274 dyads). Theoretical and practical implications of our study are discussed.

title: Accommodation in the vertical supply chain: Implications of manufacturer dual tracking
abstract: Abstract Research Summary The prevalence of dual tracking, in which upstream manufacturers simultaneously produce branded and private‐label products for downstream retailers, has increased substantially in recent years, driven by growing consumer demand for private‐label products. This paper examines the implications of manufacturer dual tracking by exploiting a setting in the ready‐to‐eat breakfast cereal industry where a leading branded manufacturer began supplying both products to retailers. We find that, because of this change in the vertical relationship, private‐label product introductions and advertising declined for products that directly imitated the dual‐tracking manufacturer's branded products. Changes in retailer behavior suggest that retailers accommodated the dual‐tracking manufacturer by selectively adjusting their private‐label portfolios. Dual tracking can therefore improve a manufacturer's bargaining position against retailers and reduce downstream imitation. Managerial Summary Manufacturers have increasingly produced not only their own branded products but also private‐label products for retailers that compete with those brands. This phenomenon, known as dual tracking, carries benefits and risks for manufacturers. While producing private‐label products can utilize excess capacity, these products directly compete with the branded counterpart. We study the implications for firms engaging in dual tracking and show that doing so gives manufacturers greater bargaining power in their relationships with retailers. Firms can leverage this change in bargaining power to reduce imitation by retailers' private‐label products, lessening competition concerns. Our results show that retailers reduced the introduction and advertising of private‐label products that directly compete with the dual‐tracking manufacturer.

title: From accidents to assets—The value pathways of patents for serendipitous inventions
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Firms often celebrate accidental inventions that lead to major breakthroughs, yet little is known about how the value of serendipitous inventions materializes. Using data from 8530 patented inventions across 23 countries, our research shows that these inventions differ from planned R&D outcomes. Serendipitous inventions are less likely to have a strong technological impact, be turned into marketable products, or serve as effective blocking tools in patent strategy. However, they are more likely to generate value through licensing, indicating that while they may not fit the originating firm's strategy, they can succeed elsewhere. Hence, serendipitous patented inventions represent “option‐like” assets that offer external channels to capture value rather than relying on internal use. Managerial Summary Accidental breakthroughs like microwaves, penicillin, or Velcro are often celebrated, but their potential to create value in practice remains unclear. Analyzing data from 8530 patented inventions across 23 countries, we find that such serendipitous inventions differ fundamentally from planned R&D outcomes. They are less likely to yield major technological impacts, products, or strategic patents but more likely to generate value through licensing, functioning as “option‐like” assets that are valuable externally more than internally. Thus, relative to planned inventions that benefit from downstream complementary assets, serendipitous patented inventions pay off more for firms with strong licensing or technology‐selling capabilities.

title: The Relational Dynamics of Multiparty Alliances: An Interdependence‐Based View
abstract: Abstract Despite the increasing relevance of multiparty alliances, existing research remains fragmented and predominantly organized around functional purposes or structural forms, overlooking the relational dynamics among alliance partners. Such an omission prevents a systematic understanding of what fundamentally distinguishes multiparty alliances from their dyadic counterparts and how different types of multiparty alliances vary from one another. This paper addresses this gap through a systematic review of research from leading management journals published between 1990 and 2025. Adopting an interdependence‐based view, we offer two main insights. First, the presence of more than two partners introduces three categorically distinct features compared to dyadic alliances: a change in membership, a change in reciprocity patterns, and the emergence of faultlines. Each of these features poses distinct challenges. Second, and more importantly, we show how pooled, sequential, and reciprocal forms of interdependence shape the emergence, evolution, and consequences of these relational features, thereby explaining systematic variations across multiparty alliances. Building on these insights, we develop an integrative framework that clarifies the distinctiveness of multiparty alliances and identifies key mechanisms and boundary conditions. This framework informs a future research agenda to redirect scholarly attention to the unique relational dynamics within and across multiparty alliances.

title: Retail investor trading and market reactions to earnings announcements
How Sustainability Transformations Quietly Lose Their Edge
abstract: As economic headwinds put pressure on sustainability and other social impact initiatives, reconciling profit and purpose is becoming increasingly challenging for teams. A study of a group of new ventures found that the likelihood of successfully meeting both goals was closely linked to the cognitive mindset of the transformation team. Those who took an either/or approach and chose to prioritize one goal in the near term were less successful than those who maintained a both/and mentality.

title: Human Capital Pathways to Sustainability: How Green Talent, Mindfulness, and Leadership Cocreate Sustainable Innovation
abstract: ABSTRACT Sustainable innovation is central to firm competitiveness, yet the mechanisms through which green human resource practices generate such outcomes remain underexplored. This study examines how green recruitment and selection drives sustainable innovation through green training and development and green mindfulness, while considering the boundary roles of green leadership and green knowledge sharing. Grounded in Human Capital Theory and the Ability–Motivation–Opportunity framework, the study conceptualizes sustainable innovation as the outcome of capability development and cognitive activation. A quantitative, three‐wave time‐lagged design was employed. Data were collected from 842 employees across mining, manufacturing, construction, and hospitality sectors. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS‐SEM) with bootstrapping was used to test the moderated serial mediation model. The findings revealed that green recruitment and selection significantly enhances sustainable innovation both directly and indirectly through green training and development and green mindfulness. A significant sequential mediation confirms that sustainable innovation emerges through staged capability and cognitive processes. Green leadership strengthens the recruitment–training and recruitment–innovation links, while green knowledge sharing enhances the training–mindfulness relationship. The study contributes to the intellectual capital literature by framing green human capital as a dynamic, process‐driven asset. It integrates capability development, cognition, and contextual enablers into a unified model, offering a clearer explanation of how sustainability‐oriented HR investments translate into innovation outcomes.

title: Deforestation‐Free Cocoa: Implications for Organizational Adaptation and Compliance Costs
abstract: ABSTRACT Mandatory due diligence is an emerging policy instrument for addressing global environmental challenges, yet how such regulations reshape firm‐level organizational structures and generate compliance costs remains poorly understood. Drawing on organizational theory, this study examines how companies in the German cocoa and chocolate sector adapt to the EU Regulation on Deforestation‐free Products (EUDR) and estimates the associated compliance costs. Based on 18 semistructured interviews with representatives of affected companies, service providers, and associations, we find that EUDR implementation constitutes a modular organizational transformation affecting governance structures, IT systems, and supply chain relationships simultaneously. Indicative total compliance costs for a reference company with approximately 500 employees amount to approximately €320,000 per year during the transition phase and €540,000 annually thereafter. The latter amount consists predominantly of price premiums for compliant cocoa, estimated at about €415,000 per year. These findings extend organizational theory by characterizing the cross‐boundary pressures inherent in extraterritorial mandatory due diligence and refine compliance‐cost frameworks by foregrounding the indirect organizational costs that such regulation generates during implementation.

title: Breaking the Silos of Sustainable Financial Measurement: A Strategic Business Environment Framework Through Multidimensional Sustainability Metrics
abstract: ABSTRACT Growing pressure on firms to align sustainability strategies with financial performance has increased the need to understand how financial mechanisms support green transformation. However, most existing studies rely on econometric approaches that explain relationships but rarely identify the relative importance and systemic interactions of sustainability‐related financial drivers. Addressing this gap, the present study examines how sustainability‐oriented finance and green innovation influence corporate performance. The study applies grey influence analysis (GINA) based on expert evaluations to analyse the interrelationships among 11 indicators covering green finance, green innovation and financial outcomes. This approach enables the identification of both direct and indirect influences under conditions of uncertainty. The findings reveal that long‐term green financing exposure and green loans are the most influential drivers, whereas green innovation, particularly process improvements and resource‐efficient operations, acts as a key connecting mechanism linking finance to performance outcomes. The study offers practical implications for managers and policymakers by identifying priority levers for sustainability‐driven value creation and demonstrating the usefulness of GINA for analysing complex sustainability–finance systems.

title: Rewiring the Circular Economy Through AI‐Informed Pathways: Structural and Distributional Drivers of Environmental Outcomes in the European Union
abstract: ABSTRACT This study investigates the structural and distributional factors that influence environmental performance in 27 European Union (EU) countries from 2010 to 2021, focusing especially on circular economy (CE) measures and the increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI)‐based analytical tools. It investigates how economic scale, population changes, energy productivity, land use, material trade, income inequality, and foreign direct investment affect ecological footprint results, considering differences between countries and the fact that some are members of the Eurozone. To improve the reliability of its findings and to identify nonlinear responses that are relevant for assessing environmental impact, the empirical approach uses a combination of method of moments quantile regression and finite mixture models together with machine learning methods such as artificial neural networks and random forests. The results indicate that economic scale, population, and energy productivity consistently account for environmental outcomes within different groups of countries, energy productivity appearing as the most effective policy measure, while trade in recyclable materials is found to be highly dependent on the specific context and has an effect of reducing the footprint within the Eurozone. These findings highlight the importance of AI‐guided, comprehensive transitions that combine CE practices with more fundamental changes in energy systems, land management, and social equity, and bring environmental impact assessment in line with the EU's broader carbon‐neutrality goals.

title: Two Pathways to ‘No’: Context‐Conditioned Sufficient Pathways to Formal SBTi Non‐Engagement Among Apparel and Footwear Suppliers in Bangladesh and China
abstract: ABSTRACT The apparel and footwear (A&F) industry accounts for up to 10% of global greenhouse gas emissions, much of it arising from supplier activities. While leading brands increasingly commit to science‐based targets (SBTs), formal engagement with the Science‐Based Targets initiative (SBTi) remains limited among suppliers, especially in key sourcing hubs. This study examines why suppliers in Bangladesh and China have not formally engaged with the SBTi despite external pressure and how this non‐engagement varies across institutional contexts. Rather than treating national context as an independent causal factor, the research employs a most similar systems, different‐context design to analyse how the same innovation attributes operate within different governance environments. Using Rogers' Diffusion of Innovations (DOI) framework and crisp‐set Qualitative Comparative Analysis based on 27 interviews with Tier 1 and Tier 2 suppliers, this study identifies sufficient pathways involving perceived relative advantage, compatibility, complexity, trialability and observability associated with formal SBTi non‐engagement. Results indicate context‐dependent non‐engagement logics: in Bangladesh, low perceived relative advantage within dense compliance systems; in China, either low perceived compatibility with mandate‐driven routines or high observability, a paradoxical pathway in which visible benefits coexist with non‐engagement. These findings suggest that DOI attributes are not universal drivers of supplier engagement but governance‐conditioned decision filters. This study contributes to supplier climate governance by showing that formal SBTi non‐engagement reflects context‐conditioned sufficiency, equifinality and causal asymmetry rather than merely cumulative barriers. It offers diagnostic insights for advancing climate action within global value chains, without making claims about overall global climate governance outcomes.

title: Operational constraints in professional kitchens: A theory of constraints perspective on food waste reduction
Rethinking satisfaction metrics: from online reviews to holistic experience analytics
abstract: Purpose The present study aims to question the trend of relying heavily on online reviews as the primary indicator of customer satisfaction in the hotel industry, exposes the disadvantages of the suggested strategy and suggests a more credible and multifaceted approach as an alternative. Design/methodology/approach The comprehensive re-evaluation of the existing literature concerning online reviews, behavioural economics and service quality is conducted and through the use of a critical synthesis approach, the current situation is disrupted. To a greater extent, the paper deploys the conceptual model of the Critical Reflection Paper (CRP) to not only perceive the dominant school of thought from a critical perspective but also to offer a different perspective. Findings The study identifies three major blind spots in online reviews, namely, the issues of quantifying the qualitative nuances, the influence of the platform algorithms on the perceptions of the guests and the consideration of silent visitors. It contends that using these measures in totality will result in the management making bad decisions in matters concerning resource allocation and wrong ideals about quality service. Practical implications The hotel industry is believed to view the customer reviews as the primary variable to gauge its performance and to conduct business reviews and to this end, it is suggested that the hotel managers are advised to depend more on their in-house feedback developed based on diverse sources, diminish the influence of third-party review ratings in its internal evaluations and introduce real-time information capture as an investment to secure and maintain its real service excellence. Originality/value While Holistic Experience Analytics (HEA) integrates existing analytical components, its originality lies in three novel logics: (a) a temporal dissonance weighting rule that prioritises behavioural signals over review scores when they conflict, (b) a governance protocol for auditing third-party platform biases and (c) a prospective satisfaction assumption that enables real-time, pre-review intervention moving beyond mere data aggregation to a fundamentally different measurement logic.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Strategic inertia or rational caution? Unpacking short-term rental pricing responses to hotel ADR fluctuations
abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate how short-term vacation rentals (STVRs) adjust their pricing strategies in response to hotel ADRs. While prior research has emphasized the disruptive effect of STVRs on hotel performance, the reverse relationship remains underexplored. The study addresses this gap by examining whether market-level STVR price adjustments respond to ADR movements and how market conditions such as STVR density and ADR volatility shape these dynamics. Design/methodology/approach Using a balanced panel dataset of monthly observations from October 2014 to May 2022 across 16 US cities, the study applies a two-step difference Generalized Method of Moments (GMM) estimator. Key variables include STVR price adjustments, hotel ADRs, ADR volatility and STVR density, with interaction terms and lagged specifications to capture delayed and dynamic effects while addressing endogeneity and unobserved heterogeneity. Findings Results reveal significant pricing inertia among STVRs. In the primary GMM specification, current hotel ADRs are positively associated with STVR price adjustment, while lagged hotel ADRs are negatively associated with subsequent adjustment, indicating a delayed and partially corrective response. STVR density does not significantly moderate this relationship in the primary model, whereas the role of ADR volatility is more sensitive to specification in supplementary analyses. Originality/value The study extends revenue management and behavioral economics theory by highlighting delayed and asymmetric competitive interactions between hotels and STVRs. It provides market-level evidence on how STVR pricing responds to hotel ADR signals over time, offering implications for hotels, STVR operators, platforms and policymakers concerned with market efficiency and competition.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Beyond self-reports: the neuro-service quality (NSQ) framework
abstract: Purpose The paper is a critical reflection on the prevalence of self-report in the research on the quality of hospitality service and offers a new, neuro-scientifically based framework: neuro-service quality (NSQ). It is intended to solve the validity crisis in conventional survey-based methods of assessment by providing a biological alternative. Design/methodology/approach This paper synthesises existing literature on service quality and current neuroscience research. The paper identifies gaps in the measurement of subconscious guest emotions and real-time physiological reactions and offers a multidisciplinary approach of affective neuroscience and service-dominant logic (SDL). Findings Traditional models do not adequately account for cognitive biases, retrospective distortions and the peak-end rule. The NSQ framework proposes the following metrics used as objective measures of service excellence: heart rate variability (HRV), skin conductance and neural resonance. Research limitations/implications This paper extends SDL by introducing neuro-affective value co-creation, which provides a more detailed conceptualisation of the biological roots of the guest experience. It is a critique of the old, long-standing gap model and proposes a change to experienced neural quality. Practical implications The use of non-invasive biometrics in optimising the service environment, personalising guest interaction and improving real-time service recovery applies to hospitality managers. It allows precision hospitality, in which the interventions are founded on objective physiological data. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this paper is one of the first to propose a methodological alternative to traditional survey-based methods of measuring service quality within the hospitality industry.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
authors: Alaa Mohamed Samir Mostafa M. Selim

title: How generative AI shapes eco-friendly accommodation choices
abstract: Purpose Despite the growing use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in travel planning, limited research has examined how GenAI-related characteristics influence travelers’ eco-friendly accommodation choices. Guided by the “Stimulus–Organism–Response” framework, this study aims to examine how perceived interactivity, personalization, information accuracy, usefulness, currency and anthropomorphism shape trust in GenAI, environmental awareness and environmental attitude, which subsequently influence intention to choose eco-friendly accommodations. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 371 Vietnamese leisure travelers with GenAI travel-planning experience were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling and artificial neural networks (ANNs). Findings Perceived usefulness and currency influence trust, environmental awareness and environmental attitude, while other GenAI characteristics show more selective effects. All three psychological states positively influence eco-friendly accommodation intention. ANN identifies environmental attitude as the strongest predictor, followed by environmental awareness and trust. Need for cognition strengthens the awareness-intention relationship, while need for affect strengthens the attitude–intention relationship. Practical implications GenAI-supported travel systems should prioritize useful, current and credible sustainability information rather than rely primarily on personalization or human-like interaction. Sustainability communication can also be adapted to travelers’ cognitive and affective processing tendencies. Originality/value The study moves beyond GenAI adoption by showing that distinct GenAI characteristics influence sustainable accommodation choices through different psychological routes. It also identifies the conditions under which these internal states are more strongly translated into behavioral intention.
journal_name: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management

title: Caste in the Boardroom, and Beyond: What’s Missing and Where to Next?
abstract: An empirical literature on caste in Indian firms – boards, CEOs, capital and labour intermediaries – has emerged in management journals over the past decade. This commentary reads the field’s findings against what economics has long established and asks what comes next.

title: On Becoming Who We Are: How a Social Venture Layers Its Identity in an Emerging Field
abstract: Organizational identity shapes how ventures define who they are and become; however, we know little about how identity evolves in social ventures over time. This gap is important because social ventures continually negotiate social purpose and financial sustainability while responding to shifting stakeholder and institutional expectations. Based on an 8-year inductive study of an impact investing venture, we examine how venture identity and an emerging field co-evolve. Our findings identify four phases of identity evolution: experimentation, institutionalization, maturation, and scaling. Rather than replacing earlier identity claims, the venture cumulatively layered new meanings onto them, preserving, reinterpreting, and extending prior commitments while maintaining coherence across changing contexts. As the venture articulated and refined its identity, it also shaped shared understandings of impact investing, allowing venture identity and field formation to develop together. We contribute to organizational identity research by theorizing identity evolution as a recursive process of adaptation, persistence, and cumulative layering.

title: Sustainable global careers: the role of career adaptability and cultural difference in expatriate health, happiness, and productivity
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: How Alliances Build Innovation Capabilities but Narrow Their Redeployment in Amazonian Community‐Based Enterprises
abstract: ABSTRACT Research on strategic alliances often treats supplier capability development as an outcome, but rarely asks which capabilities are built or what they can be used for. We address this through an embedded single‐case study of a lead‐firm‐orchestrated network in the Brazilian Amazon, comprising six community‐based enterprises (CBEs) supplying sociobiodiversity ingredients, drawing on 60 interviews and 43 h of observation. Sponsorship proved systematically imbalanced, concentrating in the capabilities that make these CBEs reliable suppliers and largely absent from those that would allow them to price, negotiate and sell elsewhere. In doing so, capability development converted general‐purpose biodiversity and traditional knowledge into buyer‐specific assets, narrowing redeployability in fact and in how the CBEs perceived their options. Counterintuitively, redeployment required alternative demand rather than additional capability. We name this mechanism developmental lock‐in: the progressive dedication of a supplier's resource base to a supplier through the activity that upgrades it, absent any contractual restriction. The study contributes to work on supplier development, which treats capability as the binding constraint on supplier independence, and to work on asset specificity, which treats specificity as a prior condition rather than a product of the relationship itself.
authors: Renata Elaje Azevedo da Mota Carmona Chaves

title: Toward a pendulum framework of firm internationalization
Competing evaluations of worth and fragile compromises: credential-based pay in a public sector bureaucracy
abstract: This paper examines how credential-based unequal pay is justified, criticised, and sustained within a public-sector accounting bureaucracy, the Controller and Accountant General's Department in Ghana. It analyses a dual-compensation regime under which chartered accountants receive higher remuneration than non-chartered colleagues despite substantial overlap in tasks and common appraisal criteria. The paper brings institutional logics into dialogue with Boltanski and Thévenot's orders of worth to explain both the historical emergence of the credential premium and the situated justificatory work through which it is defended and contested. In doing so, it also considers how the postcolonial history of accounting professionalisation has contributed to the institutional authority attached to professionally certified expertise. Empirically, the study draws on more than five years of research engagement in the field, including interviews, participant observation, informal conversations, and documentary analysis. The findings show that chartered accountants justify superior pay through professional logics that emphasise industrial and market principles of expertise, scarcity, professional investment, and external labour-market value, whereas non-chartered accountants advance critiques centred on civic principles of a bureaucratic logic of fairness, equality, and common contribution. The unequal remuneration regime is sustained, however, not because it commands settled legitimacy, but because organisational actors manage critique through fragile compromises, including compensatory allowances, selective accommodations, and deferred administrative and legal reviews, that contain dissent while leaving the differential compensation structure intact, though contested. The paper contributes to critical accounting scholarship by theorising remuneration as a contested technology of valuation through which public bureaucracies classify accounting labour, reproduce professional closure, and manage inequality.

title: A textual and linguistics analysis of budget documents and legitimation strategies in local government budgets
abstract: Local governments face demands from elected representatives, central government and citizens regarding expected services, yet not all demands can be met. Budgets serve as a legitimation tool in addressing these demands. Using a content analysis methodology, this study explores various textual and linguistic features of local government budget documents, including evidence of the use of legitimation strategies. Given limited prior research, this study offers two exploratory propositions, examined through an element of the annual budgets of five local governments. The findings indicate similarities and differences in legitimation strategies used across local governments, with rationalisation emerging as the dominant strategy, contrary to some prior research. The study offers several contributions. First, it suggests that standardised budget reports are shaped by context and audience. Second, it demonstrates co-occurrence of various legitimation strategies in budget documents. Third, it highlights the strategic use of moralisation as a legitimation strategy, which has received less attention in prior literature. Finally, the study shows text diversity persists despite structural constraints.

title: Integrating monetary and environmental goals: exploring the impact of green monetary policy on corporate environmental disclosure
abstract: Using a difference-in-differences (DID) methodology, this study examines how the expansion of China’s medium-term lending facility (MLF) policy to include green assets affects corporate environmental information disclosure. We construct a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2015 to 2020, including a treatment group of firms with potential green credit projects and a control group of other firms. We find that after the June 2018 MLF collateral expansion, environmental disclosure significantly increases for the treatment firms relative to the control firms. This effect is robust to a variety of specifications and additional checks. Further analyses based on difference-in-differences-in-differences (DDD) models identify two mechanisms, financing and investment, through which green monetary policy may ease financing constraints and encourage green investment, which in turn increases environmental information disclosure. We also find that the policy has stronger effects on firms in more developed regions, areas with weaker prior environmental regulation, non-state-owned enterprises, and those with less transparent information. Our findings underscore the potential of green monetary policy as a tool to incentivize corporate sustainability practices and contribute to the literature by providing micro-level evidence of monetary policy’s environmental impact.

title: Empowering communities through gender-focused CSR initiatives: a social return on investment approach
abstract: The effectiveness of gender-focused CSR initiatives depends not only on firms’ commitment but also on how collaboration is structured. This study examines how different governance configurations of collaborative CSR models influence the social impact of external gender-oriented initiatives. Grounded in value creation theory, stakeholder theory, and resource dependence theory, we adopt a theory-informed explanatory case study of an educational initiative implemented by a real network of Italian firms in partnership with a university and local actors. We use Social Return on Investment (SROI) in a comparative within-case design to assess one observed configuration and three empirically grounded counterfactual configurations, ranging from firm-centric initiatives to a multi-firm, externally supported governance model. Within the case analysed, the comparison indicates that the configuration combining inter-firm coordination and external expertise is associated with higher estimated social returns and deeper stakeholder engagement. The study contributes to the literature in three ways. First, it shows how governance configuration can shape community-level social value creation. Second, it reconceptualises collaborative CSR as a configurational mechanism rather than a binary condition. Third, it identifies an amplification mechanism in gender-focused CSR initiatives, whereby collaborative governance can enhance impact through structured interdependence and institutional legitimacy. Methodologically, the paper repositions SROI as a theory-informed comparative device rather than a stand-alone reporting tool. These findings offer new insights into how firms can operationalise the social dimension of ESG strategies and design collaborative gender-focused initiatives capable of generating measurable and durable community impact.

title: Camouflaging the damage: the consequences of negative ESG media coverage on earnings management
abstract: As media scrutiny of ESG misconduct intensifies, this study examines whether and how firms adjust their earnings management strategies in response to the costs of negative ESG media coverage. We explore this phenomenon through three perspectives: the ethical, managerial opportunism, and trade-off views. Using a panel of listed European firms from 2018 to 2022, we find that firms increase real earnings management and classification shifting following negative ESG media coverage, consistent with the managerial opportunism view. Further analyses reveal that climate risk exposure, reflected in unfavourable climate media coverage, prompts these opportunistic responses, and that earnings management operates as a shielding mechanism mitigating increases in financing costs and declines in institutional ownership. Moreover, firms operating in countries with tighter social norms, stronger regulatory scrutiny, and better control of corruption, as well as firms with more effective boards, are less likely to engage in earnings manipulation. The study contributes to the earnings management literature by extending it to adverse ESG shocks and by identifying institutional and governance conditions that shape managerial responses. The findings provide insights into how managers react to ESG scandals and offer guidance for investors, boards, and regulators seeking to enhance accountability.

title: Narrative Disclosure Strategies Around Stock‐for‐Stock M&As
abstract: Using 1,470 cash and stock‐for‐stock mergers and acquisitions from 2004–2020, we document that stock‐for‐stock bidders strategically manage the narrative content of earnings press releases in the year preceding the announcement to lower acquisition costs. Beyond inflating tone, we find that they also reshape tone dispersion, with positive language distributed more broadly across earnings press releases and negative language increasingly concentrated. Abnormal tone inflation leads to substantial short‐run gains ($22 million for the average bidder), with smaller but reinforcing effects from dispersion. These patterns are most pronounced in larger deals and weaker‐monitoring environments but reverse in the long run, as markets discount narrative manipulation.

title: Commercial or relational cues: how information salience in project titles affects crowdfunding performance
Driven to Win, Destined to Lose? A Process Model of How Sports Betting Escalates Into Gambling Harm and Shapes Help‐Seeking
abstract: ABSTRACT Sports betting has become a routine part of watching sport. Online and mobile platforms let consumers bet continuously, receive instant feedback, and respond to new odds throughout a match. Frequent betting is known to raise the risk of gambling‐related harm, but far less is known about the psychological mechanisms through which that harm develops and about the conditions under which gamblers decide to seek help. This research develops and tests a process model of the sports betting harm spiral across five studies. Studies 1a, 1b, and 1c show that higher betting intensity increases problem gambling severity through two mechanisms, where competitive intensification strengthens the drive to outperform other bettors while overconfidence bias inflates belief in predictive skill, which yields evidence consistent with the proposed ordering in which competitive motivation precedes distorted judgment. Studies 2a and 2b show that severe losses increase intentions to seek help, especially among highly engaged bettors, yet this response depends on attribution style, as gamblers who attribute losses to external causes report stronger help‐seeking intentions than gamblers who blame themselves. Theoretically, the findings integrate consumer culture theory, cognitive bias theory, and attribution theory into a single process model that explains how gambling harm escalates and when recovery‐oriented behavior emerges. Practically, the findings offer guidance for consumer protection, gambling policy, and responsible platform design.

title: The voice of small shareholders at annual general meetings
abstract: Purpose This study focuses on the voice of small shareholders in annual general meetings (AGMs) to explore how their marginalization unfolds. We investigate how managerial discourse constitutes small shareholders as marginal subjects and why they participate despite this marginalization. Design/methodology/approach We adopt a discourse analysis approach informed by the Foucauldian lens of power and governmentality to interpret the minutes of the four key AGMs of one of the world's oldest banks, which trace the bank's passage from growth to crisis. Findings The analysis shows that managers organize AGMs through the control of timing, sequencing, and procedural structures, limiting substantive dialogue with small shareholders while preserving procedural legitimacy. We interpret the AGM as a disciplinary dispositif operating through technologies of power that marginalize small shareholders. Shareholders raise concerns extending beyond investment interests to employees, consumers, the local community, and personal recognition. They continue to participate because they misrecognize the AGM as a democratic arena. Misrecognition sustains the illusion that voice may influence governance, while loyalty sustains continued engagement despite marginalization. Originality/value We explain how marginalization is reproduced over time and conceptualize shareholder marginalization as a recursive process by bringing Foucault's analytics of power and governmentality into dialogue with Habermas's concept of ideal speech. Findings highlight how seemingly participatory mechanisms can produce exclusion. This process may occur in settings where communicative events are structured to maintain authority while enacting procedural legitimacy. The risk that AGMs fall short as platforms for accountability warrants attention given the global adoption of purely virtual formats.

title: Examining visibilities and invisibilities within poverty-related accounting research
abstract: Purpose To analyse poverty-related literature within the field of accounting and outline a future research agenda. Design/methodology/approach We identify and collect poverty-related research within accounting before drawing on the writings of Brighenti (2007, 2010), in particular the notion of “field of visibility”, to analyse the literature. Findings Drawing on Brighenti (2007, 2010), we identify what exists in the literature as fields of visibility about poverty-related accounting academic knowledge. By analysing these fields of visibility, we also begin to interrogate the invisible – that is, what may be, but is not (yet), an object of attention and consideration. It is through this process of analysing the visible and interrogating the invisible that we discuss knowledge within the field, its implications and propose possible future research avenues. Originality/value Analysing the literature through Brighenti (2007, 2010) enables us to contribute to the poverty-related accounting literature by considering both visibilities and invisibilities. In addition, we contribute to methodological approaches to literature reviews within accounting through outlining an approach that departs from structured literature reviews and their variants, which are becoming increasingly popular in accounting yet are often limited in their potential to provide sufficient relevant insights into some topics.

title: Touchable cultural heritage: How alternative touch experience facilitates visitors’ cultural inheritance behavior
Sour grapes or strategic choice? Socially disadvantaged tourism entrepreneurs' pursuit of ‘break out’
Adoption of AI for Travel: Corporate Strategies and Firm Value
abstract: Tourists’ responses to the adoption and implementation of AI-based travel solutions have received considerable scholarly attention, yet investors’ reactions to such adoption decisions remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on multiple intelligences and tourism innovation archetypes theories, this study develops a conceptual framework that explains how AI adoption influences firm value and empirically tests this framework through a multi-method design combining event study analysis, propensity score matching, and sample selection modeling. Based on 903 corporate announcements, the findings reveal a positive effect of adoption of AI on firm value, that is contingent on the use of simplification and feelings-centered strategies. These moderating effects further vary according to firms’ labor efficiency and the prevalence of high-skill employees. The findings reveal a nuanced account of contingencies shaping AI adoption in tourism, travel, and hospitality contexts, which helps managers better understand how investors evaluate AI adoption strategies.

title: Epistemic Injustices in Islands of Conscious Power: Outsourcing and Epistemic Barriers in Claim-Making
abstract: Abstract Outsourcing has increasingly become a dominant trend in global production, as firms disintegrate vertically by externalizing non-core functions and procuring these services from the market. This process increasingly organizes production through inter-firm contracting arrangements, shifting hierarchical control from internal managers to external buyers who leverage market power. This article examines the epistemic injustices that workers face in the context of such transformations. Adopting a worker-centric perspective, it theorizes the epistemic barriers workers encounter when asserting their rights after outsourcing. These barriers include exclusion from internal norms, ultracomplex accountability chains, eroding incentives to speak out, and searching for an effective audience. The central claim is that outsourcing, as presently organized, often foreseeably produces epistemic harms from which firms benefit. An epistemic injustice lens helps bring this neglected dimension of labour injustice into view.

title: Think political leader — think he or she? A multi-country test of a gender-fair language intervention to reduce gendered leadership stereotypes
abstract: Women are greatly underrepresented in positions of political leadership around the world. In seeking to explain this underrepresentation, some researchers have pointed to people’s tendencies to stereotype leaders as more similar to men than women as these tendencies can support the belief that women are unsuited to leadership. This project aimed to test whether a subtle linguistic intervention was able to ameliorate this gender bias in political leadership stereotypes across different languages and national contexts (country/region N = 42, language N=30, sample N = 22,996). Specifically, this project examined whether gender-fair language (e.g., the use of paired pronouns ‘he or she’) can reduce the tendency for people to stereotype political leaders as more similar to men than women. To increase the rigor with which these stereotypes were measured, this project complemented the dominant ‘cheap talk’ measure of personal stereotype content with an incentivised community measure of this content. As expected, participants stereotyped political leaders as more similar to men than women; this pattern was stronger on the incentivised measure of community stereotypes. Unexpectedly, there was no evidence that paired pronouns reduced this bias (there was weak exploratory evidence that paired nouns increased participants’ tendencies to stereotype political leaders as more similar to women). This project suggests that the ability of gender-fair language interventions to ameliorate gender bias in the political leadership domain may be limited.

title: The Fragility of Merit: Presidential Power and the Civil Service Under Trump. By J. EdwardKellough, New York: Routledge, 2024. 152 pp. $52.99 (paperback). ISBN: 978‐1‐03‐265634‐2; $190.00 (hardcover). ISBN: 978‐1‐03‐265637‐3
abstract: The author of the book under review, Dr. J. Edward Kellough, served as the chair of the reviewer's doctoral dissertation committee at the University of Georgia.

title: Managing Collaboration Dynamics Under Pressure: Lessons From the COVID ‐19 Medical Supply Shortage
abstract: ABSTRACT In crisis responses such as the COVID‐19 medical supply shortage, senior policy makers often emphasize urgency, a strategy that prioritizes the rapid achievement of intermediate goals. While this approach can drive swift action, it also introduces challenges and trade‐offs that can hinder collaboration toward long‐term success. These challenges often arise from misalignment between organizational norms and priorities of collaborating partners, which can undermine legitimacy and performance. Policymakers should consider how personnel composition, such as large military contingents, shapes task force culture and operational dynamics. Even in fast‐moving crises, clearly aligning roles, goals, and timelines from the start can reduce confusion, while leaders must navigate cultural norms and challenge ingrained practices to support collaboration.

title: Regulatory Capture, Public Trust and Pro‐Environmental Behaviors
abstract: ABSTRACT Regulatory capture, where special interests steer regulation away from public interest, is widely discussed, but its broader public consequences remain underexplored. We explore the relationship between perceived regulatory capture, public trust and pro‐environmental behaviors using online survey data in China. Findings show that perceived material and information capture (the latter measured with a single scenario‐based proxy) have significant negative associations with public trust in local ( b = −0.154, −0.105) and central government ( b = −0.087, −0.064). Direct associations with non‐activist pro‐environmental behaviors in the public sphere are consistently negative and supported by bootstrapped confidence intervals across specifications (material: β = −0.066 to −0.082; information: β = −0.036 to −0.047), whereas several corresponding private sphere associations are not. Indirect associations are supported only in selected models. These findings highlight the public implications of regulatory capture, distinguishing material and information capture, and extend understanding of public trust and pro‐environmental behaviors.

title: Where belief is filtered: how truthfulness and source credibility shape trust, skepticism, and worry in vaccine communication
abstract: This study examines how true versus false messages shape trust in cancer-vaccine information on social media, alongside skepticism and worry, and tests the moderating roles of source credibility and deception-detection self-efficacy. In a 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment (N = 210), participants viewed a simulated cancer-vaccine post and reported their responses. The findings show that true messages elicit significantly higher levels of trust and lower levels of skepticism and worry than false messages, and that source credibility amplifies the positive effect of truthfulness on trust. Source credibility did not, however, moderate skepticism or worry, and deception-detection self-efficacy conditioned skepticism but not trust or worry. Higher confidence in detecting deception predicted greater skepticism, suggesting that perceived evaluative competence can intensify scrutiny rather than foster trust. Drawing on experimental evidence from the high-stakes, underexamined context of cancer vaccines, this study advances understanding of trust formation in digital science communication by showing that message truthfulness and source credibility operate through distinct processing routes: systematic evaluation of content and heuristic reliance on source cues, respectively. The findings offer theoretically grounded guidance for practitioners and policymakers seeking to counter misinformation and strengthen public confidence in emerging biomedical innovations.

title: Real-world cardiovascular effects of liraglutide: transportability analysis of the LEADER trial
abstract: Abstract Appropriate use of recently approved type 2 diabetes treatments depends on external validity of landmark clinical trials (RCTs) in real-world populations that may differ from trial participants. This study transported effect estimates from the Liraglutide Effect and Action in Diabetes: Evaluation of Cardiovascular Outcome Results (LEADER) trial, a placebo-controlled RCT of liraglutide on cardiovascular outcomes, onto real-world cohorts within the Veterans Affairs (VA) healthcare system. Risk differences (RD) in survival outcomes, approximated using pseudo-observations of individual survival probabilities, were estimated with augmented inverse probability weighting after balancing baseline characteristics between RCT and target samples using approximate balancing weights. Transported effects of liraglutide compared to placebo on major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) and all-cause mortality in veterans (“VA-weighted LEADER”) were larger than, though statistically consistent with, the treatment effects observed in LEADER: MACE RD at 3 years of 4.6% [95% CI 2.2, 7.0] in VA-weighted LEADER versus 1.6% [0.3, 2.9] in LEADER; all-cause mortality RD at 3 years of 2.9% [0.8, 5.1] in VA-weighted LEADER versus 0.9% [-0.09, 1.9] in LEADER. These estimates of the effects of liraglutide in veterans with diabetes provide real-world evidence that can guide diabetes treatment decisions and formulary policies for a high-risk population underrepresented in RCTs.

title: Solution or illusion? The distributional impact of minimum wage on household food security in Java, Indonesia
Childhood Maltreatment and Adult Obesity: Gender-Specific Pathways
abstract: Childhood maltreatment has been linked to adverse health outcomes across the life course, yet its association with body mass index (BMI) in middle adulthood remains underexplored. Using MIDUS Refresher Biomarker and Milwaukee African American Sample data ( N = 696), this study examined five maltreatment types and midlife BMI categories by gender. Multinomial logistic regression indicated that physical abuse (RRR = 2.41, p < .05), emotional abuse (RRR = 2.76, p < .01), and physical neglect (RRR = 1.68, p < .05) were associated with elevated BMI categories, with sexual abuse showing the strongest associations with both obesity (RRR = 2.56, p < .01) and severe obesity (RRR = 3.65, p < .01). Gender-stratified analyses revealed differences as well, as women who experienced physical abuse (RRR = 3.01, p < .05), emotional abuse (RRR = 3.17, p < .05), or sexual abuse (RRR = 4.71, p < .01) had increased risk of severe obesity, whereas men showed elevated obesity risk only with sexual abuse exposure (RRR = 3.86, p < .05). Findings underscore the need for trauma-informed, gender-sensitive approaches to obesity prevention and treatment across the lifespan.

title: Understanding nonresponse and strategies to improve response rates in a randomized controlled trial among breast cancer survivors: the FASTRACS-INSIGHT mixed-methods study
Emotional Responses to Image-Based Sexual Harassment: Examining Help-Seeking and Changes in Social Media Behavior
Managing policy expertise through think tank–state relations in Kazakhstan
abstract: The interconnections among expertise, politics, and policy making remain of persistent scholarly interest, yet they are still insufficiently examined outside consolidated liberal democracies. Addressing this gap, this article analyses think tank–state relations in Kazakhstan, approached here as a case of soft authoritarianism – a political system that imposes systematic restrictions on political rights and civic freedoms while retaining formal democratic institutions and relying more on citizen persuasion, agenda management, and depoliticization than on overt coercion. The study examines how soft authoritarianism shapes the conditions under which think tanks operate and how these conditions evolve during complex crises that heighten the demand for expertise. Empirically, it focuses on Kazakhstan over the period 2010–25. Drawing on original expert interviews, the analysis shows that think tanks in Kazakhstan operate within a selectively pluralistic yet tightly managed policy environment characterized by resource dependence, co-optation, and personalized access to decision-making. Rather than excluding or eliminating independent expertise altogether, the state strategically incorporates and manages it through informal networks, selective funding, and bounded participation in policy consultations. The findings further demonstrate that major crises create temporary openings for expert engagement and role redefinition, but do not fundamentally transform underlying power relations. By examining how expertise is incorporated, constrained, and instrumentalized under soft authoritarianism, while drawing comparisons with both de-democratizing and more restrictive authoritarian contexts, the article contributes to advancing comparative debates on think tanks and policy expertise beyond democratic environments.

title: The Political Psychology of Citizens in Rising China Yida Zhai. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 397 pp. $150.00 (hbk). ISBN 9781009489713
Public sector contracting-out for unilateral benefit: analysing the financial condition of local government and public enterprise
abstract: This study examines local public enterprises as an enterprise-based contracting-out instrument and evaluates their financial consequences for parent local governments and the enterprises themselves. Using panel data from South Korean local governments and affiliated public enterprises, we assess whether changes in the number of enterprises are associated with financial condition on both sides. The results show asymmetric effects: enterprise proliferation is generally associated with improved parent government financial condition but deteriorating enterprise financial condition. This pattern suggests an organisational boundary shift through which fiscal and operational burdens are transferred to separately accounted entities. By conceptualising enterprise creation as a strategic organisational choice, the study extends research on corporatisation and alternative service delivery and shows how reforms framed around specialisation and managerial professionalism can redistribute fiscal burdens within the public sector.

title: Toward wind-resilient cable-supported photovoltaic system: nonlinear stiffness, dynamic identification, and parametric instability
abstract: Cable-supported flexible photovoltaic (FPV) system is emerging as lightweight low-carbon power-generation structures, but their large-span, low-stiffness configuration makes them susceptible to large-amplitude wind-induced oscillations, for which the conventional small-amplitude assumption no longer provides a valid basis for dynamic analysis. This study establishes a finite-amplitude nonlinear dynamic framework for two-cable FPV systems, in which vibration-induced cable-force evolution is explicitly incorporated into the governing equations as time-varying stiffness. Based on this framework, deviations in dynamic characteristic identification are investigated, and practical testing strategies are proposed and validated through scaled aeroelastic model tests. Undamped free-vibration analysis reveals that the nonlinear stiffness of FPV systems is governed by nonlinear Mathieu and asymmetric Duffing mechanisms. The single-degree-of-freedom (S-DOF) response follows a Duffing oscillator, where the initial equilibrium state induces restoring-force asymmetry, amplitude deviation, and spontaneous shift of the oscillation center. In multi-degree-of-freedom (M-DOF) vibration, parametric resonance (PR) with bifurcation occurs near a unit torsional-to-bending frequency ratio, with unidirectional energy pumping from the lower-order to the higher-order mode. Coupled and uncoupled equivalent linear stiffness formulations are presented for frequency-domain analysis of flutter. These findings have direct implications for the operational lifespan, maintenance costs, and levelized cost of energy (LCOE) of FPV systems, as the amplitude-dependent stiffness evolution and parametric resonance identified in this study govern the cyclic stress levels and deformation amplitudes that drive fatigue accumulation in cables and connectors, as well as micro-cracking in PV cells. By linking finite-amplitude stiffness evolution to measurable modal properties and flutter-relevant design variables, the framework offers a mechanics-based route to wind-resilient design and reliable long-term deployment of FPV energy infrastructure.

title: Spatially decoupled design and AI-driven optimization for thermal uniformity and nitridation resistance in NH3-fueled micro-tubular SOFCs
abstract: Ammonia-fueled micro-tubular solid oxide fuel cells (MT-SOFCs) offer a compact route for carbon-free power generation, but the endothermic NH 3 decomposition can cause thermal non-uniformity, and local NH 3 enrichment can increase the thermodynamic risk of Ni nitridation in the anode. To address this issue, we propose a spatially decoupled MT-SOFC configuration that integrates an internal catalytic layer (ICL) into the fuel inlet tube. NH 3 decomposition kinetic experiments, multiphysics simulations and AI-assisted optimization are combined to evaluate flow resistance, electrochemical performance, thermal distribution and anode nitridation risk. The ICL shifts most NH 3 decomposition from the anode to the inlet tube, forming an H 2 -rich fuel environment while avoiding the severe pressure-drop penalty associated with packed-catalyst designs. At 100 sccm, the ICL design increases power density and electrical efficiency by 23.6% relative to the Base design and reduces the predicted Ni nitridation risk in the anode. Co-optimization of ICL geometry and operating conditions yields Pareto-optimal solutions constrained by maximum temperature gradient ( TG cell ) and anode nitridation-risk volume fraction ( V nit ). Compared with the optimized Base design* under the TG cell ≤ 10 K cm −1 constraint, the representative dual-constrained design increases power density from 962.6 to 1251.8 W m −2 and electrical efficiency from 7.8% to 19.6%. Meanwhile, it reduces the predicted V nit to 0% under the adopted thermodynamic criterion. These results indicate that spatially relocating NH 3 decomposition through safety-constrained optimization provides a potential route toward durable and efficient NH 3 -fueled MT-SOFCs.

title: Coupling modeling and optimization strategy of wind power reserves across different time-scales for frequency-constrained unit commitment
Machine learning-genetic algorithm coupled optimization of heteroatom-doped carbon electrodes for vanadium redox flow batteries
abstract: The development and optimization of high-performance carbon electrodes are critical for vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFBs). However, electrode performance is influenced by multiple interacting factors, while traditional experimental approaches are often time-consuming, inefficient, and costly. This study establishes a data-driven framework that integrates machine learning with genetic algorithms, enabling accurate prediction and global optimization of the performance of heteroatom-doped carbon electrodes under diverse conditions. A multidimensional database is constructed based on published literature and active learning, followed by the training and evaluation of multiple machine learning models. The optimal model achieves excellent predictive accuracy, with R 2 values of 0.982 and 0.991 for coulombic efficiency and voltage efficiency, respectively. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) analysis further reveals the underlying regulatory mechanisms of key parameters affecting electrode performance. Moreover, an elite genetic algorithm is employed to screen optimal electrode performance. The optimized electrode exhibits a predicted energy efficiency of 85.2% at 200 mA cm −2 with outstanding cycling stability. Experimental results show strong agreement with model predictions, with the mean absolute percentage error remaining below 3.7%. This work provides an efficient and reliable strategy for the rational design of doped electrodes, which significantly accelerates the development of next-generation redox flow batteries.

title: Battery early fault detection method adaptable to multi-condition operations and capable of multi-type identification
Building retrofit for energy and carbon reduction: identifying future research priorities and trends from a critical analysis and systematic mapping review of the global literature
abstract: Retrofitting buildings is essential for climate change mitigation and has numerous co-benefits; however relatively little is known about effective retrofit for energy and carbon reduction. The UN Buildings Breakthrough Agenda therefore calls for research priorities and knowledge gaps to be identified (UN, 2023). While previous reviews have identified key trends in existing research, none has systematically analysed the full research picture and clearly identified research gaps and priorities. This paper responds to this urgent call, offering the most comprehensive analysis to date of current quantitative retrofit research through a systematic mapping review and critical meta-analysis of 1,058 abstracts of peer-reviewed articles from 2017-2024. The analysis identifies three significant and critical gaps for the first time. First, only 2% of papers consider future climates. As the climate is already changing, this is of major significance and should be an urgent focus for retrofit research. Second, only 10% of papers analyse real-world projects, despite awareness that models offer limited understanding of real energy-use in existing buildings. Third, while embodied impacts are increasingly accepted as critical for new buildings, they are considered in under a third of retrofit papers, resulting in unmeasured carbon emissions from retrofit. This paper recommends that further studies should be prioritised on: whole life impacts of retrofit; real-world case studies of renovation; and, perhaps most critically, the understanding of appropriate retrofits for already-changing climates. In order to support progress in this essential and urgent field, the comprehensive dataset of categorised studies is provided alongside the paper.
