title: Commons without borders: How entrepreneurs can engage local actors into collective action for the governance of supra-local common-pool resources
Who are my people and what can I do? Community remapping for entrepreneurial venturing after forced migration
Audit culture: how indicators and rankings are reshaping the world
Superstition Everywhere
abstract: In Chinese culture, the digit 8 is considered lucky and the digit 4 unlucky. We find that this numerological superstition has a significant impact across China’s stock, bond, foreign exchange, and commodity futures markets, affecting asset prices in both the primary and secondary markets. The superstition effect, that is, asset prices ending in a lucky (unlucky) digit are far more (less) frequent than expected by chance, is prevalent across finance markets. We show that this phenomenon is driven by two mechanisms: sophisticated investors’ reliance on superstition as an anchor to manage ambiguity, and the overoptimism of unsophisticated investors. While the superstition effect does not lead to any systematic mispricing for assets traded primarily by sophisticated investors, it is closely associated with overpricing for assets heavily traded by unsophisticated investors. This paper was accepted by Will Cong, finance. Funding: J. (J.) Chang received financial support from the National Natural Science Foundation of China [Grant 72573148]. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2025.01449 .

title: Returnless Partial Refunds: A Large-Scale Field Experiment in E-Commerce
abstract: A large-scale field experiment shows AI-enabled returnless partial refunds increase customer value and reduce operating costs while raising strategic-behavior risks.

title: How Do Forward‐Looking Estimates of Credit Losses Affect the Judgments of Financial Statement Users?
abstract: ABSTRACT Financial accounting standard setters recently changed the accounting for estimates involving credit risk. The change shifted the accounting from an incurred‐loss model (ILM), which is based on credit‐risk conditions that exist at the time of the estimate, to a model based on expected credit losses over the life of the asset in question (ELM), which considers expectations of future conditions. Our paper is based on the theoretical premise that ELM will reduce surprise via its Day 1 forewarning, which, in turn, should lessen the potential for hindsight bias (i.e., Monday‐morning quarterbacking) and judging management as having made a poor quality lending decision if an actual credit loss later occurs. Three experiments support this premise, revealing when ELM accounting should have a differential impact relative to the prior accounting.

title: Navigating New Accounting Standards: Implications for Firms and Their Auditors
Enabling Circular Economy Performance Through Organizational Capabilities: The Mediating Role of Circular Business Model Innovation
abstract: ABSTRACT The transition to a circular economy requires firms to mobilize organizational capabilities that redesign how value is created, delivered, and captured. Although Circular Business Model Innovation (CBMI) has emerged as the central operational mechanism for circular transformation, the capability stack that triggers CBMI and the multidimensional performance outcomes it produces remain undertheorized. This study develops and tests an integrated model in which Responsible Data Governance Capability (RDGC), Sustainable Digital Infrastructure Capability (SDIC), and Organizational Agility Capability (OAC) shape CBMI, which in turn drives Circular Economy Performance (CEP), Sustainable Value Creation Performance (SVCP), and Financial Resilience Performance (FRP). The model is anchored in Dynamic Capabilities Theory, with each antecedent capability mapped onto the sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring microfoundations, and supplemented by the Natural Resource‐Based View for the sustainability outcomes. Using survey data from 305 firms engaged in circular transitions and analyzed through structural equation modeling with bootstrapped mediation, the findings show that all three capabilities significantly drive CBMI, with SDIC emerging as the strongest predictor. CBMI in turn produces robust effects on CEP and SVCP and a markedly weaker effect on FRP. Mediation analysis confirms that CBMI channels capability inputs into circular and value‐creating outcomes, but only marginally into financial resilience. The study refines the dynamic capabilities framework as applied to circular transitions, disciplines emerging optimism about the financial benefits of circularity, and offers managers and policymakers a granular vocabulary for prioritizing capability investments in pursuit of multidimensional sustainability performance.

title: Buyer–Supplier Relationships in the Modern Supply Chain: Exploring Professionals' Perspectives on Power Balance in Pursuit of Decarbonization
abstract: ABSTRACT Decarbonization is a contemporary and critical organizational agenda for meeting climate change goals, but little is known about how strategies deployed to meet decarbonization goals interact with employees' agentic capacities and coping strategies, particularly in the context of supply chain pressures and power dynamics. We address this knowledge gap through a qualitative study and collected data through open‐ended essay‐based interviews from 43 supply chain professionals from various countries. The data analyzed through the Gioia method revealed six aggregate dimensions, showing that decarbonization changes what power rests on without changing who holds it: The ability to decarbonize becomes a new, shared basis of dependence that binds partners closer, while the balance of power holds—except where capability is scarce, demand is mature, or one party dominates. Our findings extend power‐dependence theory by indicating a transition in the modern supply chain toward a collaborative dynamic rather than one based purely on power.

title: Incorporating Environmental and Social Sustainability in Supply Chain Strategy: A Case of Textile Recycling Value Chain
abstract: ABSTRACT With growing awareness of the net‐zero target, clothing brands are striving to reduce carbon emissions in their supply chains (SCs). Besides, social sustainability is gaining increasing attention to meet the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). Therefore, SC strategies are becoming more intertwined with environmental and social dimensions of sustainability. To address this issue, this research develops a dynamic supplier selection and order allocation (SSOA) model for the textile recycling industry by integrating the Best–Worst Method (BWM) with mixed‐integer nonlinear programming (MINLP) approach. The overall SC cost is minimised while ensuring that sustainability indices remain above target thresholds. Results indicate that if the sustainability target surpasses a critical level, total SC cost rises drastically. A stress test is conducted to identify critical suppliers, at different tiers, so that strategies for SC resilience can be planned. The findings provide strategic insights into cost–sustainability trade‐offs, enabling managers to design resilient and sustainable sourcing strategies. The study highlights the importance of supplier criticality assessment and targeted sustainability adoption in textile recycling SCs.

title: Whose story do we live? Experiential authorship threat in AI-mediated hospitality journeys and its consequences for meaning, memory, and engagement
abstract: AI now functions as hospitality’s concierge, curating itineraries, wellness plans, and trip narratives at scale. While such systems boost efficiency and personalisation, they raise a symbolic concern central to hospitality: when algorithms pre-write the journey, do guests still feel like the authors of their own experiences? This research introduces and validates Experiential Authorship Threat (EAT), defined as the perceived loss of agency, ownership, and self-authored meaning when AI curation displaces the guest’s narrative role. Across six studies (scenario-based, embedded-field, and interface experiments; total n = 2073), AI (vs. human) curation elevates EAT, especially under rigid itineraries (Study 1), and EAT, rather than adjacent constructs, drives symbolic and behavioural disengagement through diminished psychological ownership, particularly among guests high in narrative identity (Study 2). Framing AI as a co-creator rather than a curator, and offering editable rather than pre-filled itineraries, restores autonomy and authorship and improves engagement and satisfaction (Studies 3 and 4). The cost of EAT is greatest for symbolic, identity-relevant trips and high-identity-salience guests (Study 5) and persists in impoverished post-trip memory (Study 6). Theoretically, the research integrates self-determination, narrative identity, and meaning-maintenance perspectives to position EAT as a distinct psychological mechanism in hospitality. For managers, preserving guest authorship through framing, interface design, and symbolic sensitivity emerges as a design priority alongside accuracy and speed.

title: Employees as co-creators of the digital transformation – a Delphi study on the role of HRM and leadership for innovative work behavior
abstract: Successfully navigating digital transformation (DT) requires the active participation of employees, particularly through innovative work behavior (IWB). Existing literature highlights the pivotal role of human resource management (HRM) practices and leadership behaviors in promoting IWB. However, DT is not only increasing the importance of employee innovation but is also reshaping the HRM practices and leadership behaviors required to support it. Building on the AMO framework, we analyze which HRM practices and leadership behaviors will be most important for fostering employees’ IWB and how these practices and behaviors are expected to change in response to ongoing digital developments. Using a two-stage Delphi study with 27 experts, we identify future HRM and leadership requirements for IWB. The experts predict that fostering IWB during DT will require greater autonomy in learning and improved access to digital technologies (ability), a trusting environment and a positive error culture (motivation), as well as high levels of empowerment and involvement, along with time for experimentation (opportunity). Among the identified practices, training and leaders role model behavior are expected to undergo the most substantial transformation. These findings provide insights into how organizations can adapt HRM and leadership approaches to foster the IWB through which employees become co-creators of DT.

title: A de facto referendum: how proxy advisors set their standards through director elections
abstract: We study the standard-setting role of proxy advisors when their preferences diverge from regulatory mandates and shareholders’ choices. The say-on-pay (SOP) regulation in 2011 allowed U.S. firms to adopt non-annual voting schedules, whereas proxy advisors strongly preferred annual voting. We show that they leverage negative recommendations in compensation committee member elections (CMEs) as an alternative channel for expressing compensation-related concerns in non-SOP years. Among firms that hold triennial SOP votes, negative recommendations in CMEs are significantly more frequent during non-SOP years. Moreover, proxy advisors promote their standards even more strongly in firms where their preferences are less aligned with the voting choices of shareholders, highlighting their standard-setting role even when unpopular.

title: A Primer on Blue Accounting and Finance
abstract: This paper examines the relationship between blue accounting and blue finance and its implications for sustainable ocean‐based development. Using a conceptual review of the United Nations Sustainable Blue Economy Finance Principles, major financial instruments, and selected cases, the paper shows that blue finance creates demand for standardized and comparable information, while credible blue accounting supports activity eligibility, environmental risk assessment, performance monitoring, and the prevention of bluewashing. It conceptualizes blue accounting as a connected architecture spanning corporate or entity‐level reporting, project‐ and financial‐instrument‐level accounting, and national or subnational ocean accounts. These levels serve distinct but complementary purposes across financial decision‐making, corporate management, public policy, and environmental governance. The analysis finds that existing accounting methods, including SEEA‐consistent ocean accounts, provide an important but incomplete foundation. Persistent difficulties in valuation, reporting boundaries, recognition, measurement, materiality, attribution, data availability, and institutional capacity limit their effectiveness. Addressing these limitations requires combining established approaches with marine‐specific definitions, ecological indicators, valuation methods, and stronger connectivity across accounting levels. Blue finance should therefore be understood as part of a broader institutional transition aligning accounting, governance, and capital allocation with ecosystem resilience.

title: Retail Investor Attention and Voluntary ESG Disclosure: Evidence from Two Investor Interaction Platforms in China
abstract: This study examines the relationship between retail investor attention and firms’ voluntary environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure, drawing on a comprehensive dataset from investor interactive platforms (IIPs) in China. We document a positive association between retail investor attention and firms’ voluntary ESG disclosure, which holds across a wide range of robustness checks. Cross‐sectional evidence indicates that this association is stronger for firms with better ESG performance, larger size, stronger governance, and for those receiving more negatively toned ESG inquiries on the IIPs. The association is also more pronounced under external conditions such as policy initiatives and analyst coverage. Further analyses show that it is primarily linked to information‐seeking as opposed to gambling‐oriented attention, and to inquiries regarding financially material ESG issues. Firms issuing ESG reports during periods of heightened retail investor attention tend to experience favourable capital market outcomes. Overall, the evidence underscores the role of retail investors as a visible demand‐side force associated with voluntary ESG disclosure.

title: Manipulating Statistics to Justify Self-Serving Recommendations
The Transformative Impact of Prosthetics on Well-being of Consumers with Disabilities
Environmental performance feedback and green innovation: The moderating role of organizational slack
abstract: Prior research has highlighted a variety of external and internal drivers of green innovation (GI), yet much less is known about how firms interpret their own environmental performance and adjust GI strategies accordingly. Drawing on the behavioral theory of the firm, this study investigates how environmental performance feedback is associated with firms’ GI decisions. Using panel data from Chinese publicly listed firms, the results reveal a U-shaped relationship between performance below aspirations and GI, and an inverted U-shaped relationship when performance exceeds aspirations. Organizational slack weakens both patterns, reducing firms’ responsiveness to both negative and positive environmental performance feedback. These findings provide new insight into how firms adapt their GI strategies in response to environmental performance feedback signals.

title: Linking multiple sources of performance feedback to firm behavior: the combined effect of technological and financial performance on innovation
Unpleasant moral memory and the formation of inclusive orientation under incomplete institutional guidance
The more the better? The nonlinear innovation effect of the big data policy
abstract: Although big data policy has been widely regarded as a key instrument for promoting firm innovation in the digital era, many policies still fall short of expectations, prompting growing scholarly attention to the relationship between big data policy and firm innovation performance. Existing studies offer inconsistent insight because they examine policy effects through linear lenses such as signaling, rent-seeking, or isolated resource provision, while paying insufficient attention to the underlying resource mechanisms embedded in big data policy and how firms' internal and external contexts shape their responses. By integrating the resource-based view and neoinstitutional theory, this study develops a resource-based and institutionally embedded explanation of how big data policy intensity affects firm innovation performance. Using panel data on Chinese A-share listed manufacturing firms from 2013 to 2022, this study reveals that the big data policy intensity has an inverted U-shaped effect on innovation performance. Furthermore, the unabsorbed slack and absorbed slack exert heterogeneous moderating effects on this inverted U-shaped relationship. This study further finds that marketization and absorbed slack can jointly moderate the relationship between big data policy intensity and innovation performance. Overall, this study extends the policy–innovation literature by revealing when big data policy facilitates or constrains firm innovation, while offering practical implications for policymakers and firms.

title: Director Expertise and Compliance to Corporate Social Responsibility Regulations
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question/Issue This paper investigates whether assigning CSR‐specific expertise to the board committee legally responsible for CSR improves compliance with mandatory CSR law and shapes how firms organize that compliance. Research Findings/Insights Using Indian listed companies subject to mandatory CSR regulation, we find that CSR expertise on CSR committees is associated with higher compliance and more concentrated CSR activities across categories and locations. These associations are stronger among firms facing greater competitive or financial pressures and those without prior CSR engagement. High compliance combined with CSR expertise is also associated with higher firm value, improved creditworthiness, and greater institutional ownership. Theoretical/Academic Implications Our findings highlight how directors with CSR expertise help companies improve legal compliance with mandatory CSR regulations and pursue more focused CSR strategies. This research identifies committee‐level CSR expertise as an important governance mechanism shaping both regulatory compliance and the organization of CSR activities. It demonstrates the benefits of embedding CSR expertise within board structures. Practitioner/Policy Implications We provide evidence that directors with CSR expertise and stronger compliance positively affect firm outcomes. Governments and policymakers could use these findings to promote CSR expertise on corporate boards, incentivize compliance, and promote the convergence of financial and social goals. Our study provides empirical support for recent public policies, including the 2020 EU recommendation to appoint sustainability experts on corporate boards.

title: Collaboration or Opportunism? Supplier Equity Stakes in Customers and Audit Fees
abstract: ABSTRACT Research Question Based on relational and resource dependence theories, this study investigates the impact of supplier equity stakes in customers (SESC) on audit fees and its underlying mechanisms from the perspective of auditors' behavioral decision‐making. Research Findings The findings reveal that SESC significantly reduces audit fees, supporting the collaboration hypothesis. Mechanism analysis indicates that SESC lowers audit fees by reducing operational risk and audit complexity. Heterogeneity analysis shows that the effect of SESC on reducing audit fees is weakened when the holding level is high, the duration is short, and the supplier is state‐owned, whereas when the firm's external bargaining power and industry monopoly power are low, this reduction effect is enhanced. Theoretical Implications This study enriches the literature on supply chain characteristics by examining equity relationships and enriches the literature on the influence of supply chain characteristics on auditors' behavioral decisions from the perspective of SESC. Furthermore, this study extends the comprehension of SESC in corporate governance and auditing practices through the theoretical lens of relational theory and resource dependence theory. Practitioner Implications First, enterprises should recognize the strategic role of SESC in modern supply chain management and actively cultivate and develop this innovative relationship to enhance supply chain resilience and security. Second, auditors should pay heightened attention to changes in SESC to effectively evaluate supply chain stability and adjust audit workloads accordingly. Lastly, policymakers should strengthen policy support and incentive mechanisms for supply chain equity holding practices.

title: Mobilizing ecosystem support for architectural innovation: Broker-mediated expectation formation
Research grant effects across funding modes and industry collaboration
Turning a private surveillance service into a public disclosure: the case of Amazon's ring doorbell
abstract: This article analyses the interaction between broader political, economic and cultural changes and the local experiences of citizens using the Amazon Ring doorbell. The concept ‘luxury surveillance’ is used to study how citizens engage with the live and recorded images of the Ring doorbell. The paper empirically analyses the impact of the Ring, through (1) observations of platform use, (2) surveys on Facebook, and (3) in-depth interviews (N = 73) with owners of the Ring in four neighbourhoods in Rotterdam, the Netherlands. The findings reveal how the Amazon Ring reframes mundane interactions into mass surveillance opportunities, impacts the presumption of innocence, leads to different forms of perceived privacy, and provides a permanent sense of alertness by the owners.

title: Online activism at odds: Exploring tensions in the everyday practice of ‘professional’ and ‘social media’ activists
abstract: This paper investigates how two groups of activists – ‘professional’ (civil society members) and ‘independent’ activists (using primarily social media for activism) – construct the political power of digital technologies in everyday practice. We focus on how the daily practice of activists draws on both individual experiences and societal macro-discourses to develop a range of discursive resources and subject positions in the symbolic construction of digital activism. Based on a critical discourse analysis of 18 semi-structured interviews, the findings reveal three tensions between discourse and practice, namely: digital activism vs. boots-on-the-ground activism; horizontalism vs. formal organization; and private vs. activist (digital) lives. We argue that despite their persistence, the promises of technology for social justice offered by hegemonic techno-utopian discourses do not neatly fit activist practice. In the complex, messy, and fluid context of everyday life, such promises and ideals are often negotiated, reappropriated, adapted, or rejected by activists. Democratic values are thus not inscribed in technology: local context, organizational structure, and individual factors shape the ways digital technologies help or hinder digital activism. We advise citizen activists to critically consider dominant techno-utopian discourses, particularly their simplified picture of political decision-making processes. Such awareness can better equip citizens when dealing with the tensions generated by their own activist practice.

title: Causal inference of multiple interrelated exposures: Contributions of ischemic placental disease to preterm delivery
abstract: Ischemic placental disease (IPD) involves three obstetrical complications - preeclampsia, placental abruption, and fetal growth restriction - and is implicated in up to 55% of early deliveries. Despite substantial overlap in their etiology and epidemiologic risk profiles, existing studies have assessed their effects independently. Using data from the Consortium on Safe Labor (2002-2008; n = 203, 990), we examined the composite and separate effects of the IPD conditions on spontaneous and indicated preterm delivery (sPTD and iPTD). We systematically specified joint IPD probabilities, corresponding to combinations of hypothetical stochastic and deterministic interventions. Eliminating all IPD reduced sPTD (RR = 0.93; 95% CI = 0.92, 0.94) and iPTD (RR = 0.66; 95% CI = 0.64, 0.67) from observed levels. Eliminating preeclampsia alone reduced sPTD (RR = 0.94; 95% CI = 0.94, 0.95) and iPTD (RR = 0.72; 95% CI=0.71, 0.73). Partially reducing joint IPD co-occurrence among 58% of individuals who met criteria for high-risk, by magnitudes drawn from separate low-dose aspirin meta-analyses, yielded minimal reductions for sPTD (RR = 0.99; 95% CI=0.98, 0.99) and iPTD (RR = 0.89; 95%CI=0.88, 0.89). Preeclampsia drives IPD's association with both PTD subtypes; under the stated assumptions, hypothetically eliminating preeclampsia yielded the largest iPTD reduction.

title: Control-risk-informed spectrum-power allocation for virtual coupling of heavy-haul trains
An integrated NKDE–MGWR framework for smoothing-scale and network-coverage sensitivity in rural highway crash modeling
Coordinating fragmented global AI governance: Control, Rights, and Safety as a regime complex
abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence governance is often discussed as if it were a single global policy domain. In practice, governments confront a coordination problem across partially overlapping agendas pursued through different instruments and actor configurations. This research note conceptualizes global AI governance as a non-exhaustive regime complex organized around three analytically distinct governance logics: Control, Rights, and Safety. The three are selected because each combines a distinct problem definition, recurrent instrument bundle, actor configuration, and set of portable policy objects. Using an Overton-derived corpus of 198,823 AI-related policy documents and a monthly actor-by-regime panel for 1994–2025, I compare metadata-indexed trajectories, cross-regime overlap, leadership shares, temporal alignment, and OECD-relative post-event salience around three named policy moments. A stratified full-text calibration using 73 documents that were substantively readable by both independent coders, drawn from an initial sample of 100, produced high inter-coder reliability but only partial correspondence between metadata and full-text judgments; correspondence was strongest for Control and weakest for Safety. Within that explicitly documentary scope, Control has the highest metadata prevalence (65.8% of regime-bearing documents) but comparatively unsettled leadership and event-linked uptake. Rights is the clearest IGO-centered regime and shows a short-window post-2019 signal that does not survive stronger interpretations of convergence. Safety has the clearest hybrid public-private configuration. Most metadata-coded regime-bearing documents register one regime, while 13.3% combine two or three, locating candidate interfaces for closer examination. The results imply that coordination, coherence, and integration must be designed differently across regimes rather than pursued through a single omnibus strategy.

title: Galamsey eats our food: Reframing illegal mining as a food systems crisis in Ghana
abstract: Abstract Illegal artisanal and small-scale gold mining ( galamsey ) in Ghana is commonly framed as an environmental or economic issue. This commentary argues that such perspectives are incomplete because illegal mining fundamentally constitutes a food systems crisis. Drawing on a systems perspective, this commentary synthesizes existing literature to demonstrate how galamsey disrupts agricultural production, contaminates water resources, undermines livelihoods, and creates reinforcing cycles of environmental degradation and food insecurity. The commentary identifies key leverage points, including strengthened, politically accountable enforcement; simplified pathways to legal mining; locally viable alternative livelihoods; geospatial environmental monitoring; community participation; and restoration of degraded agricultural land. By reframing galamsey as a food systems challenge, this commentary calls for integrated policy responses that align environmental sustainability with livelihood security.

title: Widening urban-rural gaps amid narrowing regional disparities in cropland footprints of food consumption in China
Classification Drift: Decisions Passing Quietly but Compounding Inequity
abstract: Public-sector classification systems accumulate classification drift, a widening gap between what employees actually do, how their work is described, and how they are compensated. Because classification shapes pay, role comparison, and internal equity at scale, classification drift quietly compounds into measurable inequity. At a large U.S. urban public school district (the District), this drift manifested as 435 employees sharing the title “Specialist” across 24 pay grades ($47,000–$125,000). This article describes PRISM (Progressive Refinement and Intelligence Synthesis Model), a multi-model AI framework developed with a research-university partner’s Data Science Institute that introduces validation friction at high-stakes decision points. Rather than automating approvals, PRISM surfaces disagreement between independent AI models and routes ambiguous cases to human reviewers with a structured evidence package. Across 992 positions, 173 cases (17%) were flagged for escalated review. This article describes what public HR offices, with or without AI, can do to address classification drift.

title: Taming the Careerists: The Politics of Foreign Policy Implementation. By MinjuKim, New York: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 224 pp. $100 (hardback); $33 (ebook). ISBN: 9781009789721
abstract: The author declares no conflicts of interest. Data sharing not applicable to this article as no datasets were generated or analyzed during the current study.

title: Resilience-oriented planning for the optimal sizing and pre-positioning of mobile power sources in distribution networks with multiple energy hubs
abstract: High-impact, low-probability (HILP) events are arising more frequently than ever before and pose a great challenge to power system resilience. Mobile power sources (MPSs) have been gradually deployed in distribution networks as critical resources towards resilience enhancement owing to their flexibility and mobility in handling the complex coupled power network environment. In addition, as localised energy systems, energy hubs (EHs) have been widely integrated into distribution networks for the effective coordination of various small-size energy sources, which can be used to support resilience enhancement given their advanced control capabilities. Therefore, this paper develops a resilience-oriented planning framework for the optimal sizing and pre-positioning of various MPSs in the power distribution network with multiple EHs. In the planning stage, the optimal sizing of MPSs, including the power capacities of mobile energy storage system (MESS) and mobile emergency generator (MEG) as well as the number of deployed electric vehicles (EVs), is determined for the after-event dispatch. In addition, the pre-positioning of MPSs is implemented, considering possible line outage scenarios. In the post-event stage, coordinated operations of MPSs and EHs are performed towards resilience enhancement. Particularly, routing and scheduling behaviours of each individual MPS are modelled in detail to fully exploit their mobility and flexibility, capturing uncertainty in traffic conditions. Furthermore, a hybrid stochastic-information gap decision theory (IGDT) approach is implemented to handle the uncertainties in line outage, renewable generation, network electricity load and EH electricity and heat loads. Case studies are first carried out based on a modified IEEE 15-bus test system, considering different outage scenarios and risk management strategies. Results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves system resilience index of 90.43 %, 88.86 % and 92.30 % under the risk-neutral, risk-averse and risk-seeking strategies, respectively. Compared with the case without MPSs and EHs, the proposed method reduces the system cost from £ 668,889.32 to £ 176,138.70 and improves the resilience index from 55.74 % to 90.43 % under the risk-neutral strategy. Furthermore, additional tests on the IEEE 33-bus system validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for resilience enhancement in larger-scale networks.

title: A comprehensive review of machine learning in proton-exchange membrane fuel cells: From materials to intelligent systems
Modeling and analysis of the operational and investment costs of hydrogen sea transportation applied to NH3 and LH2 energy derivatives

A dynamic parallelized hybrid optimization method for 22 MW large-scale floating offshore wind turbines
Synergetic capacity planning of private and public EV charging piles via city-scale multiobjective optimization
abstract: Rapid electric vehicle (EV) expansion necessitates optimized charging infrastructure to bridge the persistent gaps between vehicle growth and charger availability. This study develops a demand-driven framework for city-scale EV charging demand assessment and charging pile capacity planning. It employs a bottom-up estimation approach to quantify electricity demand and a Harris Hawks Optimization algorithm to solve capacity planning challenges, capturing spatiotemporal demand variations across powertrain types and guiding allocation over 2022-2030 in Chongqing, China. The results show that (1) compared with June 2022, monthly EV electricity consumption tripled to 57.5 gigawatt-hours by the end of 2024, characterized by significant seasonal volatility and a structural shift in which the combined share of plug-in hybrid electric vehicles and extended-range electric vehicles reached 57.6%, necessitating a transition toward technology-specific infrastructure planning; (2) historical evaluations reveal a marked spatial mismatch, with actual deployment heavily concentrated in the urban core while public charging capacity consistently lagging behind demand, whereas the proposed optimized configuration achieved a superior comprehensive performance score of 0.28, compared to 0.65 for actual deployment, in balancing service adequacy across the "Core-Suburban-Exurban" hierarchy; and (3) by 2030, Chongqing is projected to require approximately 1.8 million charging units to sustain a stable 9:1 private-to-public ratio, a synergetic strategy expects to significantly mitigate urban-rural service disparities and enhance overall system resilience and grid compatibility. Ultimately, this study provides a versatile, spatially explicit tool for policymakers to support sustainable and cost-effective EV infrastructure deployment aligned with long-term electrification targets.

title: PV-anchored hybrid solar systems across output grade and storage horizon: an exergy-informed temporal architecture review
abstract: PV-anchored hybrid solar systems increasingly co-produce electricity, useful heat, cooling, freshwater and chemical carriers, and systems with similar total energy efficiency may deliver outputs with different thermodynamic quality and time of use, which cannot be distinguished by the component-based and end-use-based methods. Therefore, this review develops an exergy-informed temporal architecture framework organized by output grade and storage horizon, in which exergy is used as a reporting and interpretation basis, because reference states, auxiliary loads, useful-product boundaries and storage losses are not consistently across studies. The literature is synthesized into four architecture families, namely direct electro-thermal delivery, real-time exergy reallocation and cascading, thermal-service time shifting and chemical-carrier time shifting, which are distinguished by whether the useful product is delivered at native grade during collection, upgraded before use, preserved as a delayed local service or converted into a transportable carrier. PV/T desalination is shown to be a cross-cutting service rather than a fifth architecture family, since it can be driven within any of them. By linking output grade, storage horizon and final service identity, the review provides design rules and a minimum reporting checklist for more rigorous energy, exergy, economic and environmental comparison of multi-output solar systems.

title: Market-driven equilibria for distributed photovoltaic panel investment
abstract: This study investigates long-term investment in distributed photovoltaic panels by individual investors. We consider a setting where investment decisions are driven by expected revenue from participating in short-term electricity markets over the panel lifespan. These revenues depend on short-term market equilibria, including prices and allocations, which are endogenously influenced by the aggregate installed panel capacity. We model interactions among investors as a non-atomic game and develop a framework that links short-term market equilibria to the resulting long-term investment equilibrium. Within this framework, we analyze three market mechanisms: (a) a single-product real-time energy market, (b) a product-differentiated real-time energy market that treats solar energy and grid energy as different products, and (c) a contract-based panel market that trades rights to future production from panel capacity ex ante, rather than realized solar production ex post. For each mechanism, we derive short-term equilibrium outcomes and associated expected revenues, and analytically characterize the corresponding long-term Nash equilibrium capacity. We compare these investment equilibria with a benchmark social optimum and establish that, in the baseline risk-neutral setting, the product-differentiated market attains this benchmark, while the single-product market induces lower investment. We also show that the contract-based market can lead to over-investment when users’ additional valuations for solar energy are small. We further study extensions incorporating time-varying operating conditions and investor risk aversion, showing how these considerations affect expected revenues and investment incentives while broadly preserving key insights from the baseline analysis. Finally, we evaluate our theoretical findings through a numerical case study.

title: Multi-objective unit commitment for renewable energy considering entropy-based uncertainty costs and carbon flow driven emission allocation
Certifiable Stackelberg coordination of multiple virtual power plants with continuous pricing under uncertainty
Dynamic economic and ecological impact assessment and performance benchmarking of decentralized hydrogen production in manufacturing systems
abstract: High-temperature manufacturing processes remain major contributors to industrial greenhouse gas emissions due to their persistent dependence on fossil fuels, positioning the sector at the center of current decarbonization policies. Hydrogen-based indirect electrification is a widely discussed and promising approach for reducing emissions in high-temperature applications that requires only moderate infrastructural modifications compared to direct electrification. However, the economic and the ecological viability of decentralized hydrogen production is significantly impacted by fluctuations of the electricity prices and the greenhouse gas intensity of the electrical grid. This limits the effectiveness of conventional static Life Cycle Costing and Life Cycle Assessment approaches for making informed strategic investment decisions for decarbonization. Therefore, this paper introduces a novel, integrated method for dynamically assessing and benchmarking the performance of decentralized hydrogen production in manufacturing systems. The proposed approach extends established life cycle-oriented assessments by a systematic dynamization. This enables the temporally resolved evaluation of the levelized costs of energy and the levelized emissions of energy for decentralized hydrogen production. As the method is able to capture dynamic energy demand profiles of manufacturing systems and dynamic energy market conditions, it reveals performance characteristics that static analyses fail to detect. The method is validated through an industrial case study and a complementary sensitivity analysis, demonstrating its applicability, robustness, and relevance as a decision support tool for hydrogen-based industrial decarbonization.

title: A real-time energy management strategy for hybrid electric aircraft based on PSM-CNN-BiLSTM prediction and PPO-warm-started MPC
Can they compete? Cost competitiveness of non-light-water reactors for heat and power supply in a decarbonized european energy system
abstract: Recent pledges to triple global nuclear capacity by 2050 suggest a "nuclear renaissance," bolstered by unconventional reactor concepts such as sodium-cooled fast reactors, high-temperature reactors, and molten salt reactors. These technologies claim to address the challenges of today's high-capacity light-water reactors, i.e., cost overruns, delays, and social acceptance, while also offering additional non-electrical applications. However, this analysis reveals that none of these concepts currently meet the prerequisites of affordability, competitiveness, or commercial availability. Our cost analysis reveals optimistic FOAK cost assumptions of 5,623 to 9,511 USD per kW, and NOAK cost projections as low as 1,476 USD per kW. At FOAK cost, the applied energy system model for Europe in 2040 includes no nuclear power capacity, and thus indicates that significant cost reductions would be required for these technologies to contribute to energy system decarbonization. In lower-cost scenarios, reactors capable of producing high and medium temperature heat compete with other technologies and dominate the system once costs fall below 5,000 USD per kW. Electricity shares reach current levels of approx. 20% once costs are reduced to 3,000 USD per kW or less We conclude that, for reactor capacities to increase significantly, a focus on certain technology lines and streamlined regulation in necessary. Further remaining technological challenges, e.g., new waste streams, must be resolved.

title: Modeling and validation of hydrogen-oxygen impurity in alkaline electrolyzers under multiple operational states for hydrogen-based microgrid scheduling
abstract: Hydrogen-based microgrids play a critical role in the consumption of distributed renewable energy sources, though their operational safety is often compromised by gas impurities in electrolyzers. Conventional scheduling models typically treat electrolyzers as static energy conversion units, neglecting the dynamic behavior of hydrogen-to-oxygen (HTO) crossover during non-operating states such as standby and shutdown. To address this limitation, this paper proposes a day-ahead scheduling framework for a hydrogen-based microgrid that explicitly incorporates gas-related safety constraints across all the states. A physics-informed dynamic model of HTO crossover is first developed and experimentally validated for operating, standby and off states, which accurately captures the exponential decay behavior over non-operating periods and transient impurity surges during state transitions. The validated model is then introduced into the hydrogen-based microgrid scheduling framework, in which electrolyzer state transitions are explicitly represented. The resulting highly nonlinear mixed-integer optimization problem is solved by using a Benders decomposition approach in conjunction with the tightened McCormick relaxation. Experimental results from a 40-kW alkaline electrolyzer system demonstrate that the proposed model achieves high accuracy in predicting HTO, with R 2 > 0.98 . The effectiveness of the proposed scheduling framework is further confirmed by comparative analyses across multiple case studies, showing that it can efficiently handle strong nonlinearities and accurately track HTO concentrations with a mean approximation error reduced by up to 89.3% compared with the benchmark methods, thereby reliably ensuring electrolyzer operational safety.

title: Unlocking contingency-exclusive flexibility for interruptible load via extreme operating modes of aggregated residential appliances
Copula-based joint distributionally robust chance-constrained low-carbon operation of renewable power-to-methanol systems
Conditional remaining useful life prediction of lithium-ion batteries under specified future working conditions
abstract: Remaining useful life (RUL) is a critical metric for long-term battery management and decision-making. Most existing Lithium-ion battery RUL estimation methods rely on the individual historical data and assume a fixed coupling between the current cycle and future working conditions, thereby yielding only a single RUL prediction at current cycle. This implicit assumption fundamentally limits the predictive capability and practical applicability of conventional RUL metrics. To enable a more flexible and complete decoupling between data and working conditions across different stages of battery operation, this paper proposes a novel concept termed Conditional Remaining Useful Life (C-RUL). C-RUL is defined as the remaining life of a battery cell at current aging state under a specified future working condition. This definition explicitly indicates that RUL is conditioned on the working condition, such that multiple RUL values may exist in same current aging state under different working conditions. By relaxing the fixed coupling between current and future working conditions, C-RUL significantly extends the scope of conventional RUL formulations and enhances the practical value of RUL for predictive analysis and decision-making. The proposed framework is validated using the open-access ISU-ILCC battery aging dataset and achieves accurate prediction performance, with a root mean square error (RMSE) of 247.54 cycles and an R 2 of 0.8975 on the generated test samples. It is further validated on another benchmark dataset with an R 2 of 0.94, which shows the method’s generalization capability. Additionally, the potential of the method for several application scenarios is investigated, including working-condition control under target optimization objectives, safety-aware charging policy design under partial uncertainty in future discharging behaviors, and C-RUL-based balancing of battery cells with heterogeneous aging states. The results show the effectiveness of the proposed framework on established datasets and highlight its potential for informed decision-making in future battery management systems.

Recent advances in combustion/explosion hazards and suppression strategies for metal hydride hydrogen storage materials
abstract: Metal hydride solid-state hydrogen storage materials show strong potential for large-scale hydrogen energy applications because of their high volumetric hydrogen storage density, mild operating conditions, and relatively sound inherent safety. However, combustion and explosion hazards remain during preparation, storage, utilization, and disposal. These hazards mainly arise from hydrogen release during endothermic dehydrogenation, subsequent exothermic combustion of released hydrogen and oxidation of active metal residues, formation of combustible dust clouds, and rapid interaction with air. This review examines the process features and associated combustion and explosion hazards of the primary preparation routes for metal hydrides. It further analyzes the combustion and explosion behavior and multiphase reaction mechanisms of representative metal hydrides, with particular emphasis on how the dehydrogenation-oxidation coupling process intensifies flame propagation and explosion severity. In addition, the review summarizes the suppression mechanisms of inert gases, solid inhibitors, and composite inhibitors, highlighting physical dilution and cooling, free-radical scavenging, and protective film formation. The reviewed evidence indicates that preparation process control and appropriately selected suppression strategies can lessen combustion and explosion hazards and provide practical guidance for the safer engineering deployment of metal hydride hydrogen storage materials.

title: Deep underground energy storage solutions for data centers driven by artificial intelligence energy consumption
abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) has driven an unprecedented surge in electricity consumption by data centers (DCs). Although renewable energy and ground-based energy storage technologies are being widely adopted, they still face inherent limitations in scalability, safety, structure and stability. This review proposes deep underground energy storage (DUES) as a new approach and discusses three specific technologies: hydrogen storage, compressed air energy storage, and flow batteries. Firstly, it is found that DUES can align with AI load curves. The three technologies span storage durations from quarterly to hourly scales and response times from minutes to seconds, matching respectively the sustained high loads of AI model pre-training, the intermittent loads of fine-tuning, and the stochastic loads of inference. Secondly, we further develop a “Source-Grid-Production-Storage-Computing” model, in which DUES serves as the regulating hub bridging the intermittency of renewable energy with the stability of DCs. Subsequently, an economic assessment indicates that the levelized cost of storage for flow batteries ranges 0.340∼0.455 yuan/kWh, while that for compressed air energy storage ranges 0.746∼0.998 yuan/kWh, making them cost-competitive. Although the cost of hydrogen storage is 1.085∼1.658 yuan/kWh, it possesses strategic value. Finally, in view of challenges such as siting and stability of storage facilities, and system conversion efficiency, we recommend launching DUES for DC pilot projects in the short term, advancing multi-scenario applications in the medium term, and achieving industrialization in the long term. In summary, DUES represents a feasible, economically viable, and scalable solution to the energy challenges faced by AI-driven DCs.

title: From cross-border power links to a digitalized regional market: A critical review of the ASEAN power grid as a catalyst for decarbonization
A comprehensive review of phase change heat transfer enhancement with particular focus on nano/microscale liquid film
A review and comparative study of spectral correction models for photovoltaic performance under different atmospheric regimes and PV technologies
abstract: ABSTRACT Spectral effects can cause non-negligible deviations in photovoltaic performance modelling, yet the applicability of existing spectral correction models remains insufficiently understood across different climates, weather conditions, and PV technologies. Most existing spectral correction models have been developed under clear or all-sky conditions, while their performance under cloudy conditions has not been systematically investigated. This limitation is critical, as cloudy conditions account for a substantial fraction of operating periods in many regions, and the spectral distribution varies substantially with cloud cover and cloud properties, introducing additional uncertainty in model accuracy and generalisability. This study provides a comprehensive review of recent advances in PV spectral correction modelling, including spectral variability drivers and characterization approaches, and further conducts a unified benchmarking analysis. Using a public dataset comprising measurements from three climatically distinct sites, eight representative spectral correction models were evaluated for four PV technologies under both clear-sky and cloudy-sky conditions. The results reveal a strong weather-regime dependence in model performance. Under clear-sky conditions, multi-parameter formulations based on precipitable water (PW), particularly f(AMa_PW) and f(AMa_AOD_PW), generally show better prediction performance than the other evaluated approaches. Under cloudy conditions, formulations based on the clear-sky index, generally show improved prediction performance compared with the basic f(AMa) formulation. In contrast, the widely used single-parameter model f(AMa) performs poorly under both regimes, while f(APE) shows mixed performance but may remain useful for specific PV technologies such as a-Si. Cloudy conditions account for a substantial fraction of annual operating periods and should not be neglected in long-term PV performance assessment. Overall, no single spectral correction model is universally optimal across all climates, weather conditions, and PV technologies. Model suitability instead depends on whether its predictors capture the dominant physical processes controlling spectral variability under the corresponding operating regime. These findings provide practical guidance for the development of more adaptive and climate-aware spectral correction methods for PV performance modelling.

title: Creating a Circular Economy Vision for the Data Centre Industry
Entropy as a diagnostic for time-related constraints on circular transition: Evidence from plastic waste management in the OECD–EU countries
abstract: This study examines time-related constraints on circularity by applying Shannon entropy to measure distributional dispersion across end-of-life fates in plastic waste management. Using OECD data for 1990–2018, end-of-life shares for recycling, incineration, landfill, mismanaged, and littered waste are combined with entropy to assess structural change over time. Entropy makes that structural shift visible and comparable across time. During the early 1990s, plastic waste management was highly predictable due to landfill dominance. From the mid-2010s onward, entropy stabilized at a high level despite continued growth in recycling. That plateau is consistent with persistent dispersion across competing end-of-life routes rather than convergence toward recycling dominance.

title: Functional interdependence and spatial spillover in the regional metabolism: a spatial econometric study of an interconnected network of cities in Belgium
The Time Architecture of Circularity
Mechanisms of Hexavalent Chromium Reduction in Fe(II)-Bearing Clay Mineral and Fe (hydr)oxide Binary Systems: Competitive Adsorption versus Mediated Electron Transfer
abstract: Abstract Fe(II)-bearing clay minerals are widespread reductants of hexavalent chromium (Cr(VI)) in subsurface environments. However, the influences of coexisting Fe (hydr)oxides on Cr(VI) reduction by Fe(II)-bearing clay minerals remain elusive. Here, Cr(VI) reduction was investigated in premixed systems of reduced nontronite NAu-2 (rNAu-2) and various Fe (hydr)oxides. Results showed that coexisting ferrihydrite significantly facilitated Cr(VI) reduction during the quick stage (0–2.5 min) across pH 5.5–9.0. During the subsequent slow stage (2.5–205 min), ferrihydrite inhibited Cr(VI) reduction at pH 5.5–7.0 but enhanced it at pH 9.0. In contrast, coexisting goethite had negligible effects. Without Fe (hydr)oxides, direct reduction by rNAu-2 dominated for Cr(VI) removal. In the presence of Fe (hydr)oxides, competitive adsorption was found to inhibit direct Cr(VI) reduction, yet Fe (hydr)oxide-mediated electron transfer effectively offset this inhibitory effect. Both competitive adsorption and mediated electron transfer were influenced by the type and dosage of Fe (hydr)oxides, as well as solution pH. Kinetic modeling revealed that ferrihydrite-mediated electron transfer contributed 1.8–71.5% of the total Cr(VI) reduction, with greater contributions observed at higher solution pH and ferrihydrite dosage. Our findings provide new insights into mineral–mineral electron transfer and its role in regulating Cr(VI) fate in subsurface environments.

title: Trace Hydrogen Sulfide Enhances Plasmid-Mediated Antibiotic Resistance Gene Transfer under Anaerobic Sewer-Like Conditions: Associations with Contact and Energy-State Responses
abstract: Abstract The dissemination of antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) in sewer systems poses a potential threat to public health. However, it is currently unclear how hydrogen sulfide (H2S) in anaerobic sewers affects plasmid-mediated ARG transfer. Here, we evaluated the effects of environmentally relevant concentrations (1–100 μmol·L–1) of H2S on ARG transfer across different sewer microbial communities. The results demonstrated that H2S significantly enhanced the transfer frequency of plasmid pKJK5 in sediment-derived (2.06–3.06-fold), sewage-derived (1.50–2.81-fold), and bioaerosol-derived (2.42–4.68-fold) recipient communities in standardized liquid anaerobic conjugation assays. In mixed-community models, H2S increased total acyl-homoserine lactone (AHL)-equivalent signals and was associated with selective enrichment of polysaccharides in extracellular polymeric substances (EPS), coinciding with enhanced microbial aggregation and contact. In single-strain models, H2S was associated with reductive-stress-like responses, lowered the NAD+/NADH ratio, enhanced phosphofructokinase and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase activities, strengthened proton motive force, and increased ATP content. Inhibitor experiments and structural equation modeling suggested ATP availability as the strongest intracellular predictor of enhanced transfer, with AHL-associated EPS changes acting as a potential extracellular contributor. These findings identify a concentration-dependent sulfide effect on conjugation under anaerobic conditions and support a testable pathway-level framework for future in situ sewer studies.

title: Elucidating Olivine Carbon Mineralization Behaviors under Weakly Acidic to Alkaline Conditions for CO2 Storage
abstract: Abstract Olivine ((Mg,Fe)2SiO4), an ultrabasic mineral primarily found in peridotite rock, is earth-abundant and thus has great potential to store anthropogenic CO2 at a scale relevant to climate change mitigation. The groundwater from geologic formations composed of peridotite, such as the Samail Ophiolite in Oman, has an ultrahigh pH (>10), which is underexplored as a direct carbonation condition. This study investigated a wide range of initial pH (3–14) to elucidate the roles of pH and alkalinity during the direct carbonation behavior of olivine at a high temperature (185 °C). Despite the expected negative correlation between pH and olivine dissolution kinetics, this study revealed that alkaline pH conditions significantly enhance direct carbonation kinetics. The study also determined the effects of initial total alkalinity and the roles of different alkalinity sources, offering valuable perspectives for estimating direct carbonation behavior across a wide range of reaction conditions.

title: Harnessing the Microbial Iron Redox Chain: Liquid Organic Acid Fertilizer and EDTA-Fe Drive Unexpected Cadmium Passivation in Alkaline Upland Soils
abstract: Abstract The immobilization of cadmium (Cd) in weakly alkaline upland soils, a major agricultural system in northern China, remains a challenge. This study examined whether liquid organic acid (OA) fertilizer and EDTA-Fe could stimulate Fe redox to stabilize Cd. OA fertilizer (active ingredients: citric acid, lactic acid, and glucose) induced microbial Fe(III) reduction and acidification within 1 day, shifting Cd from Fe/Mn-oxide and organic fractions to exchangeable and carbonate forms. Iron reduction and acidification contributed 52.0–55.8% and 44.2–48.0% of Cd activation, respectively. Subsequent Fe(II) oxidation over 60 days reimmobilized Cd into Fe/Mn-oxide and residual fractions. Adding EDTA-Fe enhanced Fe(III) reduction (raising Cd activation by 35.4%) while slowing Fe(II) oxidation and increasing Cd passivation by 31.8%. Such passivation was driven by newly formed secondary Fe oxides and Fe–Al–Si minerals, and ceased when Fe(II) oxidation was inhibited. Simulations supported Cd association with Fe–Al–Si phases, and EDTA-Fe enhanced immobilization via surface complexation/coprecipitation. Unlike paddy soils, Cd dynamics in alkaline soils are distinct despite both being Fe redox-driven, underscoring the need for alkaline-specific strategies. This approach works across diverse soils (pH 7.41–8.43; Cd 1.33–30.06 mg kg–1), reducing available Cd by 19.4–51.6%, and provides new insights into Fe redox-controlled Cd stabilization in upland soils.

title: Single-Cell Insights into Virus–Microbe Interactions in Emerging Contaminant Degradation
abstract: Abstract Viruses are increasingly recognized as critical regulators of microbial ecology, yet their roles in pollutant degradation remain largely unexplored. Here, we integrate Raman-activated cell sorting–stable isotope probing (RACS-SIP) and single-cell genomics to elucidate virus–microbe interactions underlying methylnaphthalene biodegradation in petroleum-contaminated soils. Microcosm experiments demonstrated up to 80% removal of methylnaphthalene within 36 days, accompanied by pronounced shifts in microbial and viral communities. Correlation analyses suggested potential virus–host associations, with Ochrobactrum and an unclassified Caudoviricetes phage emerging as key contributors to degradation. RACS-SIP enabled in situ identification and isolation of active degraders, and single-cell genomic analysis indicated that viral auxiliary metabolic genes, including methyltransferases, aldehyde dehydrogenases, and decarboxylases, may complement host pathways for the multistep conversion of methylnaphthalene to naphthalene. Subsequent mineralization occurs through canonical catechol and gentisate pathways encoded by the host genome. This study provides preliminary evidence that viruses may act as metabolic collaborators rather than passive parasites in pollutant degradation, potentially enhancing host metabolic capacity and influencing biodegradation outcomes. Beyond revealing a virus-inclusive metabolic network, the RACS-SIP framework overcomes key limitations of traditional metagenomic methods by resolving virus–host linkages at the single-cell level. These findings broaden our understanding of viral ecological functions and highlight novel leverage points for bioremediation technologies targeting emerging contaminants.

title: Cross-Radical Knowledge Sharing via Graph Neural Networks for Unified Prediction of Aqueous Organic Contaminant Second-Order Radical Reaction Rate Constants
abstract: Abstract Selecting among hydroxyl (HO•), sulfate (SO4•–), and carbonate (CO3•–) radical advanced oxidation processes requires reliable intrinsic second-order rate constants, yet the corresponding curated data sets contain 1250, 493, and 248 records, respectively. Reframing this imbalance as a cross-radical few-shot learning problem, we introduce maco, a radical-conditioned graph neural network that uses shared molecular representation learning, oxidant/pH cross-attention, residual adapters, and a two-stage curriculum to transfer structural knowledge from the data-rich HO• task to the lower-data SO4•– and CO3•– tasks. On similarity-stratified held-out tests, maco achieved R2 = 0.855 (95% CI 0.711–0.906) for SO4•– and 0.815 (0.269–0.944) for CO3•–; on the more stringent scaffold-disjoint Murcko tests, the corresponding values were 0.652 (0.447–0.779) and 0.715 (0.500–0.825). Temperature-conditioned sensitivity analyses showed no statistically discernible generalization gain under the highly asymmetric temperature coverage. Functional-group attention analysis identified radical- and pH-dependent reactive-site patterns, while applicability-domain assessment and ensemble uncertainty quantified prediction reliability for target-radical scaffold-novel contaminants. maco provides a reproducible screening input for prioritising radical–contaminant measurements and process-specific evaluation. A browser-accessible WebUI further provides single-compound predictions, uncertainty estimates, and applicability-domain flags without local installation.

title: Methanotroph-Derived Reactive Oxygen Species Facilitate Arsenic Oxidation in Paddy Soils
abstract: Abstract Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are increasingly recognized as important oxidants in soil redox processes, with microbially produced ROS contributing broadly to elemental transformations. Given the active methane oxidation in paddy soils, methanotrophs have considerable potential to generate ROS yet their role in As(III) oxidation remains unclear. Here, we identify methanotroph-derived ROS as an important yet previously overlooked pathway for As(III) oxidation in paddy soils. Soil microcosm experiments and pure culture experiments revealed that methane oxidation enhanced ROS-mediated As(III) oxidation, with H2O2 identified as the dominant ROS. Inhibitor assays and functional gene analyses indicated that oxygen activation and respiratory electron transfer were closely associated with ROS generation during methane oxidation. These findings reveal methanotroph-derived ROS as a distinct route contributing to As(III) oxidation beyond dedicated arsenite oxidases. By revealing an overlooked connection between methane metabolism and arsenic transformation, this work expands our understanding of arsenic biogeochemistry and provides a conceptual basis for the coordinated mitigation of methane emissions and arsenic toxicity in agroecosystems.

title: Is Electro-Stimulation Always Effective for Methanogenesis? A Holistic Assessment of Electric Potential and Current Effects in Highly Conductive Systems
abstract: Abstract Electro-stimulated anaerobic digestion (EAD) typically relies on voltage-only regulation, neglecting the impacts of the associated response current, particularly in highly conductive systems. Herein, we investigated an EAD system for treating iron-containing sludge digestate. Unexpectedly, under appropriate applied voltages of 0.9 to 1.2 V, the high conductivity triggered excessive currents, which subsequently inhibited methanogenesis. By decoupling the dual potential–current effects, integrated with metatranscriptomics analysis, we revealed that excessive currents induced severe, localized oxidative stress on anodic biofilms (up to 2.3-fold of the CF group) and hindered carbon metabolism. Concurrently, lower cathodic potentials triggered microenvironmental alkalinization, accelerating calcite and ankerite deposition, which increased the mass transfer resistance by up to 1.4-fold. Consequently, the positive biological effects of electro-stimulation (e.g., Geobacter enrichment, upregulated methanogenic genes) were counterbalanced by these current-induced physical and biochemical barriers. This study highlights the necessity of comanaging electric potential and current when deploying electro-microbial technologies in highly conductive systems toward energy-efficient AD facilities.

title: Maternal Epigenetic Signatures Linking Prenatal Serum PFAS Concentrations to Birth Size in an African American Maternal–Child Cohort
abstract: Abstract Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) exposures have been linked to reduced birth size, but the underlying epigenetic mechanisms remain unclear. Among 296 mother–infant dyads in the Atlanta African American Maternal–Child Cohort (2016–2020), early pregnancy maternal blood samples (8–14 weeks) were processed for serum PFAS assessment and blood mononuclear cell (PBMC) DNA methylation profiling. We assessed birth size using sex-specific birth weight z-scores (BWZ) and small-for-gestational-age (SGA) status. Individual and mixture PFAS methylation associations were estimated by using robust generalized linear regression and quantile g-computation. We also conducted differentially methylated region (DMR), gene ontology, sex-specific, and exploratory mediation analyses. Overall, 132 CpGs were associated with at least one PFAS (FDR < 0.05), including 34, 60, 32, and 10 linked with PFHxS, PFOS, PFOA, and PFNA, respectively. PFOS showed the largest effects and appeared to drive the mixture associations. Six CpGs (annotated to EVA1A, FCRL1, CTIF, ABHD12, and WDYHV1) were associated with PFAS levels and birth size indicators. We identified 2–9 DMRs associated with individual PFASs and their mixture. Sex-specific PFAS methylation associations were observed. The PFAS-associated genes are involved in the inflammatory response, immune activity, and lipid homeostasis. Prenatal serum PFAS concentrations were associated with alterations in maternal DNA methylation, which in turn were associated with infant birth size.

Evaluating the impact of BRI toward greener energy and carbon neutrality
abstract: Belt and Road Initiative (BRI) has primarily been studied for its economic benefits; its role in promoting greener energy transitions and carbon neutrality goals is not well explored. This study examines the effects of BRI across 90 BRI countries from 1995 to 2021 with a focus on greener energy transition and carbon neutrality. Quantile Treatment Effect (QTE) models are used to compare the effectiveness of BRI across quantile levels and groups of countries. In general, results show evidence that BRI has effectively reduced CO 2 emissions and enhanced renewable energy consumption, with the effects being more pronounced in countries that exhibit high CO 2 and renewable energy consumption. The developed countries and countries with high renewable energy potential and high pollution levels are most benefitted from joining BRI. The impact of BRI in the developing and low-income countries is less prominent. In summary, the BRI tends to create the most significant environmental benefits in countries that already have a relatively high level of development, allowing them to leverage new technologies and investments for further decarbonization.

title: Manure Composting as a Strategy to Mitigate Antibiotic Resistance Dissemination in Agricultural Systems
abstract: ABSTRACT Livestock manure is a valuable agricultural resource but may introduce antibiotic residues and antibiotic resistance genes (ARGs) into the environment. This review critically evaluates the fate of antibiotics and ARGs during manure composting and identifies the principal factors controlling their attenuation. It integrates composting‐system configuration and phase‐specific operating conditions with antibiotic properties, microbial‐host succession, extracellular DNA, mobile genetic elements (MGEs), post‐application risks, and alternative manure‐treatment technologies. Composting can reduce many antibiotic residues by 80%–90% or more, although apparent removal may reflect degradation, transformation, sorption, or reduced extractability and remains strongly compound‐ and process‐dependent. ARG responses are more variable and often non‐linear. Sustained thermophilic conditions can reduce ARG‐carrying microorganisms and MGEs, but selected genes may persist or rebound during maturation because of microbial recolonization, residual selection pressure, extracellular DNA persistence, and horizontal gene transfer (HGT). Temperature and exposure duration, aeration, moisture, C:N ratio, bulking materials, biochar, and microbial inoculants are therefore key determinants of treatment performance. Composting substantially mitigates antimicrobial‐resistance risks but does not guarantee complete elimination of transmissible ARGs. Standardized monitoring, full‐scale validation, and long‐term assessment of soil and crop compartments are required to support safe agricultural use of composted manure.

title: Asynchronous Response of Plant Productivity and Soil Aggregate Nutrients to Grazing Exclusion Duration in Alpine Steppe
abstract: ABSTRACT Grazing exclusion is a critical restoration measure for degraded alpine steppe ecosystems. However, research remains limited on the key factors influencing soil aggregates that affect plant productivity and the mechanisms influencing nutrient distribution across aggregates of different size fractions during long‐term grazing exclusion. We examined alpine steppe ecosystems in northern Tibet with a space‐for‐time substitution approach to analyze dynamic changes in plant productivity and soil aggregate nutrients across different exclusion durations (0, 2, 6, 13, and 18 years). Community aboveground biomass and Stipa purpurea biomass initially increased and peaked after 6 years of exclusion, followed by a gradual decline. In contrast, long‐term exclusion (≥ 13 years) significantly increased the proportion of soil macroaggregates and their associated organic carbon, nitrate nitrogen, and available phosphorus contents. Spearman correlation analysis revealed that nitrate nitrogen stored in macroaggregates was negatively correlated with plant productivity. These results indicate an asynchronous response between vegetation recovery and soil aggregate nutrient dynamics during ecological restoration. Plant productivity recovered rapidly in the short term but did not synchronize with improvements in soil structure and nutrient pools. Although prolonged enclosure enhanced total soil nutrient stocks, nutrients became increasingly physically protected within stable macroaggregates, reducing their accessibility to plant roots. Soil aggregate‐scale nutrient distribution regulates alpine steppe productivity under grazing exclusion. These findings deepen our understanding of alpine steppe ecosystem restoration dynamics and the coordination of ecological conservation with sustainable pastoral development.

title: Eternal chattel? Or, how to live in a moveable house when liberal time isn’t enough
abstract: Examining the ways that a redistributive politics of possession is haunted by Lockean moral claims regarding land, this paper is a conceptual exploration of the entanglement of land possession and race as mercurial artifacts of colonialism. Thinking from the Caribbean reveals the need for a mode of storying that exposes and undoes the colonial boundary-making on land and bodies that produced these artifacts. I explore this first through the contradictory capacity of moveable houses in Jamaica to stay put because they can move. Rejecting the habitually truncated narration of Caribbean histories and places, I then put the wood house in relation to deeper timescales and broader geographies of archipelagic placemaking. In doing so, I consider the wood house as a guide towards the commensurability of anticolonial projects to live land otherwise. Ultimately, the house’s capacity for motion signals not merely the power of (dis)possession, but an ongoing relational potentiality.
journal_name: Environment and Planning C: Politics and Space

title: Terrain, visibility and temporalities of mountain autonomy
abstract: This article explores the role of terrain in configuring political boundaries among local communities, market forces, and the state. Built upon fieldwork conducted between 2021 and 2024, the article addresses the role of terrain volume as a constitutive agent shaping, particularly in the central mountain areas of Chile, a layer of political negotiation between practices carried out by residents—especially drovers or cowboys (arrieros) of smaller livestock and landowners—and the state’s mandate. This article pays attention to residents' practices of space navigation and their use of terrain to create temporary autonomy from the state. Autonomy here is attained by people keeping themselves at the edge of the state, thus eluding public officials as illustrated by new forms of visibility arising from the interaction between pumas and cattle breeders. Local spatial practices and terrain knowledge are key to modulating whether residents interact with state's heteronomy or enact autonomy. We conclude by showing how mobility is a defining feature in the creation of alter-spaces and regulating the affordance that people have in the face of the state and market’s presence and their environmental effects.
