Propagation of Immigration Shocks through Firm-to-Firm Trade Networks,
abstract: Abstract This paper investigates the extent to which an immigration shock to a region propagates through supply chains. Using the unexpected arrival of Syrian refugees, who are densely concentrated in border regions of Turkey, we estimate how firms across the country are affected in terms of sales, employment, and wages. We also examine the impact of the shock on interprovincial trade, focusing on trade volume and network formation. The results reveal positive spillover effects of immigration for firms with pre-existing links to Syrian refugee-hosting regions through upstream and downstream supply chain connections. Furthermore, we find evidence that the shock expands inter-provincial trade and contributes to the formation of new firm-to-firm linkages between provinces. Finally, we show that traditional spatial approaches that compare regions with differing migration rates may conflate cross-province propagation with the direct effect of migrants; in our setting, this conflation overstates direct effects on sales and employment at both the firm and regional levels of aggregation and masks a negative direct wage effect at the firm level.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Inattention, Information Provision, and (Failures of) Revealed Preference,
abstract: Abstract Economists often estimate preferences by looking at how demand for an option changes as its attributes change or as beliefs about them change in response to information. I show in a multi-attribute induced-preference experiment that this method can be substantially biased due to differential inattention. Attention is systematically distorted at baseline, with participants reacting much more to some attributes than others. Further, attention is highly malleable: information telling participants about the value of a desirable attribute—even when the information is already known, transparently redundant, and explicitly randomly assigned—greatly increases attention to the attribute it describes and distracts from other attributes. It also boosts average demand for the good, implying that inattention takes the form of neglect rather than shrinkage toward a prior. These results combine to imply that information experiments with passive control groups can be greatly misleading about preferences and can even have the wrong sign: in my experiment, reducing overoptimism about an attribute nonetheless boosts demand for its associated good. I show, both theoretically and experimentally, that active control-group experiments yield preference estimates with the correct sign but biased magnitudes. Finally I show that parallel active control-group experiments (PACEs) can solve this problem: PACEs yield unbiased estimates of preferences under an equal induced-attention assumption, which is testable (and satisfied) in my experiment.
journal_name: Journal of the European Economic Association

title: Equilibrium selection in pure bubble models by dividend injection
Correlated perfect equilibrium
abstract: Abstract We propose a refinement of correlated equilibrium based on common perturbations of the mediator’s recommendation distribution, which we call correlated perfect equilibrium (CPE). In finite games, the set of CPEs is nonempty and forms a finite union of convex polyhedra. Like perfect equilibrium, a CPE never assigns positive probability to any weakly dominated strategy. We provide a dual representation of CPE, which yields an iterative procedure for identifying CPEs. These perturbations provide a common source of off-equilibrium beliefs, a feature that distinguishes CPE from two existing refinements of correlated equilibrium—acceptable correlated equilibrium (Myerson, 1986) and perfect direct correlated equilibrium (Dhillon and Mertens, 1996)—as we demonstrate through examples.

title: Platform development in incumbent firms: The interplay of data and actor interests in adding platforms to existing businesses
abstract: Abstract Research Summary Despite growing interest in platform transitions, limited research examines how firms navigate challenges of building platform businesses alongside existing products. Through a longitudinal case study of a financial services firm launching a platform, we develop a process model revealing how data bottlenecks shape platform development. These bottlenecks arise from the interplay of technological limitations and control tensions over data aggregation, sharing, and usage. We identify five sequential bottlenecks, where resolving one reconfigures constraints, giving rise to the next. We theorize how data heterogeneity, variation in strategic sensitivity, and actors' absorptive capacity create opportunities for platform sponsors to capture value without competing with complementors. We extend resource dependency theory by showing how peripheral units overcome power imbalances by demonstrating value creation potential with limited data. Managerial Summary When established firms launch platforms alongside existing product businesses, they face significant data‐related obstacles. Drawing on a four‐year study of a financial services firm building a platform connecting SMEs with lenders, we show how firms must navigate challenges in collecting data from internal units and customers, making incompatible data sources work together, and persuading partners to share and use data in new ways. We find that these obstacles emerge in sequence, where resolving one creates the conditions for the next. We also find that not all data is equally useful to all partners, and that these differences can open market segments the platform sponsor can serve without competing with its own partners. Managers can maintain momentum by combining short‐term data workarounds with longer‐term structural solutions.

title: Analyst visibility and earnings forecast quality
abstract: Abstract This study examines how a reduction in analysts’ visibility, resulting from brokerages’ switch to anonymous forecasts on Eikon, affects earnings forecast quality. Using a difference-in-differences design, we find that treatment analysts respond by issuing more accurate forecasts in the post-anonymization period. Treatment analysts who improve forecast quality the most can sustain visibility, as reflected in their coverage by the financial media, enhance their likelihood of being voted as star analysts, and induce greater client trading. These results are consistent with analysts’ incentives to offset the reduced visibility so as to advance their careers and increase trading commissions for their brokerages. We further show that treatment analysts use a set of visibility-enhancing strategies, including issuing broader and more frequent forecasts and setting bolder target prices. Our findings suggest that reduced visibility can prompt analysts to respond strategically in ways that can improve information quality.

title: Do Incentive‐Based Policies Reduce Firm‐Level CO2 Emissions? Evidence From EU Cohesion Policy
abstract: ABSTRACT We examine whether incentive‐based policies reduce emissions among beneficiary Italian firms, using project‐level data from European cohesion policy. Exploiting quasi‐random variation in the timing of EU‐funded projects, we apply a staggered difference‐in‐differences design. We find robust evidence that EU climate‐related incentives lower firm emissions. Recipient firms reduce emissions per unit of assets by 4.6% relative to non‐recipient firms, while a 1% increase in EU funds per unit of assets leads to a 1.1% reduction in emissions. The effects are larger in less developed and transition regions, where policy resources are more concentrated, and among energy‐sector firms. We further show that emission reductions are mainly driven by increased R&D activity: firms receiving green EU funds raise patenting by 3.0%–3.6%, with no significant effects on employment or tangible assets. These findings highlight the potential of incentive‐based climate policy.

title: When Does SDG Adoption Increase ESG Risk? The Mediating Role of Risk Management
abstract: ABSTRACT Corporate engagement with the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) has expanded rapidly, yet its implications for firms' environmental, social and governance (ESG) risk remain insufficiently understood. Prior research has focused on the performance outcomes of SDG adoption while largely overlooking its potential to generate ESG risk. This study addresses this gap by analysing the relationship between SDG‐aligned ESG practices and ESG risk through the lens of legitimacy theory. We distinguish between symbolic and substantive alignment and test whether ESG risk management mediates this relationship. Using a panel of 1589 firms, we examine the circumstances in which SDG adoption can generate ESG risk. Our findings suggest that SDG‐aligned practices can increase ESG risk when they are not supported by effective risk management, whereas substantive SDG alignment embedded in robust ESG risk management mitigates ESG risk. These findings provide insights for managers, investors and regulators seeking to develop credible sustainability strategies.

title: Mitigating the Heat: The Role of AI Technology in Shielding Corporate Environmental Performance From Extreme Temperatures—Difference‐in‐Differences Evidence From Chinese Listed Firms
abstract: ABSTRACT Extreme heat has become a recurring operational challenge that disrupts production, raises energy and maintenance needs, and makes it harder for firms to sustain environmental performance. However, it remains less clear whether AI‐related capability is associated with firms' ability to maintain environmental performance under recurring extreme‐heat exposure. We develop a conceptual framework in which heat exposure diverts organizational attention and slack resources toward operational continuity, whereas AI‐related capability may support monitoring, prediction, coordination, and resource optimization. Empirically, using data from Chinese listed companies between 2011 and 2022, we employ a staggered difference‐in‐differences model to infer causal relationships. Specifically, AI‐related capability is proxied by AI‐related patents, extreme high temperature is defined as the occurrence of days exceeding 40°C, and environmental performance is derived from the environmental (E) component of third‐party ESG ratings. Our findings reveal that extreme heat significantly reduces corporate environmental performance. In the baseline intensity specification, one additional extreme‐heat day is associated with a 0.178‐point decline in firms' environmental performance score. However, in firms that have adopted AI technology, the negative effects are mitigated, with notable heterogeneity across industries. These findings suggest that AI‐related capability may act as resilience‐oriented intangible capital, helping firms reduce the environmental costs of operating under climate stress. The study adds to research on climate risk and ESG performance by providing evidence that AI‐related capability may condition firms' environmental vulnerability to recurring heat exposure, with practical implications for AI‐related innovation, digital capability building, and climate adaptation policy.

title: Alleviating user anxiety towards AI health assistant platforms: integrating HAII-TIME and perceived control perspectives
The impact of platform verification badges on social media influencer engagement
Biodiversity reporting in the coal mining industry: an institutional theory perspective
abstract: Purpose This study is motivated by the progressive loss of biodiversity, the impact of coal mining on it, and the need for companies to report transparently on biodiversity. The study aims to investigate how the largest coal mining companies across major coal-producing regions (Australia, China, India, Indonesia, the EU, and the USA) account for biodiversity in their corporate reports and examines the institutional pressures associated with these reporting practices. Design/methodology/approach We adopt an exploratory qualitative design and perform a cross-regional analysis of 28 major coal mining companies from six regions. We apply content analysis to examine biodiversity reporting and employ institutional theory to evaluate the coercive, mimetic, and normative pressures associated with these practices. Findings Our findings indicate weak and fragmented biodiversity reporting, with a notable trend towards more comprehensive reporting in Indonesia and India. We identify a pattern of fragmented isomorphism, in which common reporting responses coexist with substantial regional variations associated with differences in institutional pressures across regional contexts. Practical implications We recommend mandatory reporting obligations aligned with recognised voluntary standards, including species- and context-specific indicators to support more substantive biodiversity impact disclosure. We further emphasise the importance of biodiversity expertise in reporting processes and strengthening biodiversity-related competencies in business education. For companies, industry-specific frameworks can support them in identifying context-specific biodiversity impacts and developing science-based, time-bound biodiversity targets. Originality/value The study contributes to biodiversity reporting and institutional theory by identifying fragmented isomorphism within a single high-impact industry, where differences in institutional pressures across regional contexts are associated with non-uniform reporting patterns.

title: What Does Representation Represent? Disaggregating Demographic and Behavioral Components
abstract: ABSTRACT Representative bureaucracy research has often linked demographic representation directly to favorable outcomes, inferring active representation post hoc while rarely separating the behavioral component presumed to accompany such associations from the representation variable itself. This study addresses such gap by drawing on gender differences in leadership literature to operationalize supportive leadership as one behavioral component associated with female supervisory representation and examine the constituent elements of what has been interpreted as a representation effect. Using gender pay inequality across US federal agencies as the empirical context, the findings show that while both female supervisory representation and supportive leadership are each positively associated with nonsupervisory salaries when examined separately, the association attributed to representation loses significance once both are modeled together. These findings do not suggest that representation is unimportant; rather, they indicate that prior representation effects may partially reflect a behavioral component that has not been separately identified.

title: The DOGE Experiment: Algorithmic Governance, Operational Capture, and the Case for Hybrid Intelligence
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) as a case of algorithmic governance whose stated purpose, improving federal efficiency, diverged systematically from its operational effect: enabling unprecedented private‐sector access to federal data systems while dismantling the oversight and civil‐service infrastructure that constrains such access. Drawing on state capacity, bounded rationality, organizational learning, and public value theory, the analysis demonstrates that the conventional efficiency‐failure reading, though correct on its own terms, obscures what made DOGE structurally distinct from the Grace Commission, the National Performance Review, the President's Management Agenda, and Program Assessment Rating Tool, and the Government Performance and Results Modernization Act. The article advances hybrid intelligence, structured human‐AI collaboration with protected institutional capacity, as a paradigm resisting both reform failure and algorithmic capture. International implementations operationalize it. The analysis contributes a stated‐versus‐operational‐goal analytic to the AI governance literature and identifies legislative grounding as a precondition for durable reform.

title: Artificial Intelligence, Regulatory Capacity, and the Adaptive State
abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence is changing not only what regulators govern but the informational environment through which regulation is conducted. Regulators increasingly use advanced analytics to process evidence and target supervisory attention, while regulated organizations deploy AI across their operations. This paper develops the concept of the adaptive regulatory state to analyze how changing informational capabilities generate behavioral and institutional adaptation. Comparative cases from financial supervision, competition, tax administration, and electronic communications identify three possible trajectories: constructive learning, governed co‐evolution, and adversarial escalation. Effective oversight does not require technological parity with regulated firms, but sufficient informational, organizational, and verification capabilities to respond as the regulatory environment changes. Four institutional principles follow: functional rather than technological capacity; effective inspectability and proportionate assurance; learning with bounded revisability; and coordinated but accountable capacity. The adaptive regulatory state is defined by whether regulatory institutions remain capable, accountable, and legitimate as their informational environment evolves.

title: Contested Coexistence: Transnational Private Governance and Public Regulatory Reform in Global Value Chains
abstract: ABSTRACT This article examines how a transnational coalition of NGOs, unions, and labor rights organizations drove both private and public regulation on gender‐based violence and harassment in Lesotho's garment sector, and how the resulting regulatory systems coexist despite ongoing tension between them. Drawing on 15 months of ethnographic fieldwork, stakeholder interviews, and archival analysis, we show that the coalition leveraged reputational and diplomatic pressures, enabled by Lesotho's structural dependence on the United States as both buyer and donor, to secure the Lesotho Agreement and subsequent public regulatory reforms. The same dependencies that enabled these reforms also generated sustained tensions once the regulatory systems were in place. We term this dynamic contested coexistence —a governance configuration in which a supplying country's structural dependence on a buyer country forecloses rejection of a private regulatory system while constraining open endorsement of it—and identify it as a new form of private‐public interaction within Cashore et al.'s framework.

title: A Replication of “It is Not Merely About the Content: How Rules Are Communicated Matters to Administrative Burden”
abstract: ABSTRACT This study replicates prior research to examine how rule communication forms shape administrative burden, while also extending their research by investigating how artificial intelligence (AI) services moderate this relationship. AI services are understood to perform two distinct functions: the labeling function, where chatbots output policy rules directly from databases in response to user queries without further processing, and the optimization function, where chatbots collect, analyze, and distill rule information to present users with simplified, prioritized key points. In Study 1, the original research is replicated in the context of natural disaster relief applications in China. The findings demonstrate that bureaucratic language raises learning and compliance costs, stress, and autonomy loss, while complex information structures also increase learning costs, compliance costs, and autonomy loss. These results confirm that rule communication shapes administrative burden across policies, countries, and languages. However, differences emerge compared to the original study, in which bureaucratic language induced stigma and information complexity had no effect on compliance or autonomy loss, potentially due to contextual factors such as the complexity of Chinese logographic writing. Building on this, the extension experiment in Study 2 demonstrates that AI services reduce administrative burden. Notably, and contrary to expectations, the labeling function reduces learning, compliance, and psychological costs, while the optimization function achieves even greater reductions across all dimensions. Collectively, these findings provide empirical evidence supporting the use of AI to improve rule communication and ease administrative burden.

Auditable Automation of Activated Sludge Modeling for Wastewater Treatment Diagnosis Using LLM-Agents
abstract: Abstract Wastewater treatment plants (WWTPs) need mechanistic models that explain carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus transformations under changing operating conditions. Building activated sludge models (ASMs) still depends heavily on expert choices about boundaries, components, and reactions. We developed AutoWWTP-ASM, an auditable large-language-model agent (LLM-Agent) workflow for library-constrained ASM configuration, execution, and calibration. The workflow converts wastewater-process descriptions into structured configurations and combines a predefined ASM library with boundary specification and optional human review. In a coupled carbon−nitrogen−phosphorus task, AutoWWTP-ASM instantiated a model containing 21 state components and 41 biochemical reactions. Across 37 evaluation tasks, the average accuracy scores of ten LLM backbones ranged from 0.596 to 0.627, indicating a narrow range of backbone-level performance within the tested workflow. Ablation experiments evaluated the knowledge, planning, and reflection modules. Comparisons with a single agent, an 8B LLM, and human modelers assessed deployment and efficiency trade-offs. Additional evaluations using six IWA BSM1 scenarios and data from a full-scale WWTP provided further evidence of applicability under standardized and real-data conditions. We provide open-source LangGraph code, together with Codex, Claude Code, and Agent Skill implementations, to support the reproducible development of auditable LLM-Agent workflows for environmental modeling.

title: Redox Transformation of Platinum Mediated by Natural Organic Matter Revealed by X-ray Absorption Spectroscopy
abstract: Abstract Platinum (Pt) is an emerging environmental contaminant due to its increasing anthropogenic use, yet the processes controlling its speciation remain poorly understood. Here, we investigate Pt redox transformations in the presence of natural organic matter (NOM) using X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS). Under anoxic conditions, NOM promotes the progressive reduction of Pt(IV) to Pt(II), with Pt(II) detectable within 24 h and only ∼10% of Pt(IV) remaining after 2 months. In contrast, no reduction occurs under oxic conditions. The resulting Pt(II) is predominantly associated with reduced sulfur functional groups, highlighting the role of thiols in controlling Pt speciation. These results reveal a previously overlooked pathway for Pt transformation mediated by NOM. Such redox processes are likely to control Pt speciation in reducing environments including stratified freshwater water columns, hyporheic sediments, wetlands, and saturated soils. The formation of reduced Pt species may enhance Pt mobility, bioavailability, and potential toxicity, with important consequences for its environmental fate.

Drainage regulation enhanced the spatial heterogeneity of C, N, P, and S cycling genes and their microbial hosts along a cascade damming river
abstract: Understanding how seasonal hydrological regulations by cascade reservoirs affect biogeochemical processes is crucial for sustainable river management. This study used metagenomic sequencing and genome binning to explore the spatial dynamics of carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus, and sulfur (C, N, P, and S) cycling genes and their microbial hosts in a cascade-damming river, along with the associated regulatory mechanisms. The results revealed that multi-element biogeochemical cycling genes displayed significant seasonal variations, with pronounced spatial heterogeneity in the spring drainage period relative to the autumn storage period. Specifically, spring cascade-regulated reaches exhibited elevated gene abundances for carbon fixation and nitrification, alongside diminished potentials for carbon degradation and denitrification compared to natural river reaches, thereby corroborating the gene differentiation. The reduced residual of VPA (0.086 versus 0.742) and the elevated explanatory percentages of RDA (57.6% versus 31.4%) during spring suggested that hydrogeochemical variables explained greater variance in the cycling of C, N, P, and S in spring than in autumn, with hydrological regulations identified as the primary driver by PLS-PM. Spring drainage regulated the spatial heterogeneity of C, N, P, and S cycling through enhancing the longitudinal gradients of physicochemical parameters and nutrients. Conversely, autumn storage weakened longitudinal connectivity and flattened hydrogeochemical gradients. Raup-Crick null-model analysis revealed a higher contribution of stochastic processes in autumn than in spring (31.7% vs. 28.3%; p < 0.05). The metagenome-assembled genome further showed that hydrological regulations promoted the community's shift from the coexistence of diverse lineages during the drainage period to the dominance of a few core taxa during the storage period, reducing host turnover and intensifying functional homogenization in autumn. The findings necessitate season-specific management to mitigate spring eutrophication risks through optimal discharge and nutrient control and to preserve autumn functional complementarity through dynamic impoundment and water-level regulation.

Universal Portfolio Shrinkage
abstract: We introduce a nonlinear covariance shrinkage method for building optimal portfolios. Our universal portfolio shrinkage approximator (UPSA) is built from closed-form basis portfolios, is cheap to implement, and improves on existing shrinkage methods. Rather than uniformly penalizing all principal components of returns or discarding low-variance ones, UPSA instead reweights components to explicitly optimize expected out-of-sample portfolio performance. In empirical applications using a large cross-section of anomaly factors, it delivers robust improvements over alternative shrinkage methods in the literature.

Affordable Housing, Unaffordable Credit? Concentration and High-Cost Lending for Manufactured Homes
abstract: This paper shows that high market concentration in the U.S. manufactured home loan market allows lenders to charge markedly higher interest rates than in the mortgage market for site-built homes. Borrowers in counties with higher lender concentration face significantly higher rates, and evidence from bunching at a regulatory rate threshold, an instrumental variable analysis, and a difference-in-differences analysis suggests a causal link. Integrated lenders, which play an outsized role in this market, charge particularly high rates, and we provide evidence suggesting that these lenders exploit their market power over borrowers. We discuss factors that may explain limited lender entry.

Gendered Effects of the Minimum Wage
abstract: ABSTRACT Women work disproportionately in low‐hours jobs, which pay lower wages and are more exposed to minimum‐wage policies. We estimate an equilibrium search model with worker and firm heterogeneity, jobs differing in wages and hours, and imperfect compliance. Applied to Germany, the 8.50 € minimum wage reallocates women toward higher‐hours jobs and reduces non‐employment, although firm adjustments dampen this effect. Stronger enforcement amplifies the reallocation. Raising the minimum wage up to 14 € reduces gender gaps in wages and hours; at 11 €, changes in hours account for 44.8% of the reduction in the gender income gap.

Using Distribution Regression Difference‐in‐Differences to Evaluate the Effects of a Minimum Wage Introduction on the Distributions of Wages, Earnings, and Working Hours
abstract: ABSTRACT We estimate the causal effects of the introduction of the minimum wage in Germany on the distributions of hourly wages, monthly earnings, and hours worked, combining rich large‐scale data sources. We compare linear and non‐linear versions of distribution regression difference‐in‐differences (DR‐DiD) and also estimate bivariate DR‐DiD. We show that the introduction of the minimum wage in 2015 led to shifts in low hourly wages around the minimum wage threshold including spillover effects up to 50%–70% above. We present evidence for working hours effects in different parts of the hours distribution, though the magnitudes are small. The minimum wage explains a sizeable share of the recent fall in wage and earnings inequality. We show that groups that were later more strongly affected by the minimum wage already experienced higher wage growth before the introduction, leading to an overestimation of minimum wage effects if not accounted for.

title: The last days of LIBOR
Insurance as commitment?
abstract: Abstract Most insurance decisions combine risk management and an intertemporal dimension. Yet while non‐canonical behavioral models have been applied extensively to the risk management aspect, they are mostly missing from the intertemporal component. We expand insurance demand theory by showing that individuals who perceive themselves as present‐biased value insurance as a commitment device to counteract time‐inconsistent behavior. We test our theoretical prediction with an incentive‐compatible experiment. Among all participants, we find a near‐zero average treatment effect on the willingness to pay for the commitment aspect of insurance. When considering only the present‐biased subsample, we find tentative evidence for the theoretical mechanism, but it is not robust across between‐ and within‐subject analyses. Our findings suggest that the commitment function of insurance contracts is not a major driver of insurance demand in our experimental setting, directing future research toward other settings in which it might be more important or toward alternative behavioral mechanisms.

title: I Think You Think I Think: Hierarchical Belief Learning and Endogenous Volatility Dynamics
What drives happiness in 15 European Union countries? The role of income inequality, democracy, and environmental quality
abstract: This study examines happiness as a key dimension of sustainable development by focusing on its socio-economic, political, and environmental correlates. In recent years, it has become increasingly accepted that happiness cannot be explained solely by economic prosperity but is strongly influenced by structural factors such as income distribution, democratic institutions, and environmental conditions. Despite growing interest, empirical studies examining the simultaneous effects of these three fundamental factors on happiness are scarce. This creates a noteworthy gap in the literature. This study aims to fill this gap by empirically examining the effects of income inequality, democracy, and environmental degradation on happiness in 15 European Union countries, including the United Kingdom for comparability, between 2011 and 2022. Per capita income and health expenditure are included as control variables. Methodologically, the study employs MMQR and assesses the robustness of the findings using FGLS, PCSE, and HPJ approaches. The findings suggest that income inequality and environmental degradation are negatively associated with happiness, whereas democracy is positively associated with individuals' happiness. Furthermore, it is found that per capita income and health expenditure are found to be positively related to happiness. The results point to the need for sustainable development goals to be addressed within a holistic framework rather than independently, offering important implications for policymakers.

title: Introduction: five vectors of FinTech disruption
abstract: Financial Technologies (FinTech) such as mobile payments, blockchain and artificial intelligence are transforming financial services by powering faster payments and new forms of money in both developed and developing countries. FinTech is not only disrupting finance, we contend, but also contemporary politics by spurring divergent policy responses to cryptocurrencies, stablecoins and Central Bank Digital Currencies (CBDCs) and extending Big Tech’s societal reach and market power. FinTech is often presented as a catalyst for financial inclusion, but it can be a vehicle for criminality and corruption, and has intersected with the rise of right-wing populism. In this introduction, we identify five vectors of FinTech disruption covering (1) the international monetary order, (2) political authority, (3) security and trust, (4) inclusion, development and growth, and (5) financial governance. FinTech can be a force for good, but, if left unchecked, it has the potential to create a new monetary disorder.

title: Financial bureaucracy featuring innovation bureaucracy – insights from diverging pathways in Estonia and Lithuania
abstract: The paper investigates the integration of innovation-centric characteristics within traditional financial bureaucracies as they confront the rise of the FinTech sector. From the financial governance perspective, FinTech acts as a significant disruptive force, challenging the established operational mandates of state financial institutions and compelling them to reassess their role in the digital economy. The paper explores this dynamic through the theoretical lens of ‘transformative capacity’, which analyses how organisational roles, resources and abilities enable or constrain adaptation to a socio-technical change underpinned by FinTech, focusing on the core tension between fostering innovation and ensuring financial market integrity and stability. Using a comparative case study of Estonia and Lithuania, the research reveals divergent national trajectories. Lithuania displays a change-embracing, ‘innovation-oriented’ bureaucracy (at least initially), characterised by strong leadership, a unified institutional structure and robust coordination and learning mechanisms. In contrast, Estonia exhibits a fragmented, ‘stability-oriented’ bureaucracy marked by resource constraints, weaker coordination and a reactive posture that leverages its e-state capacity more for internal efficiency than sector-wide support. The study concludes that institutional structures, resource allocation and leadership are critical in shaping a financial bureaucracy’s capacity for agile stability, thereby determining the state’s effectiveness in navigating the FinTech landscape.

Timeless: Karl Weick's Enduring Influence on Management Studies
abstract: Abstract The essay by Patriotta and Weick (2026) constitutes one of the last scholarly contributions by Karl Weick. In this Introduction, we position the essay vis‐à‐vis Weick's broader scholarship, and we outline how the ideas articulated in this piece complement theorizing on sensemaking. We also reflect on the more general influence of Weick on scholarship in management studies, including work published in JMS . We develop the argument that Weick's enduring legacy is not only confined to the introduction and articulation of some core and highly influential ideas to the field, but that his distinct ways of thinking, writing, and interpretation of what it means to be a scholar will have an at least equally lasting impact on present and future generations. In particular, in the age of artificial intelligence and the acceleration of academia, we propose that we have much to learn from Weick's mode of scholarship. In this sense, Weick's influence will be timeless and enduring; spanning concepts, the idea of having a distinct voice, and a model of scholarship.

title: Option Value of Auditing: Evidence from Post-Audit Career Advancement
The Power of Data: Assessing Primary Care Performance Using Routinely Collected Emergency Department Data
abstract: This paper develops and validates an approach to assess the impact of individual primary care practices (PCPs) on demand for emergency department (ED) services. Using operational data from two geographically adjacent EDs in England, we focus on attendances for ambulatory care-sensitive (ACS) conditions, which are more appropriately and cost-effectively treated outside the ED. We employ a variance-decomposition approach that controls for observed and unobserved heterogeneity and explicitly accounts for socioeconomic differences. The analysis shows that approximately 52% of the variation in ACS attendance proportions is attributable to systematic differences across PCPs and that these differences are operationally meaningful. Using this methodology, we construct a PCP-level measure of systematic variation in ACS attendances and show that it correlates with patient feedback from National Health Service surveys, Quality and Outcomes Framework scores, and PCP staffing decisions. This measure outperforms existing metrics based on ACS admissions in identifying PCP-level variation and is robust to alternative modeling choices. The modular nature of the approach allows it to be applied to data from one or multiple hospitals, providing policymakers with a practical tool to evaluate PCP-level interventions and their downstream effects on ED demand. This paper was accepted by Carri Chan, healthcare management. Funding: The authors acknowledge financial support from the London Business School Research and Materials Development Fund and from the Erasmus School of Health Policy & Management Career Development Research Fund. Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2023.03234 .

title: The Asymmetric Nature of Social Hierarchies: Unpacking the Dynamic Relationship Between Power and Status
abstract: Scholars and practitioners alike have long presumed that power and status, two foundational bases of social hierarchy, share a symmetric, mutually reinforcing relationship. However, support for this presumption has largely taken the form of theoretical accounts due to the prevalence of static research designs and a dearth of dynamic methodology in organizational research. Drawing on the Dual Perspective Model, we propose that one’s status is more likely to drive changes in one’s power than vice versa because status has a stronger connection to communion—an important component of interpersonal evaluations—than does power, and communality is an important predictor of both power and status. Using data from two studies involving project teams and a contemporary methodology from developmental psychology for modeling dynamic relationships (bivariate dual change score models), we illustrate that there is indeed a mutually reinforcing relationship between power and status over time, but this relationship is asymmetric. In three additional experiments, we find that perceptions of communality explain this asymmetry. We also find similar effects whether power is formal—attached to a position or role—or involves control over informal resources. Across all studies, we find that the path from status to changes in power is stronger than the path from power to changes in status.

title: Financing the Twin Transition: How Patent Pledges Leverage Intangible Assets for Digital–Green Synergistic Transformation
abstract: ABSTRACT Against the backdrop of aligning digital expansion with green growth objectives, exploring effective financial support pathways for firms' digital–green synergistic transformation (DGST) holds significant theoretical and practical value. This study examines the impact, mechanisms, and heterogeneity of patent pledge financing on firms' DGST, using data from Chinese A‐share listed companies between 2010 and 2022. The results show: First, patent pledges significantly promote DGST, and this finding remains robust after robustness checks and endogeneity treatments. Second, mechanism analysis confirms that alleviating financing constraints and optimizing innovation structure are the key channels through which patent pledges drive DGST; by addressing funding bottlenecks and improving the allocation of innovation resources, they provide dual support for integrated digital–green development. In addition, patent pledges enhance managerial incentives, further promoting DGST. Third, we uncover significant regional and corporate divergence in how patent pledges drive DGST. The impact intensifies for high‐tech entities and those with robust banking ties and large‐scale firms, whereas regional factors such as heightened green commitment and digital maturity further amplify these benefits. Fourth, debt default risk weakens the positive effect of patent pledges on DGST. Moreover, both digital patent pledges and green patent pledges significantly promote DGST, whereas only invention patent pledges exhibit a significant transformation effect, highlighting the importance of patent quality and financing capacity. This study enriches the literature on intellectual property finance and DGST, offering empirical evidence and policy implications for improving patent pledge financing systems and promoting high‐quality corporate transformation.

title: Financial Market Effectiveness of Sustainability Initiatives in Green Bond Markets: Evidence Synthesis and Research Framework
abstract: ABSTRACT This research synthesizes prior evidence on the effectiveness of financial market sustainability initiatives (FMSIs) in green bond markets. Our analysis of 45 peer‐reviewed studies, including 42 quantitative empirical studies with 169 codable FMSI–outcome relationships, shows that FMSIs are most consistently associated with favorable financial market outcomes when they improve credibility, comparability, or interpretability of green bond information. Pricing evidence differs between primary and secondary markets. Across both segments, greenness assurance provides the broadest pricing evidence base, whereas regulation and policy show the most favorable evidence balance on a narrower base. Outside pricing, evidence remains limited for issuer behavior, relative green allocation, and environmental attribution. We propose a life cycle–based research framework linking information and agency problems to five stages of the green bond process and identify future research directions concerning FMSI interactions, institutional conditions, and participation costs. Our findings provide design implications for issuers, investors, regulators, and information intermediaries.

title: Microfoundations of Dynamic Capabilities for Eco‐Innovation in SMEs: Evidence From Industrial Case Studies
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines the microfoundations, that is, skills, processes, structures and decision rules that underlie the dynamic capabilities enabling SMEs to achieve sustained eco‐innovation performance. Building on dynamic capabilities framework, we adapt it to the SME context to explain how firms sense opportunities and threats, seize them and maintain competitiveness by reconfiguring tangible and intangible assets. Using an inductive and abductive design grounded in five in‐depth case studies of industrial SMEs in water technology, urban manufacturing and technical apparel in the Basque Country, we develop a framework capturing how eco‐innovation emerges from organisational innovation. The analysis reveals how dynamic capabilities are anchored in the orchestration of microfoundations across multiple organisational dimensions, including leadership, strategic intent, people management, business practices and external relations. By extending Teece's model to the SME context, we offer contextualised, transferable insights for companies operating under similar conditions, along with practical pathways to strengthen their eco‐innovation capacity. The framework also informs policymakers designing targeted support measures for industrial SMEs operating in comparable regional ecosystems, encouraging more adaptive, collaborative and scalable sustainability transitions.

title: From Farm to Global Markets: Enhancing Rural Livelihoods Through Sustainable Superfood Supply Chains
abstract: ABSTRACT This research examines the cultivation and distribution business strategies of rural superfoods aimed at sustainable development. Superfoods have the potential to sustainably improve rural livelihoods, promote healthy consumption and enable integration into global markets as health consciousness rises. Accordingly, the study has explored the Sustainable Business Development Factors (SBDFs) that could contribute to the attainment of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) including poverty alleviation (SDG 1), health awareness and sustainable wellness (SDG 3), business modernization and structural development (SDG 9), sustainable harvesting and dietary habits (SDG 12) and collaboration for collective success (SDG 17). The research uses Fuzzy Analytical Hierarchy Process (FAHP), Pareto analysis, and Fuzzy DEMATEL to identify, rank and analyse causal relationships among the SBDFs. Analysis shows that social motivation, sustainability‐driven behaviours and government support lead to success. The prominent causal SBDFs identified were local and regional food systems, rural development and infrastructure, information governance and digital infrastructure and institutional support and capacity building. They influence social responsibility and ethical standards, supply chain transparency and traceability, sustainable packaging and transportation, health and safety standards and carbon footprint reduction. This analysis enables superfoods to integrate environmental, social and governance (ESG) sustainability, providing smallholders with actionable knowledge to develop sustainable, digitally enabled business models.

title: What Should Scholars Study About Family Offices? A Practitioner-Informed Research Agenda
abstract: This study engages directly with family office professionals to develop a practitioner-informed research agenda. Using an exploratory sequential mixed-methods design, we conduct 27 semi-structured interviews followed by a survey of 331 respondents. Practitioners identify that the most important areas to research are the benefits of strong governance, how succession planning should be implemented within the family office, and how to engage the next generation. Building on these insights, we develop a research agenda across three primary dimensions and identify nine gaps to inspire future research, offering both theoretical directions for scholars while maintaining practical relevance for family office professionals.

title: A hybrid machine learning framework for supplier risk prediction and segmentation: an automotive supply chain case study
abstract: Purpose This study aims to develop a hybrid data-driven framework for supplier risk assessment in automotive supply chains. It seeks to integrate predictive modeling with clustering techniques to proactively identify and categorize supplier risks, enabling enhanced operational stability and resilience. The research focuses on creating a decision-support tool that combines expert-validated risk indicators with advanced machine learning (ML) methods to address gaps in traditional risk management approaches. Design/methodology/approach A systematic methodology was used, combining Delphi-based expert validation (28 indicators from 36 initial factors) with ML. Data from 500 suppliers were preprocessed (K‑nearest neighbor (KNN) outlier removal, MinMax scaling), and feature selection was performed using PCA/LASSO/Ridge. Six regression models were optimized (Grid Search and Optuna), with support vector regression (SVR) showing best performance. Agglomerative clustering segmented suppliers based on risk profiles. Findings Support vector regression achieved superior predictive accuracy among tested models. Clustering revealed a significant future shift toward higher-risk supplier segments, with low-risk suppliers decreasing notably. The study confirms that increasing budget allocation does not automatically reduce risk or enhance resilience. Expert-validated indicators proved crucial for accurate risk assessment, while the hybrid framework effectively segments suppliers for targeted risk mitigation strategies. Originality/value This research contributes a novel hybrid framework integrating prediction and clustering for supplier risk management. It introduces expert-validated indicators through Delphi methodology and demonstrates their critical role in risk modeling. The study provides automotive manufacturers with a practical decision-support tool for proactive risk mitigation and resource allocation, bridging the gap between theoretical risk models and practical supply chain challenges.
journal_name: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal

title: The enabling and constraining effects of workplace accommodations on the careers of people with disabilities
abstract: This study uncovers a paradox in the use of workplace accommodations by exploring their unintended consequences on the career advancement decisions of people with disabilities. Drawing on 30 interviews with German employees across a range of disabilities, we examine how accommodations – typically intended to foster person-job fit and inclusion – can simultaneously constrain career advancement. Our findings reveal that when accommodations lead to a strong sense of fit but are perceived as non-transferable, they may foster dependency, reduce external mobility, and limit career advancement aspirations. By problematizing the dominant narrative of accommodations as purely empowering, we offer a critical reframing: accommodations can facilitate inclusion in the short term while quietly narrowing long-term career advancement. We call on practitioners to recognize and mitigate this tension by reassessing accommodations over time, encouraging open dialogue about career goals, and ensuring that support systems extend beyond initial placement to enable both stability and progression.
journal_name: The International Journal of Human Resource Management

title: Inheriting from Bankrupt Firms? Evidence on Long-term Performance of Local Firms
Geopolitical Risk and Firms’ Eco-Innovation: International Evidence
Earliest-announcer audits, information spillovers, and audit quality
Managing through polycrises: Integrating geopolitics and climate change into global strategy
abstract: The climate crisis and geopolitical instability both affect firms' global strategies, but research has typically studied these risks separately. Further, scholars have generally situated climate and geopolitical risks as exogenous forces with which firms must contend. We argue this approach is now inadequate because these two forces not only coexist in parallel but also interact, creating compounding effects that increase asset vulnerability and disrupt multinationals' operations in unpredictable ways. We also propose that, in addition to being affected by these forces, firms have direct and unambiguous influences on them. In this theoretical paper, we explain the bidirectional interactions between environmental and geopolitical risks, and their effects on firms' global strategies and how firms, in turn, influence those global challenges. We advance a more integrative view of firms' strategy by explaining how the combination of these two risks leads firms to select between extractive environmental capabilities (abilities that enable firms to maximize cost efficiency by externalizing environmental costs) and regenerative environmental capabilities (abilities that enable firms to go beyond mitigating environmental damage and actively restore and renew the natural systems they inhabit). We finally call for future research to move beyond single-risk and static frameworks to those that examine how interdependent global disruptions jointly reconfigure firm behavior, performance, and governance over time.

title: Disclosure Complexity and Tax Enforcement Outcomes
journal_name: The Journal of the American Taxation Association

title: Capturing the system-level effects of innovation policy: An assessment of publicly funded innovative entrepreneurship in Sweden
abstract: A new generation of innovation policies has placed renewed attention on understanding the innovation processes taking place on and affecting the system level. On one hand, there is a growing demand for policy instruments addressing the need for system change. On the other hand, there is still a lack of understanding of how innovation policy instruments contribute to a system-level impact. We address this gap by taking a programme perspective and proposing an analytical framework for assessing three types of effects: first-order, second-order, and system-level. Our approach is inspired by the functions of technological innovation system literature (TIS). We apply the analytical framework to the analysis of an innovative entrepreneurship instrument, the Swedish Innovation Agency VINNOVA’s Innovative SME programme. We find that the public support programmes contributed significantly to SMEs’ ability to influence system functions. Based on the findings, we argue that the analysis of innovation policy programmes should move beyond a narrow assessment of direct effects and consider more the second-order and system-level effects.

title: Onboarding and Agency: Responding to Episodic Loneliness in Immersive Services
abstract: ABSTRACT Loneliness is a growing concern in long‐duration immersive services, where consumers not only transition into the service but also experience multiple identity transitions and life events while in the service. We argue that loneliness in these settings emerges not only as a chronic experience from a lack of social opportunities, but also episodically from difficulty navigating social landscapes after a life change. Drawing on consumer agency as a differentiating factor between aloneness and loneliness, we reconceptualize onboarding as a dynamic, multi‐actor process through which providers and co‐consumers restore agency and address loneliness throughout the service experience. Using qualitative evidence from retirement villages and residential aged care, we examine the onboarding structures supporting agency within these later‐life immersive services. Onboarding unfolds in three phases, the third of which returns as a cycle: pre‐service experience, initial transition, and cycles of integration and transition. These phases involve distinct social support types (action‐facilitating and nurturant) delivered by individual, vertical (organizational), and horizontal (co‐consumer) actors. Crucially, changes in consumer context create a need for re‐onboarding to foster agency and mitigate loneliness. Comparing the two service settings reveals onboarding stages require different actors, sequencing, and intensity depending on entry conditions. We contribute a dynamic, agency‐centered conceptualization of onboarding and provide guidance for resource allocation to mitigate loneliness risk.

title: Which AI? A Comparative Evaluation of Generative AI and Neuro‐Symbolic AI for Silicon Sampling
abstract: ABSTRACT This study examines how the choice of AI model and its architecture influences distributional fidelity in silicon sampling. Silicon samples, AI‐generated synthetic respondents used to simulate human survey responses, are increasingly proposed as substitutes for traditional market research participants, yet evidence regarding their accuracy remains mixed. Across four studies, we benchmark two AI models with distinct architectures, generative AI (GenAI) and neuro‐symbolic AI (NSAI), against human data. Our findings show that the evaluated GenAI models introduce systematic distributional distortions, including demographic bias, compressed variability, and divergence from human response patterns, even when enriched with statistical data. In contrast, the evaluated NSAI system demonstrates substantially closer correspondence with human benchmarks across the examined tasks. The findings suggest that distributional fidelity in silicon sampling is not architecture‐neutral: it depends in part on the alignment between AI architecture and the statistical demands of respondent‐level simulation. Rather than asking whether AI can replace human respondents in general, the study argues that the accuracy of silicon samples depends on which AI models are used, for which research tasks, and under what validation conditions.

title: Closing the Gap, Carrying the Burden: How Gender and Prosocial Motivation Shape Workplace Recognition
abstract: ABSTRACT Despite progress toward gender equity, women remain disadvantaged in gaining workplace recognition. We theorize that prosocial motivation helps women achieve parity in workplace recognition by providing a role‐congruent path to becoming valued advice sources. Drawing on social role theory and role congruity theory, we propose that women are less likely than men to occupy central positions in advice networks, but that high prosocial motivation closes this gap. Advice centrality, in turn, functions as a peer‐conferred signal of workplace recognition that supports leadership emergence and performance ratings. Across a time‐lagged, multi‐source field study and two online experiments, we find support for this model. Study 1 ( n = 275) shows that women occupy less central positions in advice networks than men, but that high prosocial motivation closes this gap. Advice network centrality further mediates the interactive effects of gender and prosocial motivation on leadership emergence and performance ratings. Two online experiments (Study 2a, n = 247; Study 2b, n = 248) provide converging causal evidence for these effects. These findings show that prosocial motivation helps women achieve parity with men in workplace recognition, while raising the possibility that such parity may rest on demands that fall asymmetrically on women.

title: Governing Fairness in Insurance Pricing: The Trilemma of Actuarial Adequacy, Solidarity, and Causal Legitimacy
Skills, Not Just Will: Experimental Evidence From Uganda on Transparency in Public Procurement
abstract: ABSTRACT Governments are usually the largest purchasers of goods and services, creating significant opportunities for corruption. We study whether offering training and technical assistance to procurement officials in 50 Ugandan districts prompted them to publish procurement actions on an online public portal, as legally required. Among districts that received the training and technical assistance program, we randomized whether procurement officials received information in advance about their eligibility to earn a public award for adherence to these transparency standards. We use national administrative data across multiple financial years and 134 district governments to evaluate impacts. The training and technical assistance program increased the number and value of procurement actions uploaded several‐fold, while award eligibility did not have similarly large effects. These results suggest that motivation problems may be overemphasized in the fight against corruption. Building capacity in accounting and transparency could provide effective guardrails against corruption.

title: Role strain and job crafting in China’s digitalizing street-level bureaucracy
Guidance over guidelines? Unpacking the uses and concerns of generative AI in communication science
Afterword: the waning power of the fix
abstract: This commentary offers some reflections on the ‘power of the fix' in cybersecurity and its wider implications for technological democracy. I begin with a discussion of the discrepancy between the discourse of solutionism and everyday practices of securing IT systems (Elgaard Jensen et al, 2026). Whereas the former posits that problems are neat and can be solved by means of technology, the latter must confront what Röhle (2021) has called the ‘permanent brokenness' of computational infrastructures. A peculiar form of ‘infrastructural reversal' can then be observed in the field of cybersecurity: here, disruption, breakdown and failure are not the exception, but the default (Collier et al, 2025; Fouad, 2025). This has implications for the role of public disclosure of technological vulnerabilities in the governance of digital systems (Bozzini, 2025). The endemic nature of disruption in computational infrastructures puts at risk the transformative capacities of publicity in technological politics. This also affects social studies of technology insofar as this field has long relied on disruption, failure and breakdown as empirical occasions for making visible how technology works and does not work in practice.

title: Digital responsibility, skills and environmental awareness for digital sustainability
abstract: This study investigates how digital competencies and environmental awareness interact to shape eco-friendly digital practices, contributing to the field of digital sustainability. Drawing on a representative sample of adult internet users in the United Arab Emirates (N = 1016), it explores (H1) whether individual responsibility predicts environmentally conscious digital practices; (H2) whether environmental awareness moderates the effect of perceived digital competence on behavior; and (H3) whether sustainable digital behaviors are associated with perceived digital competence, with awareness as a moderator. Using linear and moderated regression analyses, the findings confirm that individual responsibility is a significant predictor of pro-environmental digital behavior, and that perceived digital competence is positively associated with such behavior, an association that is modestly strengthened, rather than enabled, by environmental awareness. The reverse association, from behavior to perceived digital competence, is not moderated by awareness, pointing to an asymmetrical pattern that the cross-sectional design does not allow us to interpret causally. By integrating digital inequality frameworks with environmental psychology, this study advances the understanding of digital sustainability as a site where perceived competence and responsibility jointly shape sustainable digital engagement.

title: Beyond poverty and education: measuring structural racism in neighborhoods to understand racialized birth outcome disparities
abstract: Neighborhood context is a root cause of poor health and racial health disparities, including disparities in adverse birth outcomes. In a recent article, XXXX et al. leveraged a multi-generationally linked dataset of South Carolina birth certificates to construct life course trajectories of census tract-level neighborhood affluence and disadvantage (Am J Epidemiol 2025;XXX(XX):XXX-XXX). This innovative study contributes to the literature on neighborhood context and perinatal health by highlighting the relevance of a life course approach, interrogating the role of neighborhood affluence and disadvantage on racial disparities, and extending this research to the U.S. South. In this commentary, we reiterate and expand on these points. First, we argue for the importance of explicitly integrating life course theory into neighborhoods and reproductive health research and assessing neighborhood context at several time points. Second, we encourage future studies to develop exposure measures that have a clear point of intervention and address the complex process of structural racism, rather than focusing on neighborhood composition. Finally, we emphasize the importance of considering the life course of neighborhoods themselves. Future research should interrogate historical and contemporary practices of neighborhood-level marginalization to create clear calls to action on how we can intervene to improve perinatal outcomes.

title: Residential Segregation and Fecundability in the Black Women’s Health Study
abstract: Residential segregation can influence reproductive outcomes, yet few studies have investigated its effects on fertility. We used data from the Black Women's Health Study, a U.S. prospective cohort study, to estimate the effect of racialized economic segregation on fecundability, the per-cycle probability of conception. Participants enrolled in 1995 and completed biennial follow-up questionnaires. A supplemental module in 2011 asked participants to report, for each birth, whether the pregnancy was planned and the number of months to conceive. Participants also reported any attempts to conceive for ≥ 12 months without success. We operationalized racialized economic segregation using the census tract level Index of Concentration at the Extremes (ICErace + income). We fit proportional probabilities regression models with generalized estimating equations to estimate fecundability ratios (FRs) and 95% CIs, adjusting for age, calendar year, geographic region, early life socioeconomic position, and educational attainment. The analysis included 2857 planned pregnancy attempts from 2183 participants (mean age = 34 years). Relative to participants living in the most privileged group, FRs for participants in the most marginalized, mixed (marginalized) and mixed (privileged) groups were 0.88 (95% CI, 0.74, 1.04), 0.89 (95% CI, 0.78, 1.02), and 0.91 (95% CI, 0.80, 1.04), respectively. Associations were stronger among college-educated and nulliparous participants.

title: Refining Allostatic Load Measurement: Mortality Associations of an Empirically Derived Three-Component Score in the Women’s Health Initiative
abstract: Allostatic load (AL) is a multisystem index of physiological dysregulation due to chronic stress. Although widely applied, its operationalization remains inconsistent, limiting reproducibility and equity. Streamlined indices based on common biomarkers may enhance feasibility across settings. Using data from 150 293 postmenopausal women in the Women's Health Initiative, we evaluated the construct validity of a streamlined, multisystem AL index. Biomarkers across cardiovascular, metabolic, and immune domains were screened for stable associations with mortality. The final three-component AL index included systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, and white blood cell count. Cox proportional hazards models estimated associations with all-cause, cardiovascular, and immune/inflammatory mortality, adjusting for demographic and clinical covariates. Higher AL scores were strongly associated with mortality. Hazard ratios for all-cause mortality were 1.34 (95% CI, 1.30-1.38), 1.74 (1.68-1.80), and 2.27 (2.15-2.39) for scores of 1, 2, and 3 versus 0 (Ptrend < 0.001), with similar patterns observed for cardiovascular and immune/inflammatory mortality. A streamlined, multisystem AL index comprised of systolic blood pressure, waist circumference, and white blood cell count demonstrated robust associations with mortality outcomes, supporting the feasibility of such an operationalization of AL, which may enhance reproducibility and extend the applicability of AL indices in large-scale and resource-limited contexts.

title: Comparing causal estimands from sequential nested versus single point target trials: a simulation study
HMI warning strategy based on radar-video fusion perception for freeway merging areas: A risk field approach considering beyond-visual-range event
abstract: Under beyond-visual-range conditions where the driver’s sight is obstructed for the freeway merging area, the merging vehicle may seriously affect the mainline driver’s safe passage. This study aims to evaluate the mitigation effect of radar-video fusion-based human–machine interface (rHMI) warnings on the interaction risk imposed on a mainline vehicle by a merging vehicle, addressing the risk warning under beyond-visual-range conditions. Three rHMI warning schemes were developed and tested through driving simulation. They are no radar-video fusion perception without rHMI warning (Baseline), partial coverage of radar-video fusion perception with one-level rHMI warning (Warning I), and full coverage of radar-video fusion perception with two-level rHMI warning (Warning II). The study constructed the kinetic energy field incorporating speed difference (KEF-SD). A convolution operation was used to extract the field strength’s time-varying characteristics. The KEF-SD was compared with surrogate safety measures (SSMs) to demonstrate its performance. Results indicate: (1) rHMI warnings help mainline drivers to effectively reduce speed. The progressive intervention of two-level warning induces earlier speed adjustment; (2) The KEF-SD is reliable and valid. It can more accurately and finely explain the vehicle interaction process under beyond-visual-range conditions; (3) Compared to Baseline, Warning I and Warning II achieve maximum field strength reductions of 56.33 % and 89.38 %. Under the progressive intervention of two-level warning, the interaction risk mitigation is significant; (4) The provision and earlier supplementation of rHMI warnings stabilize field strength and reduce instantaneous risk mutations to zero. rHMI warnings may alleviate drivers’ workload, and the two-level warning performs best; (5) It is recommended to prioritize full detection coverage of the merging area to maximize risk mitigation through staged rHMI warning for beyond-visual-range merging events. Results provide preliminary evidence for application of risk detection and warning in specific scenarios, enhancing safety in merging areas.

title: Congolese BaYaka children's learning and exploring in a village context
abstract: Childhood is a key period for acquiring and transmitting cultural knowledge and skill. Hunter-gatherer children, such as the Congolese BaYaka, learn autonomously through exploration, play, and participation in foraging and domestic activities. Most previous work has focused on how BaYaka allocate time to learning activities while living in forest camps. By focusing on a village context, we aim to further investigate BaYaka learning ecologies by examining (1) how children sample their social and physical environments, (2) whom they spend time with, and (3) how they allocate their time to play, work-themed play, and work. We do so by analysing video observations of 57 children aged between 7 and 16 years old. BaYaka children spent 75% of their time in the village, where they had extensive opportunities to sample their social surroundings. They spent most of their time alone or in child-only groups, rather than with adults, highlighting the potential for horizontal transmission and individual learning as prominent pathways to knowledge acquisition. Finally, children spent a third of their time in play activities and another third in foraging and domestic tasks, suggesting that play and work are complementary flexible learning mechanisms. These results illustrate how embodied capital is co-constructed by children and their environments, with children actively investing time and effort in activities that are both developmentally rewarding and contextually relevant, thereby shaping the repertoire of skills and knowledge they carry into adulthood.

title: Secret or superpower? A narrative reflection on navigating dual identities as cancer survivors and cancer scientists
abstract: Abstract Purpose International research policy increasingly recognises lived experience as a form of expertise, encouraging meaningful involvement of lived experience expertise in research. However, such guidance often assumes a binary distinction between researchers and those with lived experience, offering little direction for individuals who embody both identities. This commentary examines the tensions, opportunities, and ethical considerations faced by adolescent and young adult (AYA) cancer survivors who also work as psycho-oncology researchers. Methods Drawing on our positionality as survivor-scientists, we reflect on how disclosure of lived experience is shaped by academic culture, career stage, mentorship, and evolving norms regarding experiential expertise. Results Our narratives illustrate divergent pathways: one characterised by caution, driven by concerns about credibility and perceived bias, another enabled by mentorship that explicitly valued lived experience as an asset to rigorous research. Situating these reflections within existing literature on identity negotiation among AYA cancer survivors, we extend this work by examining how these challenges are intensified within academic and healthcare settings. Conclusions We call for a shift from binary thinking about research and lived experience expertise, toward a continuum of expertise. Clear guidance and cultural change are needed to enable the lived experience expertise of academic cancer researchers to enhance the inclusivity, relevance, and quality of cancer research. Implications for Cancer Survivors This commentary highlights that lived experience of cancer should not undermine the credibility of academic cancer researchers. Rather, increased guidance and culture change can open pathways through which survivor-scientists can contribute their expertise safely and authentically.

title: Together and Apart: Dual Attachment Bonds to Cohabiting and Separated Partners Predict Relationship and Psychological Outcomes During COVID-19 Lockdowns
Reframing Self-Objectified Women’s Loneliness Experience: The Mediating Roles of Intrasexual Competition and Romantic Interpretation Bias
abstract: Abstract Despite the fact that women’s self-objectification is a psychological process embedded within interpersonal interactions, few studies have investigated the interpersonal consequences of self-objectification. Even though some studies linked women’s self-objectification with loneliness, an experience commonly occurring in interpersonal contexts, they produced inconsistent results regarding the association and still explained it from an intrapersonal perspective. Through the lens of interpersonal dynamics, this research attempted to reframe the relationship between self-objectification and loneliness. Specifically, two studies using distinct methods were conducted to investigate whether stronger intrasexual competition tendency when interacting with women and stronger romantic interpretation bias (RIB) when interacting with men, respectively, could explain how self-objectification among women affects loneliness. Study 1, a seven-day diary study, found that female university students experiencing strong self-objectifying feelings on a given day were more likely to engage in intrasexual competition, resulting in increased loneliness that day, even after controlling for their trait self-objectification, self-perceived attractiveness, social desirability, and demographic factors, such as relationship status. Similarly, Study 2, an experiment, revealed that women primed with high self-objectification exhibited stronger intrasexual competition tendencies and heightened feelings of loneliness, even after controlling for self-perceived attractiveness, social desirability, relationship satisfaction, and demographic factors such as relationship status. Although the promoting effect of women’s self-objectification on RIB was detected in both studies, RIB could not in turn predict reduced loneliness. Our study contributes to the literature on self-objectification by exploring its interpersonal consequences and provides directions for interventions aimed at reducing women’s loneliness.

title: A Legal Theory of State-Owned Enterprises: The China Experience James Si Zeng. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 2026. 278 pp. $140.00 (hbk). ISBN 9781009457682
Announcing the 2024 and 2025 best article awards
Exploring the role of renewable energy communities in the Italian flexibility markets
abstract: The increasing penetration of distributed generation, mainly from variable and scarcely predictable renewable energy sources, requires new forms of system flexibility. Renewable Energy Communities (RECs) can contribute by aggregating demand-side flexibility and participating in ancillary service markets. This paper analyses the participation of an Italian REC in the Ancillary Services Market, focusing on load flexibility and its interaction with the shared energy incentive scheme. Using real consumption and generation data, multiple flexibility scenarios are simulated and evaluated in terms of balancing revenues, shared energy, and overall community cash flows. Results show that flexibility provision is economically attractive even at moderate levels, while the impact on shared energy remains limited and, in some cases, positive. The study confirms the potential of RECs as effective flexibility providers in decentralised electricity systems.

title: Non-uniform degradation mechanisms of PEMFCs under dynamic load conditions of high temperature and low humidity
abstract: Proton exchange membrane fuel cells (PEMFCs) face durability challenges under dynamic load and high-temperature, low-humidity (HTLH) conditions. While in-plane non-uniform degradation in large-area fuel cells (LAFCs) is acknowledged, the spatiotemporal degradation patterns remain not fully understood. This study investigates a 291 cm 2 PEMFC during a 200-h HTLH dynamic load cycling test. Utilizing periodic electrochemical diagnostics and microstructural characterizations, it is revealed that performance degradation is a non-linear, spatially-dependent process. The cell operates under a continuous slow degradation state (e.g., 0–120 h and 180–200 h), primarily governed by the cathode inlet and anode inlet/outlet regions. In these areas, progressive mechanical defects and severe ionomer redistribution significantly elevate concentration polarization. Concurrently, the cell faces a risk of sudden rapid degradation (manifesting as loading failure). It is strongly associated with abrupt mechanical damage (cracking and delamination) specifically at the cathode outlet region, once accumulated humidity cycling stresses reach a critical threshold. To mitigate this risk, an in-situ recovery strategy based on high-current operation is proposed. The water produced under high-current conditions promotes ionomer hydration and swelling. This process partially fills mechanical defects and helps the cell return to the baseline slow-degradation state. Furthermore, ECSA loss is attributed to coupled catalyst layer degradation, involving Pt oxidation/dissolution-related processes, limited Pt coarsening, ionomer redistribution, and reduced electrochemical accessibility of Pt sites. This study highlights that spatial degradation severity is governed by sealing constraints and the local water state, providing a theoretical foundation for optimizing heavy-duty LAFCs under HTLH operating conditions.

title: Wind resource assessment in complex terrain using the spatio-temporal downscaling coupling of WRF-steady RANS simulation
abstract: The meso -micro coupled numerical simulation method has been gradually adopted for high-resolution wind resource assessment. However, the accuracy of downscaling from mesoscale to microscale in complex mountainous terrain remains a huge challenge. In this study, a numerical simulation method of wind field based on meso-micro coupling suitable for wind resource assessment in complex terrain was proposed to improve the accuracy of downscaling.
